q: There was an English physician. Clinical syndrome sharing features of Parkinson's disease. Which word grew out of it?
f: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817 and noted he had studied some of his cases only by watching them in the street. His name was attached decades later by a French neurologist who thought he deserved it.

q: There was a German neurologist. First described progressive dementia in 1906. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Alois Alzheimer's first case was a woman named Auguste Deter, who told him: I have lost myself. He kept her file, and when he examined her brain after death he found the plaques and tangles that still define the disease.

q: There was an English physician. Identified a unique lymphatic cancer. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Thomas Hodgkin described seven cases in 1832 and nobody noticed for thirty years. Another doctor read the paper later, confirmed it, and insisted the disease carry Hodgkin's name — a rare act of credit in medical history.

q: There was an English physician. Lymphomas other than Hodgkin's disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An entire family of cancers defined by what they are not. Once Hodgkin's type could be identified under a microscope, every other lymphoma had to be grouped somewhere — and got a name built out of a negative.

q: There was an American physician. Chronic inflammatory bowel disease described in 1932. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Burrill Crohn published with two colleagues in 1932, and the paper listed authors alphabetically. Crohn came first. His two co-authors, Ginzburg and Oppenheimer, did the same work and are remembered by almost nobody.

q: There was an American neurosurgeon. Described symptoms of excess cortisol. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Harvey Cushing essentially invented brain surgery as a survivable procedure, cutting mortality from around 90 per cent to under 10. The hormone disorder named after him is a footnote in a career mostly spent elsewhere.

q: "Down Syndrome" is named after a place.
f: John Langdon Down wrote the first careful clinical description in 1866. His original name for it was withdrawn in the 1960s as both inaccurate and offensive, and the condition was renamed for the doctor instead.

q: There was an American physician. Described inherited neurodegenerative disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: George Huntington described the disease at twenty-two, in the only medical paper he ever published. He had seen it in families on Long Island, where his father and grandfather had also practised — three generations of doctors watching the same households.

q: There was an Irish physician. Autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Robert Graves was an Irish physician who also introduced the radical idea that feverish patients should be given food and water rather than starved. He suggested his epitaph should read: he fed fevers.

q: There was a Japanese physician. Autoimmune thyroiditis first described in 1912. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hakaru Hashimoto published his findings in German in 1912, as a young doctor, and then returned to rural Japan to run a country practice. His work was overlooked for twenty years before anyone realised what he had found.

q: There was an English physician. Adrenal insufficiency described in 1855. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Thomas Addison worked out that the small glands sitting on top of the kidneys were essential to life — before anyone knew what hormones were. Colleagues found him difficult; patients found him extraordinary.

q: There was an English physician. Early term for kidney disease. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Richard Bright discovered he could detect kidney disease by heating a patient's urine over a candle and watching for a cloud of albumin. It was one of the first bedside chemical tests in medicine.

q: There was an English surgeon. Bone remodeling disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: James Paget has two different diseases named after him, plus a professorship and a hospital ward. He also worked out, as a student, that the tiny specks in bad pork were a parasite — a finding his professors ignored.

q: "Ménière Disease" is named after a person.
f: Prosper Meniere showed that vertigo could come from the inner ear rather than the brain, which overturned the standard view. He published it in 1861 and died the following year, before the profession accepted it.

q: There was a british neurologist. Copper metabolism disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Kinnier Wilson described a disease in which copper builds up in the body until it damages the liver and brain. It is one of the few inherited neurological disorders that can be treated — if it is caught in time.

q: Which name or term meaning "facial paralysis" comes from a Scottish surgeon?
f: Charles Bell mapped which nerves carry movement and which carry sensation, work so foundational that a whole law of neurology carries his name too. The sudden facial paralysis is what most people know him for.

q: There was an English physician. Clinical sign named after him. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Thomas Hodgkin's name attaches to a lymphoma, a clinical sign, and a form of anaemia. He was also a Quaker campaigner who lost a hospital post partly for his outspoken views on the treatment of indigenous peoples.

q: There was a French neurologist. Reflex indicating upper motor neuron lesion. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Stroke the sole of an adult's foot and the toes curl down. If they fan upward instead, something is wrong with the pathway from the brain. Babinski found a whole diagnosis hiding in one reflex.

q: There was a German neurologist. Test for proprioception and balance. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Stand with your feet together and close your eyes. If you sway, you were relying on sight to stay upright rather than on your body's own position sense. Romberg turned that into a test in the 1840s.

q: There was a Polish physician. Sign of meningeal irritation. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Jozef Brudzinski found that lifting the head of a patient with meningitis makes the knees pull up involuntarily — the body protecting inflamed membranes. He described several such signs; this is the one that kept his name.

q: "Kernig Sign" is named after a place.
f: Vladimir Kernig noticed that patients with meningitis could not have their leg straightened once the hip was bent. Paired with Brudzinski's sign, it gave doctors a bedside test decades before spinal taps were routine.

q: There was an American surgeon. Pain on inspiration suggesting gallbladder inflammation. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Press under the ribs on the right and ask the patient to breathe in. If they stop short from the pain, the gallbladder is inflamed. John Murphy was a Chicago surgeon known for tests that needed no equipment at all.

q: There was an American surgeon. Point of tenderness in appendicitis. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Charles McBurney worked out that appendicitis pain settles at one specific spot, about two-thirds of the way from the navel to the hip bone. Surgeons still press exactly there, and still call it McBurney's point.

q: There was an American anesthesiologist. Rapid assessment of newborn health. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Virginia Apgar sketched five checks on a scrap of paper in a hospital cafeteria after a student asked how to judge a newborn quickly. It is now done on virtually every baby born in a hospital.

q: Which name or term meaning "first-aid procedure" comes from an American surgeon?
f: Henry Heimlich published the technique in 1974 and it was saving lives within weeks. He was ninety-six when he reportedly used it in a real emergency for the first time, on a fellow resident of his retirement home.

q: There was an American urologist. Inflatable urinary catheter. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Frederic Foley's design added a small balloon that inflates once the catheter is in place, so it stays put without strapping. He lost the patent fight to a rival, but kept the name.

q: There was a Greek physician. Cervical cancer screening test. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: George Papanicolaou spent twenty years being ignored. His test could catch cervical cancer before symptoms appeared, and the profession did not want it. Once adopted, deaths from the disease fell by around seventy per cent.

q: "Koch's Postulates" is named after a person.
f: Robert Koch set out four conditions that must all hold before you can blame a specific microbe for a specific disease. It is a rule for not fooling yourself, and it ended centuries of guesswork about contagion.

q: There was a Danish bacteriologist. Differential staining technique for bacteria. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hans Christian Gram published his staining method in 1884 and wrote that it was imperfect and would surely be improved by others. It has not been. Bacteria are still sorted into Gram-positive and Gram-negative today.

q: There was a German scientists. Acid-fast staining for tuberculosis bacteria. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Tuberculosis bacteria have a waxy coat that shrugs off ordinary dyes. Ziehl and Neelsen worked out how to force the stain in with heat and acid, making the bacteria visible as bright red rods under the microscope.

q: There was a German chemist. Stain used for blood cells and parasites. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Gustav Giemsa refined a dye mixture that colours the nucleus and cytoplasm of blood cells differently. It is still the standard way of finding malaria parasites in a drop of blood.

q: There was a Swedish scientists. Immunological assay developed in 1971. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Engvall and Perlmann built a test that uses an enzyme to make an invisible immune reaction visible as a colour change. It underpins pregnancy tests, HIV screening, and most rapid tests you have ever used.

q: There was a british scientist. Device for studying cell migration. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Stephen Boyden put a porous membrane between two fluid compartments so he could watch cells crawl through it toward a chemical signal. It is a simple piece of equipment that turned cell migration into something measurable.

q: Which name or term meaning "laboratory dish" comes from a German bacteriologist?
f: Before Petri, cultures were grown under bell jars that had to be lifted, letting in whatever was floating past. His two-part dish with an overlapping lid solved contamination with no moving parts at all.

q: "Erlenmeyer Flask" is named after a place.
f: Emil Erlenmeyer gave the flask sloping sides and a narrow neck, so it can be swirled hard without spilling and stoppered easily. It is the shape everyone draws when asked to draw a chemistry flask.

q: There was a German chemist. Funnel for vacuum filtration. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Ernst Buchner's funnel has a flat perforated plate instead of a cone, so suction can pull liquid through a filter fast. It is the difference between filtering in minutes and filtering overnight.

q: There was a Scottish chemist. Double-walled vacuum flask. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: James Dewar built a double-walled vessel with a vacuum between the layers to hold liquid gases. He never patented it. A German glassware firm did, sold it as the Thermos, and made the fortune.

q: There was a French scientist. Glass pipette associated with microbiology. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A glass tube drawn to a fine point, plugged with cotton, sterilised by flame — Pasteur's answer to moving liquid without carrying microbes along with it. The plastic version in every lab still carries his name.

q: Which name or term meaning "radiation detector" comes from a German physicist?
f: Geiger's early detectors had to be watched, hour after hour, counting faint flashes on a screen in a darkened room. He built the clicking tube partly so physicists could stop staring and start listening.

q: Which name or term meaning "wave frequency phenomenon" comes from an Austrian physicist?
f: Christian Doppler predicted the effect in 1842 using starlight. Three years later a Dutch scientist tested it by hiring a train, filling an open carriage with trumpeters, and having musicians on the platform write down what they heard.

q: There was an American physicist. Voltage produced across a conductor in a magnetic field. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Edwin Hall found that a magnetic field pushes a current sideways inside a conductor, producing a small voltage across it. He was a graduate student at the time, testing something Maxwell had said was impossible.

q: "Coriolis Effect" is named after a person.
f: On a spinning planet, anything moving in a straight line appears to curve. It steers hurricanes and long-range artillery. It does not steer water down a plughole — that scale is far too small, whatever you have been told.

q: There was a German physicist. Spinning object experiences sideways force. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A spinning ball drags air around with it, and the uneven airflow pushes it sideways. Heinrich Magnus was investigating why cannonballs curved off target; footballers have been exploiting the same physics ever since.

q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Pressure decreases as fluid speed increases. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Daniel Bernoulli found that fast-moving fluid exerts less pressure than slow-moving fluid. He came from a family of mathematicians so competitive that his own father, jealous of a prize, threw him out of the house.

q: There was an Austrian physicist. Radar using the Doppler effect to measure velocity. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Bounce a radio wave off something moving and it comes back at a shifted frequency — so you can measure speed, not just position. It is why forecasters can see a storm rotating before a tornado forms.

q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a william Thomson?
f: William Thomson worked out there is a coldest possible temperature, where molecular motion stops, and built a scale starting there. He was made Lord Kelvin after the river running past his Glasgow laboratory.

q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a Swedish astronomer?
f: Anders Celsius put 0 at boiling and 100 at freezing — the exact reverse of today's scale. It was flipped after his death, and the version everyone now uses is upside down from the one he actually proposed.

q: Which name or term meaning "temperature scale" comes from a German physicist?
f: Fahrenheit set his zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably reproduce: a mixture of ice, water and salt. That is why the scale's landmarks look so arbitrary — they were pinned to what he could make in a bucket.

q: "Beaufort Scale" is named after a place.
f: Beaufort's scale needs no instruments — each step is defined by what the sea and the sails are doing. Force 12 was originally described as that which no canvas could withstand.

q: Which name or term meaning "famous periodic comet" comes from an English astronomer?
f: Halley noticed that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 followed the same path, decided they were one object, and predicted its return in 1758. He died in 1742. It arrived on Christmas night, sixteen years after his death.

q: There was an American astronomer. Discovered that galaxies recede from each other, leading to the expanding universe model. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hubble measured how fast galaxies are moving away and found the farther ones move faster — which means the universe is expanding. Astronomers still cannot agree on the exact number, and the disagreement has a name: the Hubble tension.

q: Which name or term meaning "orbiting space telescope" comes from an astronomer?
f: Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by an amount thinner than a human hair. Astronauts flew up in 1993 and fitted it with corrective optics — effectively giving a telescope a pair of spectacles.

q: There was a German astronomer. Three laws describing planetary motion around the Sun. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Kepler spent years trying to fit Mars's orbit to a circle and failing by an eight-minute discrepancy he refused to ignore. Those eight minutes broke two thousand years of circular astronomy and gave him the ellipse.

q: There was a Polish astronomer. Shift from geocentric to heliocentric worldview. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Copernicus reportedly received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not just astronomy — it was the moment humanity stopped being the centre of anything.

q: There was an Italian astronomer. Large gap separating Saturn's rings. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Giovanni Cassini spotted a dark gap in Saturn's rings in 1675 — the first hint that the rings were not one solid sheet. The spacecraft sent to Saturn three centuries later was named after him.

q: "Oort Cloud" is named after a person.
f: Jan Oort proposed an enormous shell of icy bodies surrounding the solar system, a thousand times farther out than Pluto, purely from the way long-period comets arrive. Nobody has ever seen it.

q: There was a Dutch-American astronomer. Region of icy bodies beyond Neptune. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, and the reason Pluto was reclassified — once astronomers found Pluto had thousands of neighbours out there, it looked less like a planet and more like the largest of a crowd.

q: There was an astronomers. Classifies stars by luminosity and temperature. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Two astronomers independently plotted stars by brightness against temperature and found they do not scatter randomly — they fall into a narrow band. That band is the life story of a star, drawn on one chart.

q: There was an Indian-American astrophysicist. Maximum mass of a stable white dwarf (~1.4 solar masses). Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Chandrasekhar calculated the limit at nineteen, on the boat to England. Eddington, the most famous astronomer alive, publicly ridiculed it. He was right and Eddington was wrong, and he received the Nobel Prize fifty-three years later.

q: There was an astronomer. Classification system for galaxies. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hubble sorted galaxies by shape into a diagram shaped like a tuning fork — ellipticals on the handle, spirals branching into two prongs. He thought it showed how galaxies evolve. It does not, but the classification stuck.

q: There was a French astronomer. Catalog of nebulae, clusters, and galaxies to avoid confusing them with comets. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Charles Messier was hunting comets and kept being fooled by fuzzy things that turned out not to be comets. He catalogued them as a list of objects to ignore — and that list of annoyances is now the most-used catalogue in amateur astronomy.

q: There was a british astronomer. Companion catalog to Messier objects. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Patrick Moore noticed Messier's catalogue missed many fine objects, so he made a companion list. He could not use M for Moore, since Messier had it — so he used the other half of his surname, Caldwell.

q: "Roche Limit" is named after a place.
f: Get close enough to a planet and its gravity pulls harder on your near side than your far side, until the difference tears you apart. Saturn's rings sit inside Saturn's Roche limit, which is very likely how they formed.

q: There was an astronomer. Region around a star where orbiting matter remains gravitationally bound. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Around each star in a close pair is a teardrop-shaped region where its gravity still wins. Fill that region and matter spills across to the companion — which is how some stars slowly eat each other.

q: There was a German astronomer. Empirical rule approximating planetary distances. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A numerical pattern that seemed to predict planetary distances, and even pointed to a gap where the asteroid belt was later found. Then Neptune was discovered in the wrong place and the whole thing collapsed. It was never a law.

q: There was a German engineer. Most fuel-efficient orbital transfer between two circular orbits. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Walter Hohmann worked out the cheapest route between two orbits in 1925 — two engine burns and a long coast. Every mission to Mars still uses it, which is why launch windows come round only every twenty-six months.

q: There was a French mathematician. Positions where gravitational forces balance. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Five spots where the pull of two large bodies balances so a small object can sit still relative to both. The James Webb telescope parks at one of them, a million miles out, permanently shaded from the Sun.

q: There was an American astronomer. Gaps in the asteroid belt caused by Jupiter's gravity. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Daniel Kirkwood noticed empty lanes in the asteroid belt and worked out why: any asteroid orbiting in a simple ratio with Jupiter gets a repeated nudge at the same point until it is flung out. Resonance clears the road.

q: There was a british physicist. Criterion for collapse of gas clouds into stars. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A gas cloud is a contest between gravity pulling in and pressure pushing out. James Jeans worked out the mass at which gravity wins — and that threshold is where every star in the universe begins.

q: "Eddington Limit" is named after a person.
f: A star can only be so bright before its own light blows its outer layers off. Eddington calculated the ceiling — the same Eddington who told the young Chandrasekhar his white-dwarf limit was nonsense.

q: There was a German physicist. Radius defining the event horizon of a non-rotating black hole. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Karl Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations while serving in the trenches of the First World War, and posted the result to Einstein from the front. He died of illness months later, before anyone understood he had described a black hole.

q: There was a new Zealand mathematician. Solution describing rotating black holes. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Schwarzschild described a black hole that does not spin, in 1916. It took until 1963 for Roy Kerr to solve the far harder case of one that does. Every real black hole spins, so Kerr's is the solution the universe actually uses.

q: There was a british physicist. Theoretical radiation emitted by black holes due to quantum effects. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hawking showed black holes are not entirely black — they leak, very slowly, and eventually evaporate. He set out to disprove the idea and ended up proving it, which he described as the most surprising result of his life.

q: There was a british mathematician. Method of extracting energy from a rotating black hole. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Roger Penrose worked out that you could throw an object at a spinning black hole, split it in two, and have one half come back with more energy than you sent in. The black hole pays, by spinning slightly slower.

q: Which name or term meaning "optical illusion" comes from a mathematician?
f: A triangle that looks perfectly solid and cannot exist. Penrose called it impossibility in its purest form and showed it to the artist Escher, who built entire staircases and waterfalls out of the same trick.

q: There was a Dutch physicist. Mathematical basis of special relativity. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Lorentz wrote down the equations before Einstein did, but treated them as a mathematical fix. Einstein took the same equations and said they meant time and space themselves change with speed — which is why relativity is his.

q: "Lorentz Force" is named after a place.
f: A charged particle moving through a magnetic field gets pushed sideways, at right angles to both its motion and the field. It is the reason electric motors turn and the reason the aurora glows near the poles.

q: There was a Scottish physicist. Unified electricity, magnetism, and light. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Four equations that between them describe every electric motor, radio wave and beam of light in existence. Feynman said that from a long enough view of history, the nineteenth century would be remembered for these.

q: Which name or term meaning "electromagnetic shield" comes from an English scientist?
f: A metal shell keeps electric fields out, which is why you are safe inside a car in a lightning storm — the charge runs around the bodywork, not through you. Faraday tested it by sitting in a foil-lined room while assistants zapped it.

q: There was a scientist. Rotation of polarized light by a magnetic field. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Faraday showed that a magnetic field can twist a beam of polarised light. It was the first hard evidence that light and magnetism were connected at all, and it pointed straight at Maxwell's equations twenty years later.

q: Which name or term meaning "sETI paradox" comes from an Italian physicist?
f: Over lunch at Los Alamos in 1950, Enrico Fermi interrupted a conversation about aliens with one question: where is everybody? The galaxy is old and vast and should be crowded. It looks empty. Nobody has answered him yet.

q: There was a physicist. Highest occupied energy level at absolute zero. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Even at absolute zero, electrons in a metal are not still — the rules of quantum mechanics forbid them all sitting in the lowest state. The Fermi energy is the level the topmost ones are stuck at.

q: There was a physicist. Calculates quantum transition probabilities. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Fermi called it golden rule number two in his lectures, and the name stuck. He did not discover it — Dirac did — which makes it one of physics' more cheerfully misattributed results.

q: "Feynman Diagram" is named after a person.
f: Feynman replaced pages of algebra with little pictures of particles meeting, scattering and moving on. Older physicists were suspicious of anything so easy to draw. Within a decade nobody could work without them.

q: Which name or term meaning "study technique" comes from a physicist?
f: Explain the thing to a child. Wherever you stumble is exactly where you do not understand it. Feynman used this on himself constantly, and it remains the cheapest study method ever devised.

q: There was a british physicist. Relativistic equation describing electrons. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Dirac's equation had two solutions, and one of them described a particle with negative energy. Rather than discard it he suggested it was a real particle nobody had found yet. Four years later someone found the positron.

q: There was a physicists. Predicted fifth state of matter at extremely low temperatures. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Bose's paper was rejected by a journal. He posted it to Einstein, who translated it into German himself, added his own extension, and got it published. Seventy years later the state of matter they predicted was finally made in a lab.

q: There was an Indian physicist. Gas composed of bosons obeying Bose-Einstein statistics. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Satyendra Nath Bose worked out a new way of counting identical particles that behaves nothing like counting ordinary objects. Swap two of them and nothing changes at all — because there is no way even in principle to tell which is which.

q: There was an Indian physicist. Family of particles named in Bose's honor. Which word grew out of it?
f: Every particle in the universe is either a boson or a fermion, and the bosons are named after Bose. Dirac chose the name. Bose himself never received a Nobel Prize, though at least ten have been awarded for work built on his.

q: Which name or term meaning "elementary particle" comes from a british physicist?
f: Peter Higgs's paper was rejected in 1964 as being of no obvious relevance to physics. The particle it predicted was found in 2012, and he got the Nobel the following year — forty-eight years after the rejection.

q: "Higgs Field" is named after a place.
f: An invisible field filling all of space, which particles drag through like walking in water. The dragging is what we call mass. A writer nicknamed it the God particle; Higgs, an atheist, disliked the name intensely.

q: There was an Indian physicist. Inelastic scattering of light by molecules. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: C. V. Raman started wondering why the sea is blue on a voyage home from England, and ended up discovering that molecules shift the colour of light that bounces off them. It won him the Nobel Prize in 1930.

q: There was a physicist. Analytical technique based on Raman scattering. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Shine a laser at a substance and the light that scatters back carries a fingerprint of exactly which molecules are present. It identifies paint on a masterpiece or a pill in a packet without touching either.

q: There was a German physicist. Recoil-free emission and absorption of gamma rays. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Rudolf Mossbauer found that atoms locked in a crystal can emit gamma rays without recoiling, giving a beam of extraordinary precision. He was a doctoral student, and had a Nobel Prize by the age of thirty-two.

q: There was a Dutch physicist. Splitting of spectral lines in magnetic fields. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Put an atom in a magnetic field and its spectral lines split apart. Zeeman was reprimanded for wasting laboratory time on the experiment. He won a Nobel Prize for it six years later.

q: There was a German physicist. Splitting of spectral lines in electric fields. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: The electric-field twin of the Zeeman effect — spectral lines splitting under voltage rather than magnetism. Johannes Stark won a Nobel for it, then spent his later career attacking the physics of Einstein on political grounds.

q: There was an American physicist. X-ray scattering demonstrating particle nature of light. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Compton bounced X-rays off electrons and found the light lost energy, exactly as if it were made of particles colliding. It was the experiment that made physicists accept the photon as real rather than a bookkeeping trick.

q: "Hall–Petch Relationship" is named after a person.
f: Metals are made of tiny crystal grains, and cracks travel easily inside a grain but struggle to cross a boundary. Make the grains smaller and the metal gets stronger — which is why smiths have hammered steel for three thousand years.

q: Which word meaning "unit of electric potential" comes from an Italian physicist?
f: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. He demonstrated it to Napoleon, who made him a count and put him on the currency.

q: Which word meaning "unit of electrical resistance" comes from a German physicist?
f: Ohm published his law in 1827 and German academics dismissed it as a web of naked fancies. He resigned his teaching post in disgust. Recognition came fifteen years later, from England, and eventually the unit.

q: Which word meaning "unit of pressure" comes from a French mathematician?
f: Pascal built a working mechanical calculator at nineteen to help his father, a tax official, with endless sums. He also founded probability theory, largely by answering a gambler's question about how to split an interrupted bet.

q: Which word meaning "unit of force" comes from an English physicist?
f: A newton is roughly the weight of a medium apple in your hand — a coincidence physicists enjoy rather too much given the story about the tree. Newton himself told that story late in life, and only about seeing an apple fall.

q: Which word meaning "unit of energy" comes from an English physicist?
f: James Joule was a brewer who did physics on the side, and he measured heat with the precision of someone used to controlling fermentation. On his honeymoon he reportedly took a thermometer to a waterfall to see if the falling water warmed up.

q: There was an English scientist. Pioneer of electromagnetism and electrochemistry. Which word grew out of it?
f: Michael Faraday left school at thirteen and worked as a bookbinder, reading the books he was binding. He became the finest experimentalist of the century and turned down both a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society.

q: "Henry" is named after a place.
f: Joseph Henry discovered electromagnetic induction before Faraday did, but he was teaching a full timetable at a small American academy and published late. Faraday got the credit; Henry got the unit.

q: Which word meaning "unit of frequency" comes from a German physicist?
f: Hertz proved radio waves exist. Asked what use they might be, he said none whatsoever — it is just an experiment that proves Maxwell was right. Within fifteen years Marconi was sending signals across the Atlantic.

q: There was a French physicist. Discovered natural radioactivity. Which word grew out of it?
f: Becquerel expected sunlight to make uranium salts glow, so when the weather turned cloudy he shut everything in a drawer with a photographic plate. Days later the plate was fogged anyway. He had found radioactivity by being rained off.

q: Which word meaning "unit of radioactivity (historical)" comes from a scientists?
f: Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her notebooks are still radioactive and are kept in lead-lined boxes; anyone wanting to read them must sign a waiver.

q: There was a German physicist. Discovered X-rays in 1895. Which word grew out of it?
f: Roentgen called them X-rays because he did not know what they were. The first radiograph was of his wife's hand; she looked at her own skeleton and said she had seen her death. He refused to patent any of it.

q: There was a German mathematician. Major contributions to mathematics and magnetism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Told as a schoolboy to add the numbers from 1 to 100, Gauss saw that they pair up into fifty sums of 101 and answered almost immediately. He went on to contribute to nearly every branch of mathematics there was.

q: There was a German physicist. Collaborated with Gauss on electromagnetism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Wilhelm Weber built a working telegraph line across Gottingen with Gauss in 1833, years before commercial telegraphy. He was later dismissed from his professorship for refusing to swear an oath to the king.

q: "Siemens" is named after a person.
f: Werner von Siemens built his first telegraph business on a loan from a cousin and turned it into one of the largest electrical firms in the world. The unit of conductance is the reciprocal of the ohm — and it used to be called the mho.

q: What does "Diesel" mean?
f: Rudolf Diesel designed an engine that ignites fuel by compression alone, with no spark. In 1913 he boarded a ferry across the English Channel and was never seen again; his body was found floating ten days later.

q: Which word meaning "elevator brand that became synonymous with elevators" comes from an American inventor?
f: Elisha Otis did not invent the elevator — he invented the brake that catches it. At the 1854 World's Fair he had himself hoisted up, then ordered the rope cut. The platform dropped a few inches and stopped.

q: There was an American inventor. Developed rapid-fire mechanical gun. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Richard Gatling wrote that he built it hoping one man could do the work of a hundred, so armies would need fewer soldiers and fewer would die. It is among the worst predictions anyone has ever made about a weapon.

q: Which word meaning "revolver" comes from an American inventor?
f: Samuel Colt is said to have got the idea for the revolving cylinder watching a ship's wheel lock into position as it turned. He carved his first model out of wood on that voyage, aged sixteen.

q: There was an industrialist. Company popularized repeating rifles. Which word grew out of it?
f: The rifle made the family fortune. Sarah Winchester, the widowed heir, spent decades adding rooms to a California mansion — stairs to nowhere, doors opening onto walls — in a house that still stands and can still be visited.

q: There was a gunsmith. Small concealable pistol named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: Henry Deringer spelled his name with one r. Rival manufacturers copying his pocket pistol added a second to dodge the trademark, and the misspelling is the version that survived into the dictionary.

q: "Bowdlerize" is named after a place.
f: The Family Shakespeare removed everything Thomas Bowdler thought unsuitable to read aloud. His sister Henrietta did most of the editing but published anonymously, so the brother's name became the word for censoring a text.

q: Which word meaning "hypnotize" comes from an Austrian physician?
f: Franz Mesmer claimed to heal patients by redirecting an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. A royal commission including Benjamin Franklin investigated and found no fluid — but noticed the patients often got better anyway.

q: Which word meaning "tobacco alkaloid" comes from a French diplomat?
f: Jean Nicot was a French ambassador who sent tobacco seeds to the queen as a headache remedy. The plant, the genus and the addictive chemical inside it all ended up carrying the name of a diplomat who never smoked.

q: There was a diplomat. Tobacco genus named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: Linnaeus named the whole tobacco genus after Jean Nicot. It is a large family — tobacco's relatives include the tomato, the potato, the aubergine and deadly nightshade, all in the same botanical clan.

q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a Swedish botanist?
f: Named for Anders Dahl, a Swedish student of Linnaeus. The tubers were brought from Mexico to Europe partly as a possible food crop to replace the potato. Nobody liked the taste, so it was kept for the flowers.

q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a German botanist?
f: Leonhart Fuchs died in 1566, nearly two centuries before the flower was found and named for him. The colour is named after the flower, so a sixteenth-century German doctor is the reason a shade of pink has that spelling.

q: Which word meaning "flowering tree" comes from a French botanist?
f: Pierre Magnol invented the idea of the plant family — grouping species by shared structure rather than listing them alphabetically. Magnolias themselves are older than bees, and are pollinated by beetles instead.

q: "Gardenia" is named after a person.
f: Alexander Garden was a Scottish-born naturalist working in Charleston who sent specimens back to Europe for years. He was rewarded with a flower he had nothing to do with discovering — and which does not grow where he lived.

q: There was a jesuit botanist. Missionary who studied Asian flora. Which word grew out of it?
f: Georg Kamel was a Jesuit missionary and pharmacist in the Philippines. Linnaeus latinised his name to Camellus for the flower. Tea comes from the same genus, so every cup you drink is technically a camellia.

q: There was a French governor. Patron of botany. Which word grew out of it?
f: Michel Begon was a French colonial governor who collected plants and sponsored botanists. He never saw the flower named after him — it was named by a monk he had once employed, years after Begon's death.

q: Which word meaning "christmas flower" comes from an American diplomat?
f: Joel Poinsett was the first United States minister to Mexico and sent cuttings home in 1828. The Mexican name is flor de nochebuena, Christmas Eve flower — rather better than naming it after a visiting diplomat.

q: There was a Scottish horticulturist. Royal gardener. Which word grew out of it?
f: William Forsyth was royal head gardener at Kensington and a founder of what became the Royal Horticultural Society. He also sold the government a tree-wound plaster that turned out not to work, which caused a considerable scandal.

q: There was a German botanist. Described many flowering plants. Which word grew out of it?
f: Johann Gottfried Zinn was an anatomist who mapped the structures of the human eye, and died at thirty-two having also written on Mexican plants. There is a zone of the eye named after him as well as the flower.

q: There was an American physician. Anatomist and educator. Which word grew out of it?
f: Named for Caspar Wistar — with an a. The botanist who named it spelled it with an e, nobody corrected him, and two centuries later we all still misspell an anatomist's surname every time we mention the flower.

q: There was a Greek roots. Often mistaken for an eponym but derived from Greek words. Which word grew out of it?
f: This one is a trap. It looks like somebody called Philo Dendron, but it is plain Greek: philo-dendron, tree-loving, because the plant climbs. Not every scientific-sounding plant name hides a person.

q: Which name or term meaning "whole-wheat cracker" comes from an American minister?
f: Sylvester Graham was a minister who preached that bland food calmed the passions and that spices were dangerous. His cracker was designed to be dull on purpose. Modern versions are sweetened, which would have appalled him.

q: There was a health reformer. Developed coarse whole-wheat flour. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Graham insisted flour should keep the whole grain, bran and all, against the fashion for fine white flour. He was wrong about the moral effects and right about the nutrition, which is a better record than most food reformers manage.

q: Which name or term meaning "salad" comes from an Italian-American restaurateur?
f: Caesar Cardini ran a restaurant in Tijuana and was overwhelmed on the Fourth of July, 1924. Running short of ingredients, he threw what was left into a bowl and tossed it at the table for show. No Roman emperor was involved.

q: There was a british general. Dish allegedly named in his honor. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Nobody can prove the Duke of Wellington ever ate it. The name may simply be patriotic, or may come from the dish's resemblance to a brown boot. The duke has better claims to fame elsewhere.

q: Which word meaning "tortilla chips with toppings" comes from a Mexican chef?
f: In 1943 Ignacio Anaya was closing up when a group of American army wives arrived hungry. He fried some tortilla, added cheese and jalapeno, and served it. Ignacio's nickname was Nacho.

q: Which name or term meaning "pizza variety" comes from a queen of Italy?
f: In 1889 a Naples pizzaiolo made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the one in the colours of the new Italian flag — red tomato, white mozzarella, green basil — and he named it after her.

q: "Pavlova" is named after a person.
f: Created for the ballerina Anna Pavlova during a tour, and claimed by both Australia and New Zealand ever since. A researcher combing old cookbooks found the earliest recipe in New Zealand, which has settled nothing.

q: There was an Austrian chef. Invented Vienna's famous chocolate cake. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Franz Sacher invented it at sixteen, standing in for a sick head chef. A later dispute between two Viennese firms over who could call theirs the original ran for seven years in court and is still called the Sweet Seven Years.

q: There was a Russian nobleman. Dish created for his household. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Named for the Stroganovs, one of the wealthiest families in imperial Russia. Their chef is credited with the dish, possibly designed so that beef could be cut thin and cooked fast in a Russian winter kitchen.

q: Which name or term meaning "flavored tea" comes from a british Prime Minister?
f: Bergamot-scented tea named for a British prime minister who almost certainly never blended anything. The likeliest explanation is that a merchant used his name to sell it, which worked so well it outlasted his politics.

q: Which word meaning "coffee drink" comes from a WWII Italy?
f: American soldiers in Italy found espresso too strong and added hot water. Italian baristas named the result after them, not entirely as a compliment. It is now on the menu in Italy too.

q: There was a cocktail origin debated. One theory traces it to Martinez, California. Which word grew out of it?
f: Every origin story for the martini is contested: a town called Martinez in California, a vermouth brand called Martini and Rossi, a bartender of the same name. The drink is older than any reliable record of it.

q: Which name or term meaning "waterproof boot" comes from a military commander?
f: The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot that was tough enough for the battlefield and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere. The rubber version came decades later.

q: "Raglan Sleeve" is named after a place.
f: Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo and had his coats cut with the sleeve running in one piece to the collar, so he could dress himself more easily. The design turned out to be better for movement and became standard sportswear.

q: Which name or term meaning "laboratory burner" comes from a German chemist?
f: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built it to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and twice nearly died of arsenic poisoning — chemistry was a rougher trade then.

q: There was an Italian physicist. Proposed that equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Avogadro's idea was ignored for nearly fifty years, and he died before it was accepted. The number itself — about six hundred thousand billion billion — was calculated by others and named in his honour afterwards.

q: Which name or term meaning "gas law" comes from an anglo-Irish chemist?
f: Squeeze a gas into half the space and its pressure doubles. Boyle worked it out with a J-shaped glass tube and a quantity of mercury, and published it in 1662 while helping to invent the whole idea of the experiment.

q: There was a French physicist. Demonstrated relationship between gas volume and temperature. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Jacques Charles worked out that gases expand as they warm — and he was also a balloonist, making the first hydrogen balloon flight in 1783. Villagers where it landed attacked it with pitchforks, believing it was a monster.

q: There was an English chemist. Developed modern atomic theory. Which word grew out of it?
f: John Dalton was colour blind and wrote the first scientific description of the condition, using himself as the subject. He asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; they are still preserved in Manchester.

q: There was a scientist. Mineral named in his honor. Which word grew out of it?
f: A rare potassium mineral found near volcanic vents on Vesuvius, named for Avogadro. It is one of the quieter honours in science — a man who waited fifty years for recognition, given a mineral almost nobody has seen.

q: "Mohs Scale" is named after a person.
f: Friedrich Mohs ranked minerals one to ten by which scratches which — talc at one, diamond at ten. It measures nothing absolute, only the order. A fingernail is about 2.5, which is why it will mark gypsum but not glass.

q: Which name or term meaning "earthquake magnitude" comes from an American seismologist?
f: Each whole step is about thirty-two times more energy, so a magnitude 7 is not slightly worse than a 6 — it is thirty-two times worse. Richter built the scale for southern California and it was adopted worldwide.

q: There was an Italian volcanologist. Developed earthquake intensity scale based on observed effects. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Mercalli measured what an earthquake does rather than how much energy it releases — from barely felt up to total destruction. Two places at the same Richter magnitude can be far apart on Mercalli, depending on what was built there.

q: There was an engineer & Meteorologist. Categorized hurricanes by destructive potential. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An engineer and a meteorologist built it together: Saffir was studying how buildings fail in high wind, Simpson ran the National Hurricane Center. Categories 1 to 5 describe damage, not just wind speed.

q: Which name or term meaning "space observatory" comes from an astronomer?
f: Launched in 1990 with a mirror ground to the wrong shape by less than the width of a hair. Astronauts fitted corrective optics in 1993 — effectively giving a telescope spectacles — and it has been working ever since.

q: There was a Polish astronomer. Proposed heliocentric model of the Solar System. Which word grew out of it?
f: Copernicus is said to have received the first printed copy of his book on the day he died. Moving the Sun to the centre was not only astronomy; it was the moment humanity stopped being at the centre of anything.

q: Which name or term meaning "movement disorder" comes from an English physician?
f: James Parkinson called it the shaking palsy in 1817, in an essay of sixty-six pages based on six patients — some of whom he had only observed walking past in the street. His name was attached decades after his death.

q: "Asperger Syndrome*" is named after a place.
f: Hans Asperger described the pattern in 1944. The term is being retired from clinical use in favour of the wider autism spectrum, both because the boundary proved hard to draw and because later research into his wartime conduct raised serious concerns.

q: There was a French neurologist. Identified neurological tic disorder. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Georges Gilles de la Tourette described nine patients in 1885 whose tics came with involuntary sounds. He was later shot in the head by a former patient who believed he had hypnotised her, and survived.

q: Which word meaning "heat treatment of food" comes from a French chemist?
f: Pasteur was asked why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it and showed that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Applied to milk, it saved a great many children.

q: Which name or term meaning "surgical childbirth" comes from a Roman leader?
f: Probably not named after Caesar at all. Roman law required the operation on a dying mother — and Caesar's mother lived for decades after his birth. The likelier root is caedere, Latin for to cut.

q: Which word meaning "loose undergarments/trousers" comes from an American women's rights advocate?
f: Amelia Bloomer did not invent them — she promoted them in her newspaper, and the press attached her name. Women wearing them were mocked in the street, and the campaign was dropped as a distraction from the vote.

q: Which word meaning "soft felt hat" comes from a fictional character?
f: Named after a play. Sarah Bernhardt played Princess Fedora in 1882 wearing a soft centre-creased hat, and women adopted it as a symbol of the movement for women's rights before men took it over entirely.

q: Which word meaning "wide-brimmed hat" comes from an American hatmaker?
f: John Stetson made a wide-brimmed hat on a prospecting trip to keep sun and rain off, and sold it off his own head for five dollars. He called the design the Boss of the Plains and built a factory on it.

q: "Mackintosh" is named after a person.
f: Charles Macintosh spelled his name without the k. He glued two layers of cloth together with rubber dissolved in naphtha — a by-product of the gasworks — and made the first genuinely waterproof coat. The k crept in later.

q: Which word meaning "woolen face covering" comes from a crimean War battle?
f: Named for a battle, not a person. British troops at Balaclava in the Crimean winter of 1854 were sent knitted headgear from home because the army had not equipped them for the cold.

q: Which word meaning "two-piece swimsuit" comes from a pacific atoll?
f: Louis Reard named his 1946 swimsuit after Bikini Atoll, where an atomic bomb had been tested four days earlier — he wanted a name that suggested an explosion. No Paris model would wear it, so he hired a dancer.

q: There was a british statesman. Sofa style associated with aristocratic taste. Which word grew out of it?
f: The fourth Earl of Chesterfield is said to have commissioned a sofa that would let a gentleman sit upright without creasing his suit. He is better remembered for letters of advice to his son that Samuel Johnson called immoral.

q: Which name or term meaning "folding bed" comes from an American inventor?
f: William Murphy was courting a singer while living in a one-room San Francisco apartment, and etiquette forbade a woman entering a bedroom. He designed a bed that folded into the wall, turning his bedroom into a parlour.

q: Which name or term meaning "glass preserving jar" comes from an American tinsmith?
f: John Mason patented the screw-thread glass jar with a rubber-sealed lid in 1858, making home preserving safe and reliable. His patent expired, competitors flooded in, and he died poor while everyone else got rich.

q: Which word meaning "ballpoint pen" comes from a Hungarian journalist?
f: Laszlo Biro was a journalist who noticed newspaper ink dried almost instantly while his fountain pen smudged. He built a pen that used the thicker ink with a rolling ball to feed it. Britain still calls every ballpoint a biro.

q: "Tupperware" is named after a place.
f: Earl Tupper's airtight seal sold badly in shops because nobody could see why it mattered. Brownie Wise worked out you had to demonstrate the burp in someone's living room, and invented the Tupperware party.

q: There was a courtier of Dionysius I of Syracuse. Damocles envied the ruler's fortune until he sat beneath a sword suspended by a single horsehair, symbolizing the constant danger faced by those in power. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Damocles told the tyrant Dionysius how lucky he was, so Dionysius offered to swap places. Damocles enjoyed the throne until he looked up and saw a sword hanging over it by a single horsehair. He asked to leave.

q: There was a mythical king of Corinth. Condemned by the gods to roll a boulder uphill forever, only for it to roll back each time. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sisyphus cheated death twice — once by chaining up Death himself, so that for a while nobody on earth could die. His punishment was a boulder that always rolls back. Camus argued we must imagine him happy.

q: Which word meaning "to tease with something unattainable" comes from a king punished in Hades?
f: Tantalus stood in water that drained whenever he bent to drink, under fruit that swung away whenever he reached. English took his name for the very specific cruelty of something being just out of reach.

q: Which word meaning "excessive self-love" comes from a beautiful youth?
f: Narcissus saw his reflection in a pool, did not realise it was himself, and could not leave. The flower that grew where he died still bends its head toward water.

q: There was a king of Thebes. Unknowingly killed his father and married his mother, inspiring Freud's psychological theory. Which word grew out of it?
f: Oedipus was abandoned as a baby precisely so the prophecy could not come true, and it came true because he was abandoned. Freud borrowed the name in 1899 for a theory the play itself does not require.

q: Which name or term meaning "source of unforeseen troubles" comes from first woman in Greek mythology?
f: It was a jar, not a box. Erasmus mistranslated the Greek pithos as pyxis in the sixteenth century and the mistake stuck. Pandora shut the lid with one thing still inside: hope.

q: "Procrustean" is named after a person.
f: Procrustes offered travellers a bed and guaranteed a perfect fit — by stretching anyone too short and cutting down anyone too tall. Theseus eventually gave him the same treatment on his own bed.

q: There was a cypriot sculptor. His statue came to life after Aphrodite answered his prayers; later adapted in psychology to describe self-fulfilling expectations. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A teacher told that certain pupils are gifted will, without meaning to, treat them differently — and those pupils improve. Named after the sculptor who loved his statue into life, because expectation does the shaping.

q: Which name or term meaning "ability to generate wealth or success" comes from a phrygian king?
f: Midas asked that everything he touched turn to gold, and it did — including his food, his drink, and in some versions his daughter. He begged to have the gift taken back, and washed it off in a river.

q: Which word meaning "trusted adviser or guide" comes from a friend of Odysseus?
f: When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son with a friend named Mentor. Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a goddess's disguise.

q: The word "Odyssey" is named after…?
f: Ten years to sail home from a war that itself took ten years. Odysseus survives by lying, hiding and outthinking everything he meets, which makes him a strange sort of hero and a very durable one.

q: Which word meaning "requiring immense effort" comes from a Greek hero?
f: Twelve labours, each supposedly impossible: the lion, the hydra, the stables, the golden apples. He was given them as punishment, completed all twelve, and the word for an enormous task has been his ever since.

q: There was a fire-breathing monster. Composite creature with lion, goat, and serpent parts. Which word grew out of it?
f: A lion at the front, a goat rising from the back, a snake for a tail. Even the Greeks found it absurd, which is why chimera came to mean a wild impossible idea rather than an actual monster.

q: "Cerberus" is named after a place.
f: Three heads, so one is always awake. The way past was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since Romans buried honey cakes with their dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

q: Which word meaning "two-faced" comes from a Roman god of beginnings?
f: Janus guarded doorways, with one face looking back and one forward. His temple doors in Rome stood open in wartime and shut in peace. In roughly seven hundred years they were recorded as closed only a handful of times.

q: There was a Roman god of fire. Charles Goodyear named the rubber-hardening process after the god associated with fire and metalworking. Which word grew out of it?
f: Charles Goodyear spent years and several fortunes trying to make rubber stable, and found the answer by accidentally dropping a rubber-and-sulphur mixture on a hot stove. He named it for the Roman god of the forge, and died in debt.

q: Which word meaning "planet or chemical element" comes from a Roman messenger god?
f: The fastest-moving planet took the name of the fastest god. The liquid metal got it too, for rolling away the moment you touch it — and gave English mercurial for anyone whose mood does the same.

q: Which word meaning "relating to war or the military" comes from a Roman god of war?
f: Everything military traces to Mars: martial arts, martial law, court-martial. March is his month too, because it was when the campaigning season opened and Roman armies could move again.

q: Which word meaning "cheerful and good-humored" comes from a king of the Roman gods?
f: Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your temperament. Jupiter — Jove — produced the cheerful sort. Saturn produced the gloomy sort, which is why saturnine still means what it does.

q: Which word meaning "sudden overwhelming fear" comes from a Greek god of shepherds?
f: Pan was the goat-legged god of wild places, and travellers who heard an unexplained noise in an empty wood blamed him. That particular fear — sudden, irrational, contagious — is the one that kept his name.

q: "Echo" is named after a person.
f: Echo was a nymph who talked too much, and Hera cursed her to repeat only other people's last words. She fell in love with Narcissus and could never say so — only give him his own words back.

q: Which word meaning "flower" comes from a goddess of the rainbow?
f: Iris was the rainbow, and the messenger who ran along it between gods and mortals. The coloured ring of your eye is named after her, and so is the flower, and so is the word iridescent.

q: Which word meaning "plant life of a region" comes from a Roman goddess of flowers?
f: Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and spring, and her festival involved so much noise and colour that stricter Romans disapproved. Biologists took her name for all the plant life of a place.

q: Which word meaning "animal life of a region" comes from a Roman god of forests?
f: Faunus was the Roman god of forests and wild animals, and his female counterpart Fauna gave her name to all animal life. Flora and fauna are a goddess and a goddess, still working as a pair.

q: There was a Greek god of marriage. Wedding songs invoked Hymen for blessings. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hymen was the Greek god of weddings, and a hymeneal is a wedding song. Greek marriage processions called his name aloud on the way to the bride's house, which is where the word comes from.

q: Which word meaning "symbol of romantic love" comes from a god of love?
f: The Romans made him a chubby child with a bow. The Greeks knew him as Eros and took him rather more seriously — a primordial force older than most of the gods, not a decoration for a card.

q: There was a primordial deity. Personification of darkness in Greek cosmology. Which word grew out of it?
f: Erebus was darkness itself, born near the beginning of things. A British polar ship took the name, and after it was lost in the Arctic, a volcano in Antarctica was named after the ship — darkness, twice removed.

q: "Morpheus" is named after a place.
f: Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people who appear in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. His name comes from morphe, the Greek for form.

q: Which word meaning "powerful opioid analgesic" comes from a god of dreams?
f: A German pharmacist isolated it from opium in 1804 and named it after the god of dreams. He tested it on himself and on three boys, nearly killing all four, then spent much of his life addicted to it.

q: Which word meaning "artificially induced trance" comes from a Greek god of sleep?
f: Hypnos was the Greek god of sleep, brother of Death and son of Night. Hypnosis is not really sleep at all — the name was chosen before anyone understood what was happening — and its coiner later regretted it.

q: There was a Greek personification of death. Named after the god of peaceful death. Which word grew out of it?
f: Thanatos was the gentle personification of death, as distinct from the violent kind. Thanatology — the study of dying, grief and how people face the end — took his name rather than a harsher one deliberately.

q: There was a goddess of youth. Early psychiatric term derived from the youthful goddess. Which word grew out of it?
f: From Hebe, goddess of youth, because the condition was first described in adolescents. Like several psychiatric terms built from Greek gods, it has largely been retired in favour of plainer clinical language.

q: Which word meaning "memory aid" comes from a goddess of memory?
f: Mnemosyne was memory, and the mother of all nine Muses — which makes memory, in Greek thinking, the parent of every art. Sensible, for a culture that recited Homer for centuries before writing it down.

q: Which word meaning "institution preserving knowledge and art" comes from a nine daughters of Mnemosyne?
f: A museum was originally a place belonging to the Muses — a shrine to the nine goddesses of the arts. The greatest of them, at Alexandria, was a research institute with the famous library attached.

q: "Music" is named after a person.
f: Music means, literally, the art of the Muses. It covered poetry and dance as well as sound, because the Greeks did not separate them — a performance was all three at once.

q: Which word meaning "cleanliness promoting health" comes from a goddess of health?
f: Hygieia was the daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them once sick. Her sister Panacea handled cures — and gave English a word for a remedy for everything.

q: There was a Greek god of medicine. Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius. Which word grew out of it?
f: Ancient physicians claimed descent from Asclepius, god of medicine, and called themselves Asclepiads. His snake-wound staff is still the symbol of medicine — though it is often confused with a different, two-snake staff belonging to Hermes.

q: There was a Roman equivalent of Asclepius. Used to describe doctors or medicine. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Roman spelling of Asclepius. When plague struck Rome in 293 BC the Senate sent for the god, and a snake from his temple reportedly boarded the ship and slid off onto an island in the Tiber, where they built him a temple.

q: There was a legendary sage. Secret writings attributed to him gave rise to the idea of being tightly sealed or esoteric. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary sage credited with secret writings. Alchemists working in that tradition developed a way of fusing glass to seal a vessel completely — so a hermetic seal is named after a wizard.

q: There was a titan. First cervical vertebra supports the skull just as Atlas supported the heavens. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Atlas was condemned to hold up the sky forever. The top vertebra of your spine, which holds up your skull, carries his name — and the book of maps does too, from a picture of Atlas on the cover of an early collection.

q: Which name or term meaning "largest tendon in the body" comes from a Greek hero?
f: His mother dipped him in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel — the one spot the water never touched. The largest tendon in your body is named after the one weak point in a legend.

q: "Caesarian (historical adjective)" is named after a place.
f: Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of the same word. Caesarian, meaning imperial, is the direct English adjective.

q: Which word meaning "eighth month of the year" comes from first Roman Emperor?
f: Renamed for Augustus in 8 BC. The story that he stole a day from February so his month would match Julius Caesar's is a medieval invention — but the Senate really did rename it for him.

q: Which word meaning "seventh month of the year" comes from a Roman dictator?
f: Renamed for Julius Caesar after his death, in the month he was born. He had just reformed the calendar into something close to the one we use, so the honour was at least on topic.

q: There was a French diplomat. Historical term referring to nicotine poisoning or dependence. Which word grew out of it?
f: An old medical term for nicotine poisoning, built from the name of the French diplomat who introduced tobacco to his queen as a headache cure. He would probably not have chosen this particular memorial.

q: Which word meaning "oppressively authoritarian" comes from an English novelist?
f: Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four in 1948 and swapped the last two digits for the title. The word now gets used for any surveillance at all, which slightly misses the point — his real subject was the corruption of language.

q: Which word meaning "theory of biological evolution" comes from an English naturalist?
f: Darwin sat on his theory for twenty years, worried about the reaction. He only published when a letter arrived from Alfred Russel Wallace describing the same idea — and their work was presented jointly.

q: Which word meaning "relating to evolution or competitive selection" comes from a naturalist?
f: Darwin never wrote survival of the fittest — Herbert Spencer coined it, and Darwin adopted it reluctantly in a later edition. Fittest means best-suited to the surroundings, not strongest, which is the misunderstanding that persists.

q: "Mendelian" is named after a person.
f: Gregor Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants in a monastery garden and worked out the rules of inheritance. His paper was almost entirely ignored for thirty-four years, until three separate scientists rediscovered it at once.

q: There was a French biologist. Early evolutionary theory proposing inheritance of acquired characteristics. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lamarck thought a giraffe that stretched for high leaves would pass longer necks to its young. He was wrong about the mechanism, but he was arguing that species change at all, decades before Darwin — which took some courage.

q: There was a French chemist. Refers to principles or methods associated with Pasteur's work. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pasteur's germ theory met fierce resistance from doctors who resented being told they carried disease on their hands. He was also a chemist, not a physician, which the medical establishment mentioned frequently.

q: There was a German microbiologist. Pertaining to Koch's work on bacteriology. Which word grew out of it?
f: Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera, and set out the rules for proving any such link. He and Pasteur were bitter rivals, and their national newspapers cheered them on.

q: There was a geneticist. Classical inheritance principles. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mendel's laws describe how traits pass on in neat ratios — but he chose pea characteristics that happened to be unusually simple. Most inheritance is far messier, which is partly why his results looked almost too tidy.

q: There was a Swedish botanist. Creator of binomial nomenclature. Which word grew out of it?
f: Linnaeus gave every living thing a two-word name, genus then species, replacing descriptions that ran to whole sentences. He also named himself: born Carl Nilsson, he took Linnaeus from a lime tree on the family farm.

q: There was a French naturalist. Founder of comparative anatomy and paleontology. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cuvier could reconstruct an entire animal from a few bones, and proved that species go extinct — an idea many found impossible, since it implied the creation was not perfect. He rejected evolution to his last day.

q: "Buffonian" is named after a place.
f: Buffon estimated the Earth was at least 75,000 years old by heating iron spheres and timing how long they took to cool. The Church objected. He apologised in print and went on believing it.

q: Which word meaning "relating to psychoanalysis" comes from an Austrian neurologist?
f: A Freudian slip is a mistake that supposedly reveals a hidden thought. Freud's own term was Fehlleistung — faulty achievement — and he collected examples obsessively, including a great many of his own.

q: There was a Swiss psychiatrist. Based on archetypes and the collective unconscious. Which word grew out of it?
f: Jung was Freud's chosen successor until they fell out permanently over how much of the mind is sexual. He went on to argue that certain images recur across all cultures, and called them archetypes.

q: There was an Austrian psychologist. Focuses on inferiority, social interest, and striving. Which word grew out of it?
f: Adler broke with Freud over the same question and built a psychology around the drive to overcome feelings of inferiority. He gave us inferiority complex, one of the few psychiatric terms everyone uses correctly.

q: Which word meaning "automatic conditioned response" comes from a Russian physiologist?
f: Pavlov was studying digestion, not learning, and the dogs' drooling was ruining his measurements. He investigated the nuisance instead of eliminating it, and found conditioning. He was not, incidentally, ringing a bell — usually a metronome.

q: There was an American psychologist. Developed operant conditioning and behaviorism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Skinner trained pigeons to guide missiles during the Second World War, and the system worked — the military just could not bring itself to trust it. He also raised his daughter's early months in a heated, filtered climate-controlled crib.

q: There was a Swiss psychologist. Theory of cognitive development in children. Which word grew out of it?
f: Piaget worked out his stages of child development largely by watching his own three children very closely and writing down everything. He published his first scientific paper, on an albino sparrow, at the age of eleven.

q: "Maslowian" is named after a person.
f: Maslow never drew his hierarchy as a pyramid — someone else added that later, and the shape implies a rigidity he did not intend. He was interested in what healthy people do, when psychology mostly studied illness.

q: Which word meaning "relating to Descartes" comes from a French philosopher?
f: Descartes is supposed to have thought of coordinates while lying in bed watching a fly on the ceiling and wondering how to describe its position with numbers. Every graph you have ever drawn descends from that fly.

q: Which word meaning "ideal or non-romantic" comes from a Greek philosopher?
f: Platonic love, in Plato, meant a love that climbs from a particular person toward beauty and truth themselves. English flattened it into love without romance, which Plato would have considered the least interesting part.

q: There was a Greek philosopher. Based on Aristotle's philosophy and logic. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

q: Which word meaning "using guided questioning" comes from a Greek philosopher?
f: Socrates wrote nothing. Everything we have comes from students, chiefly Plato. His method was to ask questions until the other person discovered their own answer had a hole in it — which made him popular with the young and not with anyone else.

q: There was a Greek philosopher. Advocated rational pleasure and freedom from fear, later popularly associated with refined enjoyment. Which word grew out of it?
f: Epicurus taught that the greatest pleasure is freedom from pain and anxiety, and lived on bread, water and the occasional pot of cheese. English turned his name into a word for a gourmet, which reverses him completely.

q: Which word meaning "enduring hardship without complaint" comes from a Greek philosophy?
f: Named after a building. Zeno taught on a painted porch — a stoa — in Athens, and his followers were called the porch people. Their doctrine was that you control your judgements and nothing else.

q: "Cynic" is named after a place.
f: From the Greek for dog-like. The Cynics lived rough on purpose, and Diogenes is supposed to have accepted the insult and adopted it. Modern cynicism — assuming bad motives — is a long way from the original.

q: There was a Greek philosopher. Modern medical term referring to severe self-neglect and hoarding; the association with Diogenes is debated. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A modern term for extreme self-neglect and hoarding. It is arguably misnamed: Diogenes chose poverty deliberately and owned almost nothing, which is close to the opposite of hoarding.

q: There was a Greek mathematician. Father of geometry. Which word grew out of it?
f: Euclid's Elements ran as a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

q: Which word meaning "relating to right triangles" comes from a Greek mathematician?
f: Pythagoras ran what was half a school and half a secret society, with rules against eating beans. The theorem was known to Babylonian mathematicians a thousand years earlier; his followers may have supplied the first proof.

q: There was a Greek mathematician. Discoveries in geometry, mechanics, and buoyancy. Which word grew out of it?
f: Archimedes worked out how to measure the volume of a crown in the bath and, the story goes, ran into the street shouting. He was killed by a Roman soldier while drawing diagrams in the sand, reportedly telling him not to disturb them.

q: Which word meaning "normally distributed" comes from a German mathematician?
f: The bell curve turns up everywhere — heights, errors, exam marks — because adding up enough small independent effects produces it almost regardless of what those effects are. Gauss found it while analysing astronomical errors.

q: Which word meaning "binary logic" comes from an English mathematician?
f: George Boole reduced logic to algebra with two values, true and false, in 1854. He thought he was studying the laws of thought. Ninety years later it turned out he had written the mathematics of every computer ever built.

q: "Turing Machine" is named after a person.
f: An imaginary device with an infinite paper tape that reads, writes and moves one square at a time. Turing invented it to prove something impossible, and accidentally defined what a computer is.

q: Which name or term meaning "aI benchmark" comes from a computer scientist?
f: Turing called it the imitation game: if you cannot tell from a conversation whether you are talking to a person or a machine, he argued, asking whether the machine thinks is the wrong question.

q: There was a Hungarian-American mathematician. Stored-program computer architecture. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: The idea that a computer should keep its instructions in the same memory as its data — so a program can be changed without rewiring the machine. Von Neumann's name went on the report; several colleagues who helped were left off it.

q: Which word meaning "number sequence" comes from an Italian mathematician?
f: Fibonacci's real service to Europe was not the sequence but the digits: he brought Hindu-Arabic numerals west in 1202, and argued they beat Roman numerals for arithmetic. The rabbits were a small example in a long book.

q: There was a Greek mathematician. Method for finding the greatest common divisor. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A method for finding the largest number that divides two others, written down around 300 BC. It is the oldest algorithm still in everyday use — your web browser runs a version of it during encryption.

q: Which name or term meaning "non-orientable surface" comes from a German mathematician?
f: Give a strip of paper a half twist and join the ends: it now has one side and one edge. Mobius and another mathematician, Listing, both found it in 1858, independently, within months of each other.

q: There was a German mathematician. Closed non-orientable surface. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Klein called it a Kleinsche Flache — a Klein surface. Someone misread Flache as Flasche, which means bottle, and the mistranslation was too good to correct. It is a surface with no inside and no outside.

q: "Banach Space" is named after a place.
f: Banach and his colleagues did much of their mathematics in the Scottish Cafe in Lwow, writing problems in a notebook the waiters kept behind the bar. Prizes for solutions included a bottle of wine and, once, a live goose.

q: There was a German mathematician. Generalized geometry underlying Einstein's relativity. Which name or term grew out of it?
