f: Riemann described geometry on curved surfaces in a lecture in 1854, with no application in mind. Gauss, in the audience and hard to impress, was reportedly astonished. Sixty years later Einstein needed exactly that mathematics.

q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Major contributions across mathematics and mechanics. Which word grew out of it?
f: Euler went blind in his sixties and his output actually increased — he dictated to his sons. He produced so much that a project to publish his complete works has been running since 1911 and is still not finished.

q: There was a French mathematician. Differential operator central to physics. Which word grew out of it?
f: Asked by Napoleon why his book on the heavens never mentioned God, Laplace is said to have replied that he had no need of that hypothesis. The operator named after him turns up in heat flow, waves and quantum mechanics.

q: There was a French mathematician. Represented periodic functions as sums of sine and cosine waves. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Fourier showed any repeating wave can be built from simple sines added together — which is how audio compression works. He also worked out that the atmosphere warms the planet, describing the greenhouse effect in the 1820s.

q: There was a Swiss mathematician. Relationship between fluid speed and pressure. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Faster fluid means lower pressure. It is often used to explain how wings lift, which is only part of the story — the fuller answer involves the wing pushing air downwards, and physicists still argue about the best way to teach it.

q: There was an English statistician. Foundation of Bayesian probability. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Thomas Bayes never published it. A friend found the paper among his effects after his death and sent it to the Royal Society. It is now the mathematics behind spam filters, medical testing and most machine learning.

q: "Pareto Principle" is named after a person.
f: Pareto noticed that a fifth of Italy's population owned four-fifths of the land — then found the same lopsided split in his garden, where a fifth of the pea pods held most of the peas.

q: There was an American mathematician. Stable outcome in game theory where no player benefits from changing strategy alone. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A situation where nobody can do better by changing their own move alone. Nash wrote it up in a doctoral thesis of twenty-seven pages, won a Nobel Prize for it forty-four years later, and had a film made about his life.

q: There was a british economist. Advocated government intervention to stabilize economies. Which word grew out of it?
f: Keynes argued governments should spend in a downturn rather than tighten their belts. Told that markets would correct themselves eventually, he replied that in the long run we are all dead.

q: There was a british economist. Comparative advantage in international trade. Which word grew out of it?
f: Ricardo showed two countries both gain from trade even when one is better at making everything — each should do what it gives up least to make. It is counterintuitive enough that people still argue against it two centuries on.

q: There was an English economist. Predicted population growth would outstrip food supply. Which word grew out of it?
f: Malthus predicted population would outrun the food supply and reasoned it could only end in famine. He did not foresee fertiliser, mechanised farming or falling birth rates — so he was wrong, and influential anyway.

q: There was a German philosopher. Pertaining specifically to Marx's original economic and philosophical writings. Which word grew out of it?
f: Marxian points at the analysis; Marxist points at the politics. Economists who use his tools to study capitalism without wanting to overthrow it tend to insist on the first word.

q: There was a German philosopher. Political and economic ideology derived from Marx's theories. Which word grew out of it?
f: Marx spent his most productive years in the Reading Room of the British Museum, in poverty, supported largely by Engels. He is buried in Highgate Cemetery in London, a short walk from where he wrote.

q: "Leninism" is named after a place.
f: Lenin argued a revolution needed a small disciplined party to lead it rather than waiting for the workers to rise on their own. He returned to Russia in 1917 in a sealed train, permitted through Germany by an enemy hoping to destabilise Russia.

q: There was a Soviet leader. Characterized by centralized authority, forced collectivization, and extensive state control. Which word grew out of it?
f: Stalin was a name he chose — it means man of steel. He was born Ioseb Jughashvili in Georgia and trained briefly as a priest. His rule is associated with forced collectivisation and mass political repression.

q: There was a Chinese revolutionary. Adapted Marxism-Leninism with emphasis on the peasantry and prolonged revolutionary struggle. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mao adapted a theory built for industrial workers to a country that was overwhelmingly rural, arguing revolution would come from the peasantry. It was a substantial departure from what Marx had written.

q: There was a Russian revolutionary. Advocated "permanent revolution" and opposed Stalin's policies. Which word grew out of it?
f: Trotsky organised the Red Army, lost the power struggle after Lenin's death, and was exiled. He was killed in Mexico in 1940 by an assassin with an ice axe, while his followers argued for permanent revolution.

q: Which word meaning "relating to Gandhi's philosophy" comes from an Indian independence leader?
f: Gandhi's satyagraha meant refusing to cooperate with injustice while refusing to answer it with violence. In 1930 he walked 240 miles to the sea to make salt, breaking a British monopoly with a handful of mud.

q: There was a british Prime Minister. Associated with privatization, deregulation, and free-market reforms. Which word grew out of it?
f: Britain's first woman prime minister and its longest-serving of the twentieth century. Her programme of privatisation and deregulation still divides the country, which is why the word gets used as praise and insult in equal measure.

q: There was an u.S. President. Popular term for supply-side economics pursued during the 1980s. Which word grew out of it?
f: The argument that cutting taxes at the top increases total revenue by growing the economy. A journalist coined the word on air; the administration disliked it at first and then adopted it.

q: "Bonapartism" is named after a person.
f: Rule by a strong leader who claims to speak directly for the people, over the heads of parliaments. Napoleon held plebiscites to confirm his power, which made his authority look popular and left nobody able to challenge it.

q: There was a German chancellor. Associated with Realpolitik, German unification, and the modern welfare state. Which word grew out of it?
f: Bismarck unified Germany through what he called blood and iron, then introduced the world's first national health insurance and old-age pensions — partly to undercut the socialists. Ruthlessness and welfare, from the same man.

q: There was a Czech writer. His fiction portrays bewildering bureaucracy and existential anxiety. Which word grew out of it?
f: Not merely bureaucratic — Kafkaesque means the system is impossible to argue with because nobody in it will admit to being in charge. Kafka asked his friend to burn all his manuscripts. His friend published them instead.

q: Which word meaning "harsh, impoverished conditions" comes from an English novelist?
f: Dickens was twelve when his father went to debtors' prison and he was sent to paste labels on bottles in a factory. He told almost nobody for the rest of his life, and wrote about it in every book he produced.

q: Which word meaning "dramatic" comes from an English playwright?
f: Shakespeare is the first recorded user of something like 1,700 English words — though first recorded often means only that his plays survived and the pamphlets did not. Either way, he was not shy about inventing one.

q: There was an ancient Greek poet. Refers to the style or epic grandeur of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*. Which word grew out of it?
f: We do not know whether Homer was one person, several, or a tradition. The poems were composed to be recited from memory, and their repeated phrases — swift-footed Achilles, the wine-dark sea — are the scaffolding that made that possible.

q: There was an English poet. Style associated with *Paradise Lost* and elevated blank verse. Which word grew out of it?
f: Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost at night in his head, dictating each morning to whoever was available. Twelve books of epic verse, and he never saw a line of it written down.

q: "Chaucerian" is named after a place.
f: Chaucer wrote in English when serious writers used Latin or French, and largely settled which English would become standard. He also held a day job as a customs official on the London docks.

q: There was an Irish satirist. Sharp political and social satire modeled on *Gulliver's Travels*. Which word grew out of it?
f: In A Modest Proposal, Swift suggested in flat reasonable prose that the Irish poor should sell their children as food. Readers who missed the satire were exactly the point — he was mimicking the economists of his day.

q: There was an English poet. Romantic, rebellious, melancholic hero archetype. Which word grew out of it?
f: Brooding, brilliant, self-destructive and impossible to advise. Byron largely invented the type by living it; a former lover called him mad, bad and dangerous to know, and the phrase has followed him for two centuries.

q: There was a writer. Modern expression describing situations where denial itself is treated as evidence of guilt. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An accusation built so that denying it counts as proof — your protest shows how deep the problem goes. Named for Kafka's Trial, where the accused is never told the charge and cannot therefore answer it.

q: Which word meaning "impractically idealistic" comes from a cervantes' fictional knight?
f: Curiously, the word is pronounced quick-SOT-ic in English while the character is Key-HO-tay in Spanish — the adjective went one way and the name the other. Both mean chasing something noble and impossible.

q: Which word meaning "miserly person" comes from a dickens character?
f: Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in six weeks because he needed money, and published it himself. It has never been out of print, and Scrooge's name became the word for a miser within a few years.

q: Which word meaning "excessively optimistic person" comes from an eleanor H. Porter's heroine?
f: Pollyanna plays the glad game: find something to be pleased about in any disaster. The book was a bestseller in 1913, and her name turned into a mild insult for optimism that refuses to look at facts.

q: "Lothario" is named after a person.
f: From a 1703 play, The Fair Penitent, where Lothario seduces and abandons the heroine. He is on stage for a fraction of the play and is the only thing anybody remembers about it.

q: There was a Venetian adventurer. Famous for numerous romantic affairs documented in his memoirs. Which word grew out of it?
f: Casanova was a soldier, spy, violinist, and briefly a librarian at a Bohemian castle, which is where he wrote his memoirs out of boredom. They run to twelve volumes, and the romance is a small part of them.

q: Which word meaning "romantic male lover" comes from a shakespeare character?
f: Romeo is in love with a different girl, Rosaline, when the play opens, and forgets her the instant he sees Juliet. The whole tragedy takes place in about four days.

q: There was a Spanish literary character. Became the universal symbol of a seducer. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: He first appears in a Spanish play of 1630 and has been rewritten ever since — by Moliere, Mozart, Byron and Shaw. Almost every version ends with him dragged off to hell, which has not dented his popularity.

q: There was a character in *Trilby*. Manipulated others through psychological domination. Which word grew out of it?
f: In the 1894 novel Trilby, Svengali hypnotises a tone-deaf girl into a great singer who cannot perform without him. The book was a sensation, and gave English both a word and, from a character's hat, the trilby.

q: Which word meaning "enormous" comes from a giant in Rabelais' novels?
f: Rabelais's giant Gargantua was born calling for a drink, and in one episode a whole army shelters from the rain under his tongue. He is also, in the same book, sent to school and taught rather well.

q: There was a voltaire's *Candide*. Absurdly optimistic philosopher believing everything happens for the best. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dr Pangloss insists this is the best of all possible worlds while being hanged, dissected and enslaved in succession. Voltaire was mocking a real philosophical position, and did such a thorough job that the name became the argument against it.

q: "Rip Van Winkle" is named after a place.
f: He falls asleep in the Catskills, wakes twenty years later, and wanders into town still cheering for a king who has been gone since the Revolution. Washington Irving wrote it in England, homesick, in 1819.

q: Which word meaning "highly analytical" comes from a conan Doyle detective?
f: Conan Doyle modelled Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could deduce a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall and public outrage forced him to bring him back.

q: There was a holmes' companion. Explanation from within a fictional universe. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Watsonian explanation stays inside the story — Watson made a mistake in his notes. A Doylist one steps outside it — Conan Doyle forgot. Fans of every fictional world now use both terms.

q: There was a holmes' adversary. Criminal mastermind opposing the detective. Which word grew out of it?
f: Moriarty appears properly in one story and is mentioned in a handful of others. Conan Doyle invented him specifically as someone impressive enough to kill Holmes off with, and he has loomed over the canon ever since.

q: There was an English philosopher. Belief in strong centralized authority to prevent chaos. Which word grew out of it?
f: Without a strong state, Hobbes wrote, life would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short. He was writing during the English Civil War, which rather explains the mood.

q: There was an English philosopher. Emphasized natural rights and government by consent. Which word grew out of it?
f: Locke argued government is legitimate only by the consent of the governed, and that people may replace one that fails them. Jefferson borrowed the structure of that argument almost directly for the Declaration of Independence.

q: There was a French philosopher. Advocated the "general will" and natural human goodness. Which word grew out of it?
f: Rousseau opened his most famous book with man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains. He also wrote a celebrated treatise on educating children while placing all five of his own in a foundling hospital.

q: "Confucian" is named after a person.
f: Confucius held only minor office and considered himself a failure. His students wrote down his conversations after his death, and those notes shaped Chinese government, family life and education for two thousand years.

q: There was a Chinese philosopher. Based on harmony with the Tao ("the Way"). Which word grew out of it?
f: The Tao Te Ching opens by saying that the Way which can be named is not the true Way — a book that begins by warning you it cannot do its job. It is one of the most translated texts in the world.

q: Which word meaning "relating to Buddhism" comes from a religious teacher?
f: Buddha is not a name but a title meaning the awakened one. Siddhartha Gautama was a prince who left the palace, saw sickness, age and death for the first time, and spent the rest of his life on what to do about them.

q: The word "Christian" is named after…?
f: The book of Acts records that followers were first called Christians at Antioch — and it was probably a nickname given by outsiders rather than one they chose. They adopted it anyway.

q: There was a historical English term. Former English term for Muslims; now considered outdated because Muslims worship God, not Muhammad. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An outdated English term for Muslims, formed by analogy with Christian. It was dropped because it misdescribes the faith: Muhammad is regarded as a prophet, not an object of worship. Muslim is the correct word.

q: Which word meaning "protestant denomination" comes from a German reformer?
f: Luther set out ninety-five points for debate in 1517 and, thanks to the new printing press, they were all over Germany within weeks. He was arguing for reform, not a new church — the split happened anyway.

q: There was a French theologian. Emphasized predestination and divine sovereignty. Which word grew out of it?
f: Calvin turned Geneva into a model reformed city, strictly governed. The doctrine that God has already chosen the saved gave rise, oddly, to a famously hard-working culture — since worldly success might be a sign of it.

q: "Wesleyan" is named after a place.
f: John Wesley and his Oxford friends were mocked as Methodists for the methodical way they organised their prayer and study. They adopted the insult. Wesley rode an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback preaching.

q: There was a christian monk. Monastic order following the Rule of St. Benedict. Which word grew out of it?
f: Benedict's sixth-century Rule set out how a monastery should divide the day between prayer, work and reading. It is also a liqueur — made to a recipe a wine merchant claimed to have found in an old monastic manuscript.

q: There was a Spanish priest. Founded the Order of Preachers. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dominic founded an order of travelling preachers. Latin-speaking wits nicknamed them Domini canes — the hounds of the Lord — a pun the order seems to have enjoyed, since dogs turn up in their art.

q: Which word meaning "religious order" comes from an Italian saint?
f: Francis of Assisi gave away his inheritance, including the clothes he was wearing, and founded an order on absolute poverty. He is said to have preached to birds, and is now the patron saint of animals and ecology.

q: There was a Spanish priest. Society of Jesus devoted to education and missionary work. Which word grew out of it?
f: Ignatius Loyola was a soldier until a cannonball shattered his leg and he read the only books available during a long recovery. The order he founded became the great educational network of the Catholic world.

q: There was a christian theologian. Philosophy and theology derived from Augustine's writings. Which word grew out of it?
f: Augustine's Confessions is arguably the first autobiography in the Western tradition — a man examining his own mind in public. He prayed, famously, for chastity, but not yet.

q: There was a medieval philosopher. Scholastic philosophy integrating Aristotle with Christian theology. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aquinas set out to reconcile Aristotle with Christian theology and produced a work of immense length. Near the end of his life he had an experience after which he stopped writing, saying everything he had written seemed like straw.

q: "Machiavellian" is named after a person.
f: Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain who smiles while calculating exactly how to use you.

q: There was a Norwegian politician. Collaborated with Nazi Germany during WWII. Which word grew out of it?
f: Vidkun Quisling helped Germany occupy Norway in 1940, and his name became the English word for a traitor within about a week — while he was still alive to read it. He was executed in 1945.

q: Which word meaning "organized refusal to deal with someone" comes from an Irish land agent?
f: Captain Boycott was a land agent in Ireland who evicted tenants in 1880. The community simply stopped dealing with him — no worker, no shop, no post. He had to import labour under police guard to save his harvest, and left.

q: There was a virginia landowner. The term likely derives from extrajudicial punishment associated with "Lynch's Law.". Which word grew out of it?
f: Probably from Charles Lynch, a Virginia judge whose unofficial wartime court handed out floggings. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and became the name for one of America's darkest habits.

q: Which word meaning "manipulation of electoral boundaries" comes from a governor of Massachusetts?
f: In 1812 Governor Elbridge Gerry approved a district shaped so oddly that a newspaper drew wings on it and called it a salamander. His name was hard-G — so strictly it should be gerrymander with a hard sound, which nobody says.

q: Which word meaning "outline profile image" comes from a French finance minister?
f: Etienne de Silhouette was finance minister for eight months and imposed such harsh economies that anything cheap was mocked as being a la Silhouette. Cut-paper profiles were the cheapest portraits going, and the insult stuck to them.

q: Which word meaning "independent-minded person" comes from a texas rancher?
f: Samuel Maverick was a Texas rancher who did not brand his cattle. Neighbours took to calling any unbranded animal a maverick — and then any person who refuses to carry anybody's mark.

q: "Guillotine" is named after a place.
f: Joseph-Ignace Guillotin opposed the death penalty and proposed the machine as a humane step toward abolishing it. He was appalled to have it named after him, and his family later petitioned unsuccessfully to have the name changed.

q: Which word meaning "one-piece athletic garment" comes from a French trapeze artist?
f: Jules Leotard invented the flying trapeze and performed in a knitted one-piece that let the audience see the body work. He also inspired the song about the daring young man on the flying trapeze.

q: Which word meaning "knitted sweater" comes from a british general?
f: The seventh Earl of Cardigan led the Charge of the Light Brigade — a catastrophic order, gallantly obeyed. He came home a celebrity, and the knitted waistcoat his officers wore in the Crimea took his name.

q: Which word meaning "waterproof boot" comes from a british general?
f: The duke asked his shoemaker for a boot tough enough for the field and neat enough for the evening. It became so fashionable that gentlemen wore them everywhere; the rubber version arrived decades later.

q: There was a british field marshal. Sleeve style designed to accommodate his amputated arm. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lord Raglan lost his right arm at Waterloo, and asked for his sleeve to be cut in one piece running to the collar so he could dress unaided. The design turned out to allow better movement and is now standard on sportswear.

q: Which word meaning "vacuum cleaner" comes from an American businessman?
f: William Hoover made leather goods. A department-store janitor named Murray Spangler built the vacuum cleaner out of a fan, a pillowcase and a broom handle — then sold the patent to Hoover, his wife's cousin.

q: Which word meaning "photocopy" comes from a company?
f: From Greek xeros graphos, dry writing, because the process needed no liquid ink. The inventor was turned down by more than twenty companies before one took it on. Xerox now sends letters asking people not to use it as a verb.

q: Which word meaning "facial tissue" comes from a company?
f: Launched in 1924 as a disposable cloth for removing cold cream. Customers kept writing in to say they were blowing their noses on it instead, so the company changed the advertising and the market.

q: Which word meaning "vacuum flask" comes from a company?
f: James Dewar invented the vacuum flask and never patented it. A German glassware firm did, ran a public competition to name it, and a resident of Munich won with thermos — Greek for hot.

q: Which word meaning "moving staircase" comes from a company?
f: Otis owned the trademark and lost it by using the word generically in its own advertising. A court ruled in 1950 that the company had turned its own brand into an ordinary noun.

q: Which word meaning "acetylsalicylic acid" comes from a company?
f: Bayer's trademark, lost as a war reparation — the Treaty of Versailles handed the name to the Allies in 1919. It is still a Bayer trademark in Germany and generic in Britain and America.

q: Which word meaning "toy" comes from a company?
f: The toy is thousands of years old, but the name is Filipino. Pedro Flores brought it to America in the 1920s; Donald Duncan bought his company, trademarked the word, and eventually lost the trademark for being too successful.

q: Which word meaning "flying disc" comes from a company?
f: Students at Yale threw empty pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company. When Wham-O started selling a plastic flying disc they heard the students shouting Frisbie, respelled it, and used it as the brand.

q: Which word meaning "table tennis" comes from a company?
f: An English firm trademarked the sound the game makes. Everyone else had to call it table tennis, which is why the sport's governing body uses the duller name and the rest of us do not.

q: "Velcro" is named after a place.
f: George de Mestral came back from a walk and looked at the burrs stuck to his dog under a microscope — tiny hooks catching in loops. He spent eight years reproducing it, and named it from velours and crochet.

q: Which name or term meaning "search the internet" comes from a technology company?
f: The company itself lobbied against this, worried that a brand which becomes a verb can lose its trademark. A court disagreed in 2017, ruling the name still identified the company. The verb had already won.

q: Which name or term meaning "digitally alter an image" comes from a software?
f: Written by two brothers, one a PhD student and one working at Industrial Light and Magic. Adobe's style guide insists it is a proper adjective and asks people not to say photoshopped, which nobody has ever obeyed.

q: There was an inventor. Whirlpool technology became associated with relaxation and hydrotherapy. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Candido Jacuzzi built the first pump so his young son could have arthritis hydrotherapy at home. The company only realised it had a leisure product years later, when customers started asking for the pump without the illness.

q: There was a mythological king. Alternate adjective occasionally used instead of *Sisyphean*. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An occasional variant of Sisyphean. Both describe the same boulder rolling back down the same hill forever — and the fact that English cannot settle on one spelling is itself faintly Sisyphean.

q: Which word meaning "excessively harsh" comes from an Athenian lawgiver?
f: Asked why the penalty for petty theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could think of nothing worse for the large ones. Athenians said his laws were written in blood rather than ink.

q: There was a biblical king. Celebrated for wisdom and fair judgment. Which word grew out of it?
f: Two women each claimed the same baby. Solomon called for a sword and offered them half each. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.

q: "Judaic" is named after a person.
f: From Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled from the tribe to a kingdom to a Roman province, and from there into the words Judaism and Jewish.

q: There was a brother of Moses. Pertains to the hereditary priesthood descended from Aaron. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aaron was Moses's brother and did the talking, because Moses said he was slow of speech. The priesthood descended from him, so the family that spoke for Moses ended up speaking for everybody.

q: Which word meaning "relating to Moses" comes from a biblical prophet?
f: Careful — this is the Moses word, meaning of his law. The mosaic made of coloured tiles is unrelated: that one comes from the Muses, via rooms decorated in their honour. Two identical English words, two different origins.

q: There was a biblical king. Refers to the royal lineage of David. Which word grew out of it?
f: David was a shepherd boy who became king, and the line descending from him mattered enormously to later writers — both Gospel genealogies take care to route Jesus back to him.

q: Which word meaning "giant opponent" comes from a philistine giant?
f: The giant loses because David refuses to fight the way giants fight. He turns down armour, keeps his sling, and wins at a distance — which makes the story less about size than about choosing your own contest.

q: There was a biblical figure. Endured immense suffering while remaining faithful. Which word grew out of it?
f: Job loses his family, his wealth and his health, and keeps asking why. The book never really answers him. The patience of Job is proverbial, though anyone who reads it notices he complains a great deal.

q: Which word meaning "betrayer" comes from a disciple of Jesus?
f: Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later, almost nobody names a child Judas.

q: "Samaritan" is named after a place.
f: The point of the parable is who the helper was: Samaritans and Judeans despised each other. A modern retelling would have to pick whichever group the listener likes least, which is uncomfortable, and deliberate.

q: There was an American general. Defected to the British during the American Revolution. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Arnold was one of the ablest American generals of the Revolution before he changed sides. There is a monument at Saratoga to his wounded leg — a boot, with no name on it, honouring the part of him that stayed loyal.

q: Which name or term meaning "romantic balcony" comes from a shakespeare character?
f: There is no balcony in Shakespeare's text. Juliet appears at a window; the word never occurs in the play. The balcony was added by an eighteenth-century adaptation and has been there ever since.

q: Which word meaning "creator of something dangerous" comes from a mary Shelley's scientist?
f: Frankenstein is the scientist, not the creature — the monster has no name at all. Mary Shelley was eighteen when she wrote it, during a wet summer holiday where the group agreed to each write a ghost story.

q: Which word meaning "book of maps" comes from a titan?
f: Mercator put a picture of Atlas holding up the world on the front of his collection of maps in 1595, and the name transferred from the picture to the book. Atlas himself held up the sky, not the Earth.

q: Which name or term meaning "fatal weakness" comes from a Greek warrior?
f: His mother dipped him in the river Styx holding him by the heel, and that one patch stayed dry. Homer never mentions this — the heel appears in later versions, long after the Iliad.

q: There was a goddess of health. Associated with disease prevention and cleanliness. Which word grew out of it?
f: Daughter of the god of medicine, and her job was keeping people well rather than curing them. Her sister Panacea handled cures. Prevention and treatment, split between two sisters, which is roughly how medicine still divides.

q: "Thanatos" is named after a person.
f: The gentle death, as opposed to violent death, who was his brother. Freud later borrowed the name for a supposed drive toward destruction — a use the Greeks would not have recognised at all.

q: Which word meaning "massive" comes from a Greek primordial gods?
f: The Titans were the generation of gods before the Olympians, and they lost. Naming the largest ship afloat after a family famous chiefly for being overthrown was, in hindsight, an odd choice.

q: Which word meaning "majestic" comes from a home of Greek gods?
f: Mount Olympus was where the gods lived; Olympia, where the games were held, is a different place about two hundred miles away. English uses Olympian for both the majestic sense and the athletic one.

q: Which word meaning "powerful female warrior" comes from a mythical warrior women?
f: The river was named by a Spanish explorer who reported being attacked by women warriors. The bookshop was named after the river, because its founder wanted something that suggested enormous scale and started with A.

q: Which word meaning "austere" comes from a Greek city-state?
f: Spartan boys left home at seven for military training and were underfed on purpose, so they would learn to steal food. A boy caught stealing was punished — not for the theft, but for being caught.

q: There was an ancient Greek city. Renowned for ornate architecture and capitals. Which word grew out of it?
f: Corinth was rich, and its architecture showed it. In Victorian England a Corinthian also meant a wealthy amateur sportsman — which is why an English football club founded by gentlemen amateurs is called Corinthian.

q: There was an ancient Greek region. One of the classical Greek architectural orders. Which word grew out of it?
f: The order with the scrolls at the top, like a ram's horns or a rolled scroll. Greek writers considered it the feminine order to the Doric's masculine — slimmer, more decorated, and set on a base.

q: "Doric" is named after a place.
f: The plain one — no base, no scrolls, just fluting and a flat top. The Parthenon is Doric. It is the oldest of the three orders and the one that looks most like a stone version of a wooden post.

q: There was a Greek city. Most elaborate classical architectural order. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: The most decorated of the three, with carved acanthus leaves. The story goes that a sculptor saw a basket left on a girl's grave with an acanthus plant growing up around it, and built a column out of the image.

q: Which word meaning "intricate or excessively complex" comes from an ancient city?
f: The Eastern Roman Empire ran for a thousand years after Rome fell, with a court so layered in ceremony and intrigue that its name became the English word for anything needlessly complicated.

q: Which word meaning "uncultured person" comes from an ancient people?
f: The Philistines were a real people with cities, pottery and trade. Matthew Arnold popularised the cultural insult in the 1860s, aiming it at the English middle classes — so an ancient nation is now a synonym for bad taste.

q: There was a Greek city-state. Reflects austere Spartan lifestyle. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: The famous dish was black broth — pork boiled in blood and vinegar. A visitor from another city tried it and said he now understood why Spartans were so willing to die in battle.

q: There was a Greek sanctuary. Home of Apollo's oracle known for ambiguous prophecies. Which word grew out of it?
f: The oracle told Croesus that if he attacked Persia he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Delphic answers were always true and almost never useful.

q: Which name or term meaning "costly victory" comes from a king of Epirus?
f: Pyrrhus beat the Romans twice and lost so many men doing it that he reportedly said one more such victory and we are undone. Rome could replace its losses; he could not.

q: "Laconic" is named after a person.
f: Philip of Macedon warned Sparta that if he entered Laconia he would raze it to the ground. The Spartans sent back a one-word reply: If. He did not invade.

q: Which name or term meaning "laryngeal prominence" comes from a biblical first man?
f: A medieval story held that a piece of the forbidden fruit stuck in Adam's throat and left a lump in every man since. The Bible never says the fruit was an apple either — that came from a Latin pun.

q: There was a biblical figure. Pertaining to mankind's earliest state. Which word grew out of it?
f: Adam simply means man or earth in Hebrew — he is named after the ground he was made from. Adamic language means the supposed original speech of humanity, before Babel scattered it.

q: There was a biblical patriarch. Pertaining to the Flood or Noah's covenant. Which word grew out of it?
f: After the flood, the covenant with Noah is made with all humanity rather than one people, and the rainbow is its sign. Flood stories appear across Mesopotamian literature, including one a thousand years older.

q: Which word meaning "relating to Abraham" comes from a biblical patriarch?
f: Judaism, Christianity and Islam all trace themselves to Abraham, which is why they are grouped under his name. It is one of the few labels all three traditions accept.

q: Which word meaning "one restored from apparent death" comes from a biblical figure?
f: Raised after four days in the tomb. The name is now used for anything that comes back when it should not: Lazarus taxa in biology are species that reappear in the fossil record long after apparently going extinct.

q: Which name or term meaning "skeptic" comes from a disciple of Jesus?
f: Thomas said he would not believe without putting his hand in the wounds. He is remembered for the doubt rather than for what he did next, which was to believe immediately once he was shown.

q: "Prodigal" is named after a place.
f: Prodigal means wastefully extravagant, not returning — the son is prodigal in the first half of the parable, before he comes home. People use it to mean the coming back, which is exactly backwards.

q: There was a biblical follower of Jesus. Historically associated (incorrectly in tradition) with penitence. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mary Magdalene was identified with a penitent sinner by a pope in 591, on no textual basis, and the Church formally separated them again in 1969. Her name also gave English maudlin — from paintings of her weeping.

q: There was a jewish religious sect. New Testament portrayal emphasized legalism and hypocrisy. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Pharisees were a reform movement that made scripture accessible outside the Temple, and rabbinic Judaism descends from them. The English insult comes entirely from how the Gospels portray their arguments.

q: There was a jewish priestly sect. Influential group in Second Temple Judaism. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, and they rejected any belief in resurrection. When the Temple was destroyed in AD 70 they vanished with it, leaving the Pharisees to shape everything that came after.

q: There was an ancient Mesopotamian city. Symbol of grandeur, decadence, and exile in biblical tradition. Which word grew out of it?
f: Babylon really did have the scale the legends suggest — walls, ziggurats, and possibly gardens. Its reputation for decadence comes mostly from the people it conquered, who had every reason to be unkind.

q: Which word meaning "confused mixture of voices or languages" comes from a biblical story?
f: The Babylonians called their city bab-ilu, gate of the god. Hebrew writers heard it as balal, to confuse, and built the story of the scattered languages around the pun. The tower was probably a real ziggurat.

q: Which word meaning "emperor or absolute ruler" comes from a Roman ruler?
f: One family name became the word for supreme ruler in half of Europe, and outlasted the empire by fifteen centuries. Caesar himself was never emperor — the title did not exist yet when he was killed.

q: "Kaiser" is named after a person.
f: German emperors were Kaisers right up to 1918, and the word is Caesar worn down by two thousand years of German mouths. The pronunciation is actually closer to the original Latin than the English Caesar is.

q: Which word meaning "russian emperor" comes from a via Latin *Caesar*?
f: Russian rulers took the same Roman title, arguing that after Constantinople fell Moscow was the third Rome. English still uses it for anyone put in charge of a problem — a drugs tsar, a productivity tsar.

q: There was a Roman dictator. Introduced sweeping calendar reform in 45 BC. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Caesar's reform in 45 BC required one transitional year of 445 days to drag the calendar back into line with the seasons. Romans called it the year of confusion.

q: Which name or term meaning "modern civil calendar" comes from a pope?
f: By 1582 the Julian year was ten days out of step, so October simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752 and had to skip eleven.

q: There was a Roman general. Avoided pitched battles to wear Hannibal down gradually. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult. After Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack him head-on, it became a compliment, and Fabian has meant winning by patience ever since.

q: There was a Roman statesman. Returned to farming after serving as dictator. Which word grew out of it?
f: Given absolute power to save Rome, Cincinnatus won the war in about a fortnight, resigned, and went back to his farm. George Washington was compared to him constantly — and an American city is named for the society that admired him.

q: There was a Greek philosopher. Founded the school of philosophical skepticism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pyrrho argued you should suspend judgement about everything, since certainty is not available. Sceptics after him used his name. He is not the Pyrrhus of the costly victory — two different Greeks, frequently confused.

q: "Stoicism" is named after a place.
f: Named after a painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught. The core claim is that you control your own judgements and nothing else — and two of its greatest writers were an enslaved man and a Roman emperor.

q: There was a Greek philosophers. Rejected wealth and social convention. Which word grew out of it?
f: From the Greek for dog-like, meant as an insult about living rough in public. The Cynics accepted it. Their point was that convention is arbitrary; modern cynicism, assuming everyone is selfish, is a much later invention.

q: There was a Greek teachers. Known for persuasive rhetoric, sometimes regardless of truth. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Sophists were paid teachers of rhetoric in a city where winning an argument in court could save your life. Plato disliked them intensely, wrote the dialogues that survived, and their name has been an insult ever since.

q: Which name or term meaning "question-based teaching" comes from a Greek philosopher?
f: Socrates claimed to know nothing and asked questions until the other person found the hole in their own answer. Athens executed him for it, which suggests the method works better than it is welcomed.

q: Which name or term meaning "plane geometry" comes from a Greek mathematician?
f: Euclid's fifth postulate, about parallel lines, bothered mathematicians for two thousand years because it looked like it should be provable. It is not — and dropping it produces the curved geometries relativity needs.

q: There was a Greek inventor. Device for raising water. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A spiral inside a tube: turn it and water climbs uphill. It is still used to move water and grain today, and versions have been found that predate Archimedes — he may have described it rather than invented it.

q: Which name or term meaning "fundamental geometry theorem" comes from a Greek mathematician?
f: Babylonian tablets show the relationship a thousand years before Pythagoras. What his followers may have supplied is the proof — the argument that it must hold for every right triangle, not just the ones anyone measured.

q: "Eratosthenes Sieve" is named after a person.
f: Cross out every multiple of two, then of three, and keep going; what survives are the primes. The same man measured the circumference of the Earth using shadows in two cities and got within a few per cent.

q: There was a Greek mathematician. Ancient algorithm for finding the greatest common divisor. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Keep replacing the larger number with the remainder until nothing is left over. It is the oldest algorithm still in daily use, and a version of it runs every time your browser sets up an encrypted connection.

q: Which name or term meaning "medical ethical oath" comes from a Greek physician?
f: First, do no harm is not in it. That phrase comes from another of his works entirely. The actual oath swears by Apollo and includes clauses about not using a knife, which modern surgeons have quietly set aside.

q: There was a Greek physician. Classical description of facial appearance before death. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Hippocrates described the sunken, drawn appearance of a face in the last stage of illness so precisely that the description was still being used two thousand years later, before machines could measure anything.

q: There was a Greek physician. Medical practices based on Galen's teachings. Which word grew out of it?
f: Galen dissected pigs and apes because Roman law forbade human dissection, then described human anatomy from what he found. His errors went uncorrected for fourteen hundred years, because questioning Galen was unthinkable.

q: There was a Persian physician. Based on the influential *Canon of Medicine*. Which word grew out of it?
f: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was the standard European medical textbook for six centuries — longer than it was used in the world that produced it. He wrote it in Persia around 1025.

q: There was a Flemish anatomist. Founder of modern human anatomy. Which word grew out of it?
f: Vesalius dissected human bodies himself rather than lecturing while an assistant did the cutting, and found more than two hundred places where Galen was wrong. He published at twenty-eight and was attacked for it immediately.

q: "Harveyan" is named after a place.
f: Harvey proved blood circulates by simple arithmetic: the heart pumps more blood in an hour than the whole body contains, so it cannot be constantly made and consumed. It must go round. His practice suffered for saying so.

q: There was a british surgeon. Introduced antiseptic surgical techniques. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lister sprayed carbolic acid in operating theatres and death rates collapsed. Surgeons resented the implication that they carried infection on their own hands, and adoption took years longer than the evidence warranted.

q: There was an English physician. Exhibiting features of Parkinson's disease. Which word grew out of it?
f: The tremor Parkinson described is at its worst at rest and eases when the hand does something — the reverse of most tremors. That detail is still one of the first things a neurologist looks for.

q: Which word meaning "exceptionally handsome man" comes from a beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite?
f: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story travelled west from Phoenicia. So calling a handsome man an Adonis is a compliment in a language almost nobody using it knows.

q: Which word meaning "step-by-step computational procedure" comes from a Persian mathematician?
f: From al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician of the ninth century. His name latinised to Algoritmi. Another of his book titles gave English a second word — al-jabr became algebra.

q: Which word meaning "unit of electric current" comes from a French physicist?
f: Ampere founded the study of electromagnetism in a few weeks of intense work after hearing that a current deflects a compass needle. His father had been guillotined during the Revolution when he was eighteen.

q: Which word meaning "tactile writing system" comes from a French educator?
f: Louis Braille was blinded at three by an accident in his father's workshop. At fifteen he adapted a military code for reading messages in the dark into a six-dot alphabet. His school did not adopt it until after his death.

q: "Chauvinism" is named after a person.
f: Nicolas Chauvin was supposedly a soldier so devoted to Napoleon that he stayed loyal after everyone else gave up. Historians have never found evidence he existed. The word may be named after a man who was never born.

q: Which word meaning "stimulate into action" comes from an Italian physician?
f: Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch with electricity and concluded animals carry their own vital force. Volta disagreed, and invented the battery to prove it. Galvani was wrong, and English kept his name anyway.

q: There was a Scottish engineer. Revolutionized road-building with compacted crushed stone. Which word grew out of it?
f: McAdam worked out that a road needs no heavy stone foundation if it is raised, drained, and surfaced with small angular stones that lock together under traffic. Add tar to keep the dust down and you get tarmac.

q: There was a French military officer. Known for relentless drilling and strict discipline. Which word grew out of it?
f: Jean Martinet drilled Louis XIV's infantry into the best in Europe and was loathed for it. He was killed at the siege of Duisburg in 1672 by his own side's artillery, which some of his troops are said to have found fitting.

q: Which word meaning "grand tomb" comes from a ruler of Caria?
f: Mausolus ruled a small kingdom and his widow built him a tomb so vast it became one of the Seven Wonders. It stood for sixteen centuries, was destroyed by earthquakes, and its stone was carted off to build a castle.

q: Which word meaning "arch-rival" comes from a Greek goddess of retribution?
f: Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

q: There was a daughter of Asclepius. Represented universal healing in Greek mythology. Which word grew out of it?
f: Panacea and Hygieia were sisters, daughters of the god of medicine — one the cure for everything, the other the prevention. English kept both, and uses panacea almost entirely to say that no such thing exists.

q: "Sandwich" is named after a place.
f: The Earl of Sandwich asked for meat between bread so he could keep working — or keep gambling, depending on who is telling it. The gambling version comes from a political opponent, so it may be an insult that stuck.

q: Which word meaning "musical instrument" comes from a Belgian instrument maker?
f: Adolphe Sax survived falling from a third floor, swallowing a pin, drinking acid by mistake and a gunpowder explosion, all before adulthood. His mother said he was a child doomed to misfortune. He invented the saxophone at thirty.

q: There was a Greek herald. His voice was said by Homer to equal that of fifty ordinary men. Which word grew out of it?
f: Homer says the herald Stentor could shout as loudly as fifty men together. In one version he challenges a god to a shouting match, loses, and dies of it — which is a very specific way to go.

q: There was a wealthy Greek colony. Celebrated for luxury, pleasure, and extravagance. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sybaris was so wealthy that its citizens were said to have banned noisy trades from the city so nobody's sleep was disturbed. A rival city destroyed it in 510 BC and diverted a river over the ruins.

q: Which word meaning "unit of magnetic field strength" comes from a serbian-American inventor?
f: Tesla claimed to see detailed visions of his inventions before building them, and tested some purely in his head. He died in a New York hotel room, owing money, having given away most of the patents that made others rich.

q: Which word meaning "unit of power" comes from a Scottish engineer?
f: Watt did not invent the steam engine — he made an existing one three times more efficient by adding a separate condenser. He also coined horsepower, as a sales device to explain his engines to people who owned horses.

q: Which word meaning "rigid airship" comes from a German airship pioneer?
f: Count Zeppelin was fifty-two and retired when he started building airships. The Hindenburg disaster ended the industry in thirty-seven seconds of newsreel — and a British rock band took the name a generation later.

q: "Babbitt" is named after a person.
f: Sinclair Lewis invented a realtor named George Babbitt who bought whatever his neighbours bought and believed whatever his club believed. Readers recognised him instantly — and within a year Americans were calling any such man a Babbitt.

q: There was an anti-heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair. Born poor, she charmed and schemed her way up through English society without ever quite being caught. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Thackeray refused to give his novel a hero, so he gave it Becky Sharp instead: penniless, brilliant, and willing to flatter anyone who might raise her a rung. Readers were supposed to disapprove. Most of them rooted for her anyway.

q: There was an English philosopher. He judged every law and custom by one test: does it increase happiness for the greatest number. Which word grew out of it?
f: Jeremy Bentham thought morality should be arithmetic — add up the happiness, subtract the suffering, keep whatever comes out positive. He left his body to University College London, where his preserved skeleton, dressed in his own clothes, still sits in a cabinet.

q: There was a heroine of Flaubert's Madame Bovary. She read romantic novels until she could no longer see her ordinary life clearly. Which word grew out of it?
f: Emma Bovary read so many romances that her real life — a country doctor, a quiet village — became unbearable by comparison. The French coined bovarysme for that exact ache: mistaking the daydream for the life you were owed.

q: There was a land of giants in Swift's Gulliver's Travels. Gulliver, a normal man, reached a country where wasps were the size of birds and he could be carried in a pocket. Which word grew out of it?
f: Swift sent Gulliver first to Lilliput, where he was a giant, then to Brobdingnag, where he was a toy. English kept both: lilliputian for the tiny, Brobdingnagian for the colossal. Only one of them is hard to spell.

q: There was an English preacher and author of The Pilgrim's Progress. He wrote his allegory in plain, forceful English while imprisoned for preaching without a licence. Which word grew out of it?
f: John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress in Bedford jail, turning a Christian's life into a journey past the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. He had almost no schooling, and his plain thundering English outsold nearly every book in the language.

q: There was a naive hero of Voltaire's 1759 satire. He was taught that this is the best of all possible worlds, then survived earthquake, war, and shipwreck still half-believing it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Voltaire wrote Candide in three days to mock philosophers who insisted everything happens for the best. His hero endures catastrophe after catastrophe, and ends up concluding only this: we must cultivate our garden.

q: "Cassandra" is named after a place.
f: Cassandra saw Troy burn years before it happened. She warned everyone. Apollo's curse meant her family heard her perfectly and dismissed her every time — the cruellest gift in Greek myth, and now the word for any warning nobody heeds.

q: There was an enchantress in Homer's Odyssey. She fed Odysseus's crew a drugged feast and turned them into pigs. Which word grew out of it?
f: Circe welcomed Odysseus's sailors with wine and cheese, then touched them with her wand and watched them drop to all fours as swine. Odysseus, protected by a herb from Hermes, was the one guest she could not transform.

q: There was a Roman statesman and orator. His speeches set the standard for balanced, rhythmic Latin prose for the next two thousand years. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cicero could hold the Roman Senate for hours with sentences built like architecture. Renaissance scholars admired him so much that some refused to use any Latin word he had not used first — a fussiness their rivals mocked as Ciceronian.

q: There was a florentine poet. His Inferno mapped hell in nine descending circles with terrible precision. Which word grew out of it?
f: Exiled from Florence on pain of burning, Dante spent his banishment writing a tour of the afterlife — and quietly placed several of his political enemies in hell. A Dantesque scene is one of infernal, orderly horror.

q: There was an Athenian orator. He overcame a speech impediment to become the most forceful public speaker in Greece. Which word grew out of it?
f: Demosthenes is said to have practised with pebbles in his mouth and shouted over the surf to strengthen his voice. He turned that hard-won delivery on Philip of Macedon in speeches so fierce that attacks on any leader are still called philippics.

q: There was a Greek god of wine and theatre. His festivals celebrated ecstasy and loss of self, the opposite of calm reason. Which word grew out of it?
f: Nietzsche split art in two: Apollonian for order and clarity, Dionysian for ecstasy and abandon. Both named for gods — Apollo the composed archer, Dionysus the god whose worshippers danced themselves out of their own minds.

q: Which name or term meaning "a place of fabulous, unattainable wealth" comes from a legendary golden king of a South American tribe?
f: El Dorado means 'the gilded one' — originally a person, not a place. A Muisca chief really did coat himself in gold dust for a ritual on Lake Guatavita. Spanish rumour inflated one man into a city, and expeditions died searching for it.

q: "Euhemerism" is named after a person.
f: Euhemerus claimed to have found an inscription on a distant island proving Zeus had been an ordinary king. Nobody has ever located the island, but the idea stuck: euhemerism is the theory that every god started out as somebody's grandfather.

q: There was a comic knight in Shakespeare's Henry IV. Fat, cowardly, boastful and irresistibly funny, he stole every scene he appeared in. Which word grew out of it?
f: Falstaff lies about his own bravery so extravagantly that his friends count the exaggerations for sport. Legend says Queen Elizabeth enjoyed him so much she asked Shakespeare for a play showing the fat knight in love.

q: There was a scholar of German legend who traded his soul to the devil. He wanted unlimited knowledge and pleasure, and signed away eternity to get them. Which word grew out of it?
f: The real Johann Faust was a wandering German magician. Legend gave him a contract with the devil, Marlowe and Goethe gave him great plays, and English gained the Faustian bargain — a deal that pays now and ruins you later.

q: Which word meaning "a person of flawless nobility and purity" comes from a knight of Arthur's Round Table?
f: Every knight at the Round Table went looking for the Grail. Only Galahad, so pure he could sit in the one chair that killed all other occupants, was permitted to find it — and having found it, he was taken straight to heaven.

q: There was a legendary king of Phrygia. His ox-cart was tied with a knot so intricate that an oracle promised Asia to whoever loosed it. Which word grew out of it?
f: For centuries nobody untied the Gordian knot. Alexander the Great arrived, considered it briefly, and cut it in half with his sword. He went on to conquer Asia, which suggests the oracle accepted his method.

q: There was a title character of Shakespeare's tragedy. Told to avenge his father, he spends four acts examining the question from every angle. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hamlet has the proof, the motive, and the opportunity by act three — and still stops to ask whether being is better than not being. Shakespeare made indecision so gripping that the prince's name became the word for it.

q: Which word meaning "a greedy snatcher" comes from a winged snatchers in Greek myth?
f: The Harpies were storm spirits with women's faces and birds' bodies, sent to snatch the food from Phineus's table again and again. Their name comes from the Greek for 'snatchers', and it is still what we call anything that will not stop grabbing.

q: "Hectoring" is named after a place.
f: This one is unfair to Hector. In the Iliad he is the most decent man in the war — a devoted father defending his city. Later English writers recast him as a swaggerer, and to hector has meant to bully ever since.

q: There was a Greek arsonist. He burned down the Temple of Artemis purely so that history would remember his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Herostratus torched one of the Seven Wonders of the World and freely confessed his motive: fame. Ephesus made it a capital crime to speak his name, hoping to erase him. You are reading it now, which tells you how well that worked.

q: Which word meaning "keenly observant and deductive" comes from a detective created by Arthur Conan Doyle?
f: Conan Doyle based Holmes on his medical teacher Joseph Bell, who could diagnose a patient's trade and travels before they spoke. Doyle killed Holmes off at a waterfall; public outrage was so fierce he had to bring him back.

q: There was a titan of light in Greek myth. Father of the sun, moon and dawn, his name means 'he who goes above'. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hyperion fathered Helios the sun, Selene the moon, and Eos the dawn. Hamlet uses him as the measure of magnificence — comparing his noble father to Hyperion and his uncle to a satyr. The tallest living tree on Earth carries the name.

q: There was a son of Daedalus in Greek myth. Given wings of wax and feathers, he ignored his father's warning and flew too near the sun. Which word grew out of it?
f: Daedalus warned his son twice: not too low, or the sea will soak the feathers; not too high, or the sun will melt the wax. Icarus flew high anyway. The stretch of water where he fell is still called the Icarian Sea.

q: Which word meaning "a traitor, especially one who betrays a friend" comes from the disciple who betrayed Jesus?
f: Judas gave up his teacher for thirty silver coins and marked him with a kiss so the soldiers would know which man to take. Two thousand years later the name is still a synonym for betrayal, and almost nobody names a child Judas.

q: Which word meaning "a person with two violently opposed personalities" comes from a twin identities in Stevenson's 1886 novella?
f: Stevenson is said to have written the first draft in three days, burned it after his wife's criticism, and rewritten the whole thing in three more. The result gave English its standard phrase for anyone who is two different people.

q: "Jezebel" is named after a person.
f: Jezebel painted her face and dressed her hair before meeting the men who came to overthrow her — defiant to the last minute. The Bible meant it as a portrait of vanity; her name has been an insult in English for four hundred years.

q: There was a Czech-German writer. His characters are trapped by rules nobody will explain, in systems with no visible person in charge. Which word grew out of it?
f: Kafka wrote about a man arrested for a crime the court refuses to name, and a surveyor who can never reach the castle that employs him. He asked his friend to burn all of it after his death. His friend published everything instead.

q: There was a title character of Shakespeare's tragedy. He divided his kingdom between the daughters who flattered him, disinherited the one who loved him, and raged on a heath once he understood. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lear asks his three daughters to say how much they love him. Two lay it on thick; Cordelia, who means it, refuses to perform. He gives his kingdom to the flatterers and spends the rest of the play discovering his mistake in a storm.

q: There was a Roman general and famous host. He retired from war to throw banquets so extravagant they became proverbial. Which word grew out of it?
f: Asked why he had ordered a magnificent dinner when he was eating alone, Lucullus is said to have replied that tonight Lucullus dines with Lucullus. He also brought the cherry tree to Italy, which may be his more useful legacy.

q: There was a florentine diplomat and writer. The Prince advised rulers that keeping power sometimes requires setting honesty aside. Which word grew out of it?
f: Machiavelli wrote The Prince while out of a job, partly hoping to be hired again. Within decades English playwrights had turned his name into a stock villain — the Machiavel — who smiles at you while planning exactly how to use you.

q: There was a character in Sheridan's play The Rivals. She reached for grand words and grabbed the wrong ones, calling someone the very pineapple of politeness. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sheridan named her from the French mal a propos, 'badly suited'. She meant to call a man the pinnacle of politeness and called him the pineapple instead — and every mixed-up word since has carried her name.

q: Which word meaning "lacking a wise guide or adviser" comes from an odysseus's old friend in the Odyssey?
f: When Odysseus sailed for Troy he left his son in the care of a friend named Mentor. The goddess Athena kept borrowing that shape to deliver advice — so the word for a trusted guide is really the name of a disguise.

q: "Merlinic" is named after a place.
f: Merlin appears first in a twelfth-century history that presented him as fact. He is said to have aged backwards, remembering the future and forgetting the past — which is one way to explain a prophet who always knows what happens next.

q: There was an English poet. Paradise Lost set the standard for grand, sweeping epic in English. Which word grew out of it?
f: Milton went completely blind in his forties and composed Paradise Lost in his head at night, dictating each morning to whoever was available — often his daughters. Twelve books of epic poetry, and he never saw a line of it written down.

q: There was an American writer who coined the term in 1942. Wylie attacked what he saw as smothering sentimentality about American mothers. Which word grew out of it?
f: Philip Wylie coined momism in Generation of Vipers, a book so scathing that it made him famous and disliked in equal measure. It is one of the rare eponyms built not from a person's name but from what a whole country called its mothers.

q: There was a Greek god of dreams. He shaped the human figures that appear in dreams — his name comes from morphe, 'form'. Which word grew out of it?
f: Morpheus did not bring sleep; he supplied the people in your dreams, taking their shapes himself. When a chemist isolated a powerful sleep-bringing drug from opium in 1804 he named it morphine after the same god.

q: There was a Greek hero of Homer's Odyssey. He took ten years to sail home from Troy, surviving by cunning rather than strength. Which word grew out of it?
f: Odysseus escaped a cyclops by telling it his name was Nobody, so that its cries for help made no sense to the neighbours. Ten years of that kind of thinking got him home, and gave English both odyssey and Odyssean.

q: There was a wife of Odysseus in the Odyssey. Besieged by suitors, she promised to choose one when her weaving was done, then unpicked it every night. Which word grew out of it?
f: Penelope told a hall full of suitors she would remarry once she finished weaving a shroud. Each night she quietly unravelled the day's work. She held them off for three years before a servant gave her away.

q: Which word meaning "cheerfully naive" comes from a genial hero of Dickens's The Pickwick Papers?
f: The Pickwick Papers made the twenty-four-year-old Dickens famous in monthly instalments. It also gave English a strange, useful phrase: to mean something in a Pickwickian sense is to insist your insult does not count.

q: "Protean" is named after a person.
f: Proteus knew everything but hated being asked. Grab him and he becomes a lion, then a snake, then running water, then a tree — and only when you have held on through all of it does he give up and tell you the truth.

q: There was a French monk, physician and writer. His giant heroes Gargantua and Pantagruel eat, drink and joke on an enormous scale. Which word grew out of it?
f: Rabelais wrote about giants so large that a whole army once sheltered under one's tongue. His books were banned by the theologians of the Sorbonne, which did nothing to slow their sales and gave French a word for cheerful excess.

q: There was an Israelite king renowned for wisdom. Faced with two women claiming one baby, he proposed dividing it and identified the true mother by who refused. Which word grew out of it?
f: Two women each swore the baby was hers. Solomon called for a sword and offered to give each of them half. One agreed; the other begged him to give the child away instead — and he handed the baby to her.

q: There was a moneylender in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice. He held a debtor to a contract promising a pound of the man's own flesh. Which word grew out of it?
f: Shylock's bond entitles him to a pound of flesh, and the court agrees it is valid — then rules he may take flesh but not one drop of blood, because the contract never mentioned blood. He loses on the same literal reading he demanded.

q: Which word meaning "idealistic" comes from an ideal island in Thomas More's 1516 book?
f: Thomas More described a perfect island republic and named it, in Greek, No Place. Everyone since has used utopia to mean a paradise, missing the pun. More was beheaded by Henry VIII, which was not utopian at all.

q: There was an Italian physicist. He built the first battery, a stack of zinc and copper discs that produced steady current. Which word grew out of it?
f: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with brine-soaked cloth between them and made electricity flow steadily for the first time. Napoleon made him a count. The volt is named for him too, so he is one of very few people who are twice a unit.

q: There was an Athenian general and politician. Brilliant, beautiful and completely unreliable, he changed sides between Athens, Sparta and Persia. Which word grew out of it?
f: Alcibiades led Athens, defected to Sparta, advised Persia, then came home to cheering crowds. Socrates taught him and could not steady him. He is the ancient world's model for the dazzling person you should probably not trust.

q: "Antigonean" is named after a place.
f: Creon forbade the burial of Antigone's brother on pain of death. She scattered earth over his body anyway and told the king to his face that no decree of his could overrule the unwritten laws. She was walled up alive for it.

q: There was a hundred-eyed giant in Greek myth. Hera set him to guard a prisoner because some of his hundred eyes stayed open while the rest slept. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hermes eventually bored Argus to sleep with stories and killed him. Hera gathered his hundred eyes and set them into the tail of her peacock, which is why the bird still looks like it is watching you from every direction.

q: There was a Cretan princess in Greek myth. She gave Theseus a ball of thread to unwind so he could find his way back out of the Labyrinth. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Theseus could kill the Minotaur; the harder problem was leaving. Ariadne handed him thread to unspool on the way in. Mathematicians still call the technique of solving a maze by exhaustive tracking an Ariadne's thread.

q: There was a Roman god of wine. His festivals were famous for wild dancing and drinking. Which word grew out of it?
f: Rome so distrusted the Bacchanalia that the Senate banned them in 186 BC and executed thousands of participants. The god survived the crackdown, and English kept bacchic and bacchanal for any party that goes well past sensible.

q: There was a Byzantine general. He won back much of the Roman west for Justinian and was repaid with suspicion and disgrace. Which word grew out of it?
f: Belisarius reconquered North Africa and Italy for an emperor who never quite trusted him, and was twice stripped of command. A later legend, probably false, had him blinded and begging in the streets — a story too good for painters to resist.

q: There was a Greek hero who rode Pegasus. He was sent to a king carrying a sealed letter that requested his own execution. Which word grew out of it?
f: Bellerophon delivered his own death warrant, unaware, because he could not read the sealed tablet he carried. The king who received it sent him to fight the Chimera instead — and he survived that too, on the back of the winged horse Pegasus.

q: There was a hundred-handed giant in Greek myth. One of three brothers with fifty heads and a hundred arms apiece who fought for Zeus against the Titans. Which word grew out of it?
f: Zeus was losing the war against the Titans until he freed three hundred-handed giants from the underworld. Briareus and his brothers hurled three hundred boulders at once, and the Titans broke. Some jobs need more hands than others.

q: "Burkean" is named after a person.
f: Burke supported the American colonists and opposed the French revolutionaries, which sounds inconsistent until you notice his rule: mend what exists, do not tear it down and start fresh. His prediction that France would end under a general came true.

q: Which word meaning "imperial" comes from a Roman general and dictator?
f: Caesar's name outlived his empire twice over: German emperors were Kaisers and Russian ones Tsars, both worn-down forms of Caesar. The surgical caesarean also carries it, though the old story that he was born that way is almost certainly untrue.

q: There was a Roman emperor. Ancient historians recorded him as cruel and unhinged, and said he planned to make his horse a consul. Which word grew out of it?
f: Caligula was a soldiers' nickname meaning 'little boot' — he wore a miniature army uniform as a child on campaign with his father. The cuddly nickname stuck to one of the most feared names in Roman history.

q: There was a nymph in Homer's Odyssey. She kept Odysseus on her island for seven years, offering immortality if he would stay. Which word grew out of it?
f: Calypso offered Odysseus eternal youth and a beautiful island forever. He sat on the shore and wept because he wanted to go home to a middle-aged wife on a rocky one. The gods eventually made her let him go.

q: There was a Roman statesman. Famously austere and moralising, he ended every speech by demanding the destruction of Carthage. Which word grew out of it?
f: Whatever the Senate was debating — roads, taxes, anything — Cato finished his speech with the same line: and furthermore, Carthage must be destroyed. He kept it up for years. Eventually Rome destroyed Carthage.

q: There was three-headed dog guarding the Greek underworld. He let the dead in and let nobody back out. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cerberus had three heads so at least one was always awake. The trick was music — Orpheus played him to sleep — or cake, since the Romans buried honey cakes with the dead specifically as a bribe. Hence a sop to Cerberus.

q: There was a whirlpool monster in the Odyssey. She swallowed the sea three times a day, facing the six-headed Scylla across a narrow strait. Which word grew out of it?
f: Odysseus had to steer between Scylla's six heads and Charybdis's whirlpool. Choosing Scylla cost him six men; Charybdis would have cost the ship. Between Scylla and Charybdis still means a choice between two disasters.

q: "Clytemnestran" is named after a place.
f: Agamemnon sacrificed their daughter to get his fleet to Troy. Clytemnestra waited ten years, welcomed him home across a purple carpet, and killed him in his bath. Greek tragedy rarely takes a clear side on which of them was worse.

q: There was a king of Lydia. His kingdom's gold-rich rivers made him a byword for wealth while he still lived. Which word grew out of it?
f: Croesus asked an oracle whether to attack Persia and was told he would destroy a great empire. He attacked. The empire he destroyed was his own. Rich as Croesus survived him by two and a half thousand years.

q: There was a master craftsman of Greek myth. He built the Labyrinth on Crete, then wings to escape from the island he had made inescapable. Which word grew out of it?
f: Daedalus designed the Labyrinth so cunningly that he could barely find his own way out of it. King Minos imprisoned him to keep the secret, so he built wings. His son Icarus did not follow the flight instructions.

q: There was a Greek hero at Troy. In the Iliad he fights so boldly he wounds two gods, Aphrodite and Ares, in a single day. Which word grew out of it?
f: Diomedes is the only mortal in the Iliad to wound two gods in one afternoon. Athena lends him the sight to tell gods from men on the battlefield, and he uses it immediately to pick a fight with the god of war.

q: There was a daughter of Agamemnon in Greek tragedy. She urged her brother to kill their mother in revenge for their father's murder. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Jung named it in 1913 as the daughters' counterpart to Freud's Oedipus complex. Freud disliked the term and never really used it. The Electra of the plays is less a case study than a study in how long a person can hold a grudge.

q: There was a Dutch humanist scholar. He argued for reform through scholarship and gentle satire rather than schism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Erasmus produced the Greek New Testament that Luther translated from, then spent the Reformation refusing to join either side. Both sides attacked him. He said he would rather be a spectator than a soldier in a war of words.

q: There was a Greek mathematician. His Elements built all of geometry from five plain postulates and became the model of rigorous proof. Which word grew out of it?
f: Euclid's Elements was a school textbook for over two thousand years — the longest run of any book but the Bible. Asked by a king for a shortcut, he is supposed to have replied that there is no royal road to geometry.

q: "Fabian" is named after a person.
f: Rome nicknamed Fabius the Delayer as an insult; after Hannibal destroyed a Roman army that did attack, it became a compliment. Britain's Fabian Society took the name in 1884 to signal socialism by patience rather than revolution.

q: Which word meaning "of Florence" comes from a city in Tuscany, Italy?
f: Catherine de' Medici left Florence in 1533 to marry the future king of France, reportedly bringing her own cooks and a fondness for spinach. Whether or not the story is true, French menus have called spinach dishes a la florentine ever since.

q: There was an Italian astronomer and physicist. He discovered Jupiter's four largest moons and framed the principle that motion looks the same to all steadily moving observers. Which word grew out of it?
f: In January 1610 Galileo pointed a homemade telescope at Jupiter and saw three little stars beside it. Four nights later they had moved. They were moons, orbiting something other than Earth — and the sky was never the same shape again.

q: There was a statue brought to life in Greek myth. The sculptor Pygmalion fell in love with his own ivory carving and Aphrodite made her real. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pygmalion carved a woman more perfect than any living one and then could not stop loving her. Aphrodite took pity and warmed the ivory to skin. Shaw reused the plot in Pygmalion, which became My Fair Lady.

q: There was three snake-haired sisters of Greek myth. Anyone who met the gaze of a Gorgon turned instantly to stone. Which word grew out of it?
