f: There were three Gorgons, but only Medusa could be killed. Perseus managed it by never looking at her directly — he watched her reflection in his polished shield and struck at what he saw there.

q: There was a tree nymphs of Greek myth. Each was bound to one particular tree and died when it died. Which word grew out of it?
f: A dryad could wander the forest. A hamadryad could not: she lived inside a single tree and her life ended with it, so cutting one down was murder. Naturalists later borrowed the name for the king cobra.

q: There was a Roman poet. His satires teased human folly with a smile rather than attacking it with a knife. Which word grew out of it?
f: Roman satire came in two flavours: Horatian, which laughs at you, and Juvenalian, which wants you punished. Horace also gave us carpe diem — seize the day — from a poem about opening the wine now rather than later.

q: "Irenic" is named after a place.
f: Eirene was one of three sisters who kept the seasons and the social order. Athens raised a statue of her holding the infant god of wealth, making the point plainly: peace is what makes prosperity possible.

q: There was a river and river-god of Thebes. The Ismenus ran through Thebes, so poets used the name to mean Theban. Which word grew out of it?
f: Greek poets rarely said Thebes when they could say something more ornate. Ismenean, after the river running past the city, was the elegant option — the kind of word that tells you the writer had a classical education.

q: Which word meaning "majestic and genial" comes from a Roman king of the gods, also called Jupiter?
f: Jove gave English two words with opposite moods. Jovial means cheerful, because Jupiter's influence was thought lucky. Saturnine means gloomy, from Saturn. Your temperament, medieval doctors believed, depended on which planet was up when you were born.

q: There was a Greek satirist. He wrote mocking dialogues, including a voyage to the moon presented as a straight-faced travel report. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lucian wrote A True Story, about sailing to the moon and meeting its army — and opened by announcing that everything in it was a lie. Scholars call it the first science fiction, written eighteen centuries before the rockets.

q: There was a legendary lawgiver of Sparta. He is credited with the harsh code that turned Sparta into a permanent military camp. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lycurgus supposedly made the Spartans swear to keep his laws until he returned, then left and never came back — binding them forever by a technicality. Whether he existed at all is still argued over.

q: There was the mortal Gorgon of Greek myth. Her hair was a mass of living snakes and her gaze turned men to stone. Which word grew out of it?
f: Perseus cut off Medusa's head and the winged horse Pegasus sprang from her neck. He kept the head as a weapon — it worked just as well detached — and eventually gave it to Athena, who mounted it on her shield.

q: There was a Roman goddess of wisdom and crafts. She sprang fully armed from Jupiter's head, and became the patron of thought and skill. Which word grew out of it?
f: Minerva was born from her father's skull, fully grown and already in armour, after he swallowed her mother. The owl on her shoulder is why owls have stood for wisdom in Western art for two thousand years.

q: "Myrmidon" is named after a person.
f: Myrmex is Greek for ant. When a plague emptied the island of Aegina, Zeus turned its ants into people — and they kept the ant temperament: tireless, obedient, and utterly without independent opinions.

q: Which word meaning "a sea nymph" comes from an old man of the sea in Greek myth?
f: Nereus had fifty daughters and they were the good sort of sea spirit — they helped sailors rather than drowning them. Neptune's second-largest moon is called Nereid, and so is a whole class of bristly marine worms.

q: There was a queen of Thebes in Greek myth. She boasted of her fourteen children, the gods killed them all, and she wept until she turned to stone. Which word grew out of it?
f: Niobe said she was luckier than a goddess who had only two children. Apollo and Artemis — the two children in question — killed all fourteen of hers. She wept until she became a rock, and the rock kept weeping.

q: There was a legendary musician of Greek myth. His playing moved stones and trees, and persuaded the lord of the dead to release his wife. Which word grew out of it?
f: Orpheus played so beautifully that Hades agreed to release Eurydice — on one condition: do not look back until you are both in daylight. He was almost out when he turned around to check she was following.

q: There was a Greek name for Pharaoh Ramesses II. Shelley's 1818 sonnet describes his shattered statue boasting in a desert where nothing else remains. Which word grew out of it?
f: Shelley wrote the sonnet as a bet with a friend over who could write the better poem about Egypt. The inscription in it — look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair — sits on a broken statue in an empty desert.

q: There was an Athenian statesman. He led Athens through the decades that built the Parthenon and produced its greatest drama. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pericles spent the treasury of an alliance on rebuilding his own city, which the allies noticed. The Parthenon was the result. He died of plague three years into the war that ended the age named after him.

q: Which word meaning "of Phoenicia" comes from an ancient seafaring civilisation of the Levant?
f: The Phoenicians were merchants, not conquerors, and their greatest export was not cloth or cedar but the alphabet. Every letter you are reading descends from marks made by traders who needed a quick way to keep accounts.

q: "Plutonian" is named after a place.
f: Poe's raven comes from the Night's Plutonian shore. When an eleven-year-old girl suggested Pluto for the new planet in 1930, the underworld god fit — it was the coldest, darkest, farthest thing anyone had found.

q: There was a titan of Greek myth. He stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity, and was chained to a rock for it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Zeus chained Prometheus to a mountain and sent an eagle to eat his liver each day; it grew back each night. Mary Shelley subtitled Frankenstein 'The Modern Prometheus' — a warning about the cost of stealing fire.

q: There was a Greek poet of Lesbos. She wrote in a distinctive four-line stanza that now carries her name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sappho was so admired that Plato called her the tenth Muse, yet almost all of her nine books are lost — we have one complete poem and a drift of fragments, some recovered from ancient rubbish dumps in Egypt.

q: There was a Roman god and the slowest visible planet. Astrologers blamed Saturn's cold, sluggish influence for gloomy temperaments. Which word grew out of it?
f: Medieval doctors believed the planet overhead at your birth set your personality for life. Saturn, slow and cold and distant, produced the melancholy sort. The planet has moved on; the word has not.

q: There was an Athenian hero of Greek myth. He entered the Cretan Labyrinth, killed the Minotaur, and found his way back out. Which word grew out of it?
f: Athens had been sending fourteen young people into the Labyrinth every nine years as tribute. Theseus volunteered to be one of them, killed the monster at the centre, and ended the tribute — which is how you get a city named after you.

q: There was an ancient Greek city in Boeotia. Home of Oedipus, Antigone and Cadmus, it supplied Greek tragedy with its darkest family. Which word grew out of it?
f: Thebes was where Greek tragedy went for its worst stories: a king who married his mother, a daughter buried alive, brothers who killed each other at the gates. Alexander the Great later flattened the city, sparing only the poet Pindar's house.

q: There was a Greek keeper of the winds. He gave Odysseus a bag holding every wind but the one he needed. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aeolus bagged up the contrary winds so Odysseus could sail straight home. In sight of Ithaca the crew opened the bag, assuming it held treasure, and blew themselves all the way back. Geologists still call wind-blown sand aeolian.

q: "Agamemnonian" is named after a person.
f: Agamemnon won the ten-year war and survived the whole of it, only to be killed in his own bathroom within hours of arriving home. Schliemann dug up a gold funeral mask at Mycenae and cabled that he had gazed on the face of Agamemnon. It was three centuries too old.

q: Which word meaning "a figure of great strength brought down by wounded pride" comes from a Greek warrior at Troy?
f: Ajax was the wall of the Greek army — the man who never lost a duel. He killed himself over a prize he did not win. A cleaning powder now carries his name, on the reasoning that it is stronger than dirt.

q: There was a princess chained to a rock in Greek myth. She was offered to a sea monster to pay for her mother's boasting, and Perseus rescued her. Which word grew out of it?
f: Andromeda's mother said her daughter was lovelier than the sea nymphs, and a monster was sent to collect the difference. Perseus saved her mid-flight. The whole family — mother, father, hero, monster — was put in the sky as constellations.

q: There was a giant of Greek myth. He was invincible while touching the earth, his mother, and lost all strength when lifted from it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Antaeus beat every wrestler who came at him, because every time he was thrown down he got up stronger. Heracles worked out the trick, hoisted him off the ground, and held him in the air until he weakened.

q: There was a Greek god of light, music and prophecy. He stood for clarity, proportion and reason. Which word grew out of it?
f: Nietzsche paired Apollonian order against Dionysian ecstasy and argued great art needs both — the clear shape and the wild energy inside it. The Apollo space programme took the name of the god who drove the sun across the sky.

q: There was a mortal weaver of Greek myth. She out-wove Athena in a contest and was turned into a spider for the insult. Which word grew out of it?
f: Arachne's tapestry was better than the goddess's — that was the problem. Athena tore it up and struck her, and when Arachne despaired, turned her into a creature that could weave forever. Spiders are still classed as arachnids.

q: There was an athens's ancient council, meeting on the Hill of Ares. It served as the city's highest court for the gravest crimes. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Areopagus tried murder cases, and myth says its first defendant was the war god Ares himself. Milton borrowed the name in 1644 for Areopagitica, his argument against censorship — a speech to a court that no longer existed.

q: "Argonaut" is named after a place.
f: The Argonauts were named for their ship, not their leader — argonaut simply means Argo-sailor. Prospectors racing to California in 1849 called themselves Argonauts too, which was optimistic about the fleece.

q: There was an Athenian comic playwright. He put living politicians on stage and mocked them by name in front of the whole city. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aristophanes wrote a comedy attacking Socrates as a fraud who taught students to dodge debts. Twenty-four years later, at his trial, Socrates complained that the play had poisoned the jury against him long before he arrived.

q: There was a Greek philosopher. He classified everything from tragedy to squid and set the framework for European thought for centuries. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great, dissected sea creatures on Lesbos, and wrote the first surviving works on logic, physics and drama. For much of the Middle Ages, European scholars simply called him The Philosopher.

q: Which word meaning "a wild, drunken celebration" comes from a Roman god of wine?
f: The Roman Senate banned the Bacchanalia in 186 BC, calling them a conspiracy. Thousands were arrested. The festivals had grown from a small women's rite into all-night gatherings the state could neither see into nor control.

q: There was a Roman senator. He joined the plot to kill Julius Caesar, who had treated him as a friend. Which word grew out of it?
f: Shakespeare gives the dying Caesar the line Et tu, Brute — you too, Brutus. The real Caesar probably said nothing at all. Brutus insisted he acted for the Republic, not against the man, and killed himself two years later.

q: There was a founder of Thebes in Greek myth. He sowed a dragon's teeth and armed men sprang up and killed each other until only five were left. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Cadmean victory costs more than losing would have. Cadmus also, according to the Greeks, brought them the alphabet from Phoenicia — so the man behind the ruinous win is also the reason they could write about it.

q: There was Greek Muse of epic poetry. Chief of the nine Muses, she inspired Homer and the grand heroic style. Which word grew out of it?
f: Calliope was the eldest Muse and the mother of Orpheus. In 1855 an American inventor attached her name to a steam whistle organ so loud it could be heard for miles — the calliope that still shrieks over fairgrounds.

q: "Caryatid" is named after a person.
f: Six caryatids hold up a porch of the Erechtheion in Athens. One was removed by Lord Elgin and taken to London; the Athenians said for years that the remaining five could be heard at night, crying for their missing sister.

q: There was a ferryman of the dead in Greek myth. He rowed souls across the Styx, and only for those buried with the fare. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Greeks buried their dead with a coin in the mouth to pay Charon. Anyone unburied waited a hundred years on the wrong bank. Pluto's largest moon is named Charon, still ferrying alongside the underworld.

q: There was Greek Muse of history. She carried a scroll and was invoked at the opening of historical works. Which word grew out of it?
f: Clio's name comes from the Greek for 'to make famous' — the historian's actual job, as the Greeks saw it. Herodotus's nine books of history were each named after one of the nine Muses, and Clio got book one.

q: There was one of the three Fates in Greek myth. She spun the thread of each human life while her sisters measured and cut it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Three sisters ran every life: Clotho spun the thread, Lachesis measured it, Atropos cut. Even Zeus could not overrule them. Engineers borrowed the name for the clothoid, the spiralling curve that eases a road into a bend.

q: There was a titan father of Zeus. He ruled the Golden Age, and the Romans identified him with Saturn. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cronus swallowed each of his children at birth to stop the prophecy that one would overthrow him. His wife handed him a stone in swaddling clothes instead of the sixth. The sixth was Zeus, and the prophecy held.

q: There was a town near Athens. Its secret initiation rites promised a better afterlife and were never written down. Which word grew out of it?
f: For nearly two thousand years, thousands of Greeks were initiated at Eleusis — and not one of them ever recorded what happened inside. The penalty for telling was death. It remains the best-kept secret in the ancient world.

q: There was a paradise of the blessed dead in Greek myth. Heroes were sent there instead of the grey underworld, to fields of perpetual ease. Which word grew out of it?
f: Elysium was the good afterlife — sunlight, meadows, no work. Paris named a boulevard after it: the Champs-Elysees, the Elysian Fields. Anyone stuck in its traffic may question the comparison.

q: "Eumenidean" is named after a place.
f: The Furies hunted murderers without rest. Calling them the Eumenides — the Kindly Ones — was pure superstition: you did not want to attract their attention by using the real name. It is the oldest recorded nickname made out of fear.

q: There was a wife of Orpheus in Greek myth. Orpheus won her back from the dead and lost her again by glancing behind him. Which word grew out of it?
f: One rule: do not look back until you are both out. Orpheus walked the whole way up in silence, heard nothing behind him, and turned at the last step to check. She was there, and then she was not.

q: Which word meaning "of the Hebrew language, people or tradition" comes from an ancient people of the Levant?
f: Hebrew stopped being an everyday spoken language for roughly seventeen centuries, surviving only in prayer and study — then was deliberately revived, and is now the first language of millions. No other language has managed that.

q: There was a Greek goddess of witchcraft and crossroads. She was worshipped at night where three roads met, with offerings left in the dark. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hecate is often shown with three faces, watching all three roads at once. Greeks left food for her at junctions on the night of the new moon, and did not look too closely at who collected it.

q: There was a queen whose flight to Troy began the Trojan War. Marlowe called hers the face that launched a thousand ships. Which word grew out of it?
f: Careful with the spelling: Helenic is Helen of Troy, Hellenic is Greek in general. Both trace to Greece, but only one of them started a ten-year war by leaving with a visiting prince.

q: There was a Greek god of the forge. Lame and cast out of Olympus, he made the finest armour and machines of the gods. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hephaestus was thrown off Olympus as an infant and walked with difficulty afterwards — the only Greek god with a disability. He was also the only one who actually made things, including golden servants that moved on their own.

q: There was a youth of Greek myth loved by Apollo. Killed by a discus throw, and from his blood Apollo raised a flower. Which word grew out of it?
f: Apollo threw the discus, the wind blew it off course, and his friend died. The flower that grew where the blood fell carried the boy's name. Homer uses hyacinthine for hair, meaning dark and tightly curled.

q: "Iliadic" is named after a person.
f: The Iliad is not about the whole war — it covers about seven weeks near the end, and never reaches the wooden horse. Its actual subject, announced in the first word, is the anger of one man.

q: There was a daughter of Agamemnon in Greek myth. Her father sacrificed her to obtain a favourable wind for the fleet sailing to Troy. Which word grew out of it?
f: Agamemnon summoned his daughter to the coast on the pretext of a wedding. In some versions Artemis snatched her away at the last instant and left a deer on the altar — a rescue the Greeks invented later, when the original proved unbearable.

q: There was a river of forgetfulness in the Greek underworld. Souls drank from it to erase their memories before being reborn. Which word grew out of it?
f: The dead drank from Lethe so they could start again with nothing. Its opposite, Mnemosyne, ran alongside — and initiates of some mystery cults were told to refuse the first river and ask for the second.

q: There was an ancient region of southwest Anatolia. Its people carved elaborate tombs into cliff faces and kept their own language and alphabet. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Lycians cut house-shaped tombs high into sheer rock so the dead would be closer to the sky. Their alphabet borrowed from Greek but kept extra letters for sounds Greek did not have, and nobody could read it for two thousand years.

q: There was a sorceress of Greek myth. Betrayed by Jason, she took a revenge so extreme that Greek audiences were shocked by it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Medea gave up her home and her family to help Jason steal the Golden Fleece. When he left her for a princess, she destroyed everything he loved and escaped in a chariot drawn by dragons. Euripides gave her the last word.

q: There was Greek Muse of tragedy. She is shown holding a tragic mask and wearing the raised boot of the tragic actor. Which word grew out of it?
f: Melpomene started as the Muse of singing — her name means 'to celebrate with song'. She was reassigned to tragedy later. The two masks hanging outside theatres are hers and her sister Thalia's, comedy and tragedy together.

q: There was a Greek goddess of memory. She was the mother of all nine Muses, making memory the parent of every art. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Greeks made memory the mother of the arts, which is exactly right for a culture that recited Homer from memory for centuries before writing it down. Mnemonic — a memory trick — comes from the same root.

q: "Nemesian" is named after a place.
f: Nemesis did not punish crime — she punished excess. Too much luck, too much boasting, and she arrived to restore the balance. Her name now means an unbeatable rival, which is a demotion from goddess of cosmic accounting.

q: Which word meaning "of the ocean" comes from a titan of the great river encircling the world?
f: For the earliest Greeks the Ocean was not water everywhere — it was one enormous river running in a circle around the rim of a flat world, and Oceanus was the Titan who was that river.

q: Which word meaning "a four-year period" comes from a sanctuary in southern Greece?
f: An Olympiad is properly the four-year gap, not the festival — the Greeks dated events by counting them. The ancient games ran for roughly twelve centuries before a Roman emperor shut them down as a pagan rite.

q: There was a Greek hero who killed Medusa. He beheaded the Gorgon, rescued Andromeda, and was placed in the sky as a constellation. Which word grew out of it?
f: Perseus borrowed winged sandals, a cap of invisibility and a mirrored shield, which is a lot of equipment for one monster. The Perseid meteor shower every August appears to come from his constellation.

q: There was an Athenian princess of Greek myth. After a brutal wrong she was turned into a nightingale, whose song poets treated as beautiful grief. Which word grew out of it?
f: Philomela was silenced and wove her story into a tapestry instead, because nobody thought to take away her loom. The gods turned her into a nightingale — the bird that sings most beautifully after dark.

q: There was a judge of the dead in Greek myth. A son of Zeus so famously just that he was made a judge in the underworld. Which word grew out of it?
f: Rhadamanthus was one of three judges deciding where each soul went, and he had the reputation of being unbribable. His name is now the strongest word English has for a judge who will not bend, not even slightly.

q: There was a Greek goddess of the moon. She drove the moon across the night sky in a silver chariot. Which word grew out of it?
f: Selene fell in love with a shepherd and asked Zeus to keep him young forever; he granted it by putting the man into eternal sleep. The element selenium is named after her, because it was found alongside one named for the earth.

q: "Terpsichorean" is named after a person.
f: Terpsichore is the reason a dancer can be called a terpsichorean — a nine-letter way of saying it. Of the nine Muses she is the one whose job survives most recognisably: she is usually shown mid-step, holding a lyre.

q: There was a Roman god of fire and the forge. His workshop was said to lie under Mount Etna, which explained the smoke. Which word grew out of it?
f: Romans thought the rumble of Etna was Vulcan hammering underground. The island of Vulcano off Sicily was his chimney, and it gave every volcano on Earth its name — including the ones nowhere near Italy.

q: Which word meaning "of Hadria or the Adriatic" comes from an ancient town in northern Italy?
f: A small Roman town called Hadria named the whole Adriatic Sea, then lent its adjective to the emperor Hadrian, then to popes and a great many children. The town itself is now several miles inland, left behind by the silt.

q: There was a Trojan hero of Virgil's Aeneid. He carried his father out of burning Troy and sailed on to found the line that led to Rome. Which word grew out of it?
f: Virgil's stock epithet for him is pius Aeneas — not pious exactly, but dutiful. He escapes Troy with his father on his back and his household gods under his arm, and spends the rest of the poem doing what he is told by fate.

q: There was a Greek word for selfless love. Early Christian writers chose it over other Greek words for love to mean unconditional goodwill. Which word grew out of it?
f: Greek had at least four words for love, and early Christian writers deliberately picked the least romantic one. Agape is not affection or desire — it is the kind you extend to someone who has done nothing to earn it.

q: There was a queen of Greek myth. She agreed to die in her husband's place when no one else would. Which word grew out of it?
f: Admetus was allowed to escape death if someone would go instead. He asked his parents, who declined. His wife Alcestis volunteered. Heracles turned up, heard the story, and went to wrestle Death at the graveside to get her back.

q: There was a Theban general of Greek myth. In Moliere's play the true host is identified as the one who provides the dinner. Which word grew out of it?
f: Zeus disguised himself as Amphitryon to visit his wife, producing two identical husbands and a very confused household. Moliere's version settles the question with a line the French adopted: the real Amphitryon is the one who serves the meal.

q: "Anchisean" is named after a place.
f: The image of Aeneas escaping Troy with his father on his back and his son by the hand became Rome's picture of duty itself — carrying the past out and leading the future forward at the same time.

q: There was a Greek lyric poet. He wrote light verse in praise of wine, music and good company. Which word grew out of it?
f: A London gentlemen's club sang a drinking song called To Anacreon in Heaven. An American lawyer later set his poem about a flag to that same tune, and the United States ended up with a national anthem built on a Greek wine poet.

q: There was a Greek term for one who withdraws. Early Christian hermits withdrew to the desert to live alone in prayer. Which word grew out of it?
f: Anchorites went further than monks: some were sealed into a small cell attached to a church wall, with one window to the altar and one to the street, and stayed there for the rest of their lives.

q: There was first Roman emperor. Virgil, Horace and Ovid all wrote under him, making his reign the peak of Latin literature. Which word grew out of it?
f: Augustus boasted he found Rome brick and left it marble. Eighteenth-century English writers admired the period so much that they called their own era Augustan and set out to imitate it deliberately.

q: There was a region of central Greece. Athenians mocked their rural neighbours as slow-witted, and the slur stuck to the region's name. Which word grew out of it?
f: This is an ancient insult that outlived its target. Athens sneered at Boeotia as farmland full of dullards — conveniently forgetting that Hesiod, Pindar and Plutarch all came from there.

q: There was a Spanish novelist. Don Quixote mixes comedy and idealism so closely that neither wins. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cervantes lost the use of his left hand at the battle of Lepanto and spent five years as a captive in Algiers before writing what is often called the first modern novel. He died in the same week as Shakespeare.

q: Which word meaning "of the Americas or of Columbus" comes from a Genoese navigator?
f: America was named for Amerigo Vespucci, not Columbus — but Columbian survived as the poetic alternative. It is why the United States has a District of Columbia and Canada a British Columbia.

q: "Coriolanian" is named after a person.
f: Coriolanus could not bring himself to show his battle scars to voters, which was the custom. Exiled for the insult, he marched on Rome and was stopped only when his mother walked out to meet the army.

q: There was a Trojan woman in medieval and Shakespearean versions of the Troy story. She swore constancy to Troilus and transferred her affections once she reached the Greek camp. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cressida does not appear in Homer at all — she was invented in the Middle Ages and handed down through Boccaccio and Chaucer to Shakespeare, each of whom made her a little less sympathetic than the last.

q: There was a French soldier-poet, immortalised in Rostand's 1897 play. In the play he lends his eloquence to a handsome friend, wooing the woman he loves on someone else's behalf. Which word grew out of it?
f: The real Cyrano wrote science fiction about travelling to the moon. Rostand gave him an enormous nose, a duelling sword, and the finest words in French theatre — all spent under a balcony, for another man.

q: There was a florentine poet. His descent through the nine circles of hell set the standard for infernal imagery. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy in Italian rather than Latin, which scholars considered a waste of a good poem. It is the reason modern Italian sounds the way it does.

q: There was Greek Cynic philosopher. He lived in a large ceramic jar and owned almost nothing on principle. Which word grew out of it?
f: Diogenes walked Athens in daylight with a lit lamp, saying he was looking for an honest man. When Alexander the Great offered him anything he wanted, he asked him to move slightly — he was blocking the sun.

q: There was a hero of Cervantes's novel. He read so many chivalric romances that he set out as a knight and charged windmills believing them giants. Which word grew out of it?
f: Don Quixote's windmills are the most famous mistake in literature. Cervantes meant to mock outdated romances, but readers kept siding with the old man who insisted the world should be nobler than it is.

q: There was a Greek people who settled the Peloponnese. Their name attached to a musical mode and to the plainest of the classical column orders. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Doric column is the plain one — no scrolls, no leaves, just fluting and a flat top. Greeks thought of it as the masculine, unfussy order, and used it for the Parthenon.

q: "Euclidian" is named after a place.
f: Euclid's fifth postulate — about parallel lines — bothered mathematicians for centuries because it seemed like it should be provable. It is not. Dropping it produced curved, non-Euclidean geometries, and eventually general relativity.

q: Which word meaning "of the Gospel" comes from a Greek word meaning 'good news'?
f: Euangelion literally means good message — in classical Greek it was the reward you gave the runner who brought good news from a battle. English kept the messenger sense in evangelist and the enthusiasm in evangelical.

q: Which word meaning "of the modern calendar or of plainsong chant" comes from a pope who reformed the calendar in 1582?
f: To fix the drift, October 1582 simply lost ten days — people went to sleep on the 4th and woke on the 15th. Britain held out until 1752, by which time it had to skip eleven.

q: There was a narrator of Swift's Gulliver's Travels. He is a giant in one land and a doll in the next, and reports both with the same flat calm. Which word grew out of it?
f: Swift wrote Gulliver's Travels as savage political satire. It was so successful as an adventure story that it turned into a children's book, which is the fate of a surprising number of angry books.

q: There was a cambridge stable owner. He rented horses strictly in rotation: you took the one nearest the door, or none at all. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hobson had forty horses and a rule that stopped customers from wearing out the best ones. Students grumbled about Hobson's choice, and the phrase outlived every horse in the stable.

q: There was an English writer and lexicographer. He wrote a dictionary almost single-handedly and spoke in weighty, balanced sentences. Which word grew out of it?
f: Johnson spent nine years on his dictionary and slipped jokes into it — he defined lexicographer as a harmless drudge. His friend Boswell wrote down his conversation for years, producing the most famous biography in English.

q: There was a German philosopher. He argued morality means acting only on rules you could will everyone to follow. Which word grew out of it?
f: Kant kept to a schedule so exact that neighbours in Konigsberg were said to set their clocks by his afternoon walk. He never travelled more than a hundred miles from his birthplace, and rearranged Western philosophy from there.

q: "Lilliputian" is named after a person.
f: Lilliput's great political dispute is whether to crack a boiled egg at the big end or the little end — a war that has killed thousands. Swift was writing about religious conflict, and he was not being subtle.

q: There was a name meaning 'light-bringer', applied to the fallen angel. Pride made him rebel against heaven and fall from it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lucifer is Latin for light-bringer and was originally the morning star, Venus. A verse in Isaiah about a fallen Babylonian king was read as being about Satan, and the planet's name transferred to the devil.

q: Which word meaning "of Newton's classical physics" comes from an English physicist and mathematician?
f: Newton did his best work during a plague year when Cambridge closed and he went home to the farm. In eighteen months he laid out calculus, optics and gravitation. He later called it his year of wonders.

q: There was an Italian poet. He wrote hundreds of sonnets to a woman named Laura, in a form now named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: Petrarch saw Laura in a church in Avignon in 1327 and wrote poems about her for the next forty years, including twenty-one after her death. There is no evidence they ever had a conversation.

q: There was a castaway hero of Defoe's 1719 novel. His story of surviving alone on an island spawned an entire genre of imitations. Which word grew out of it?
f: Defoe based Crusoe partly on Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish sailor marooned for four years on a Pacific island. Germans coined Robinsonade for the flood of imitations, and the genre now includes Swiss Family Robinson and Lord of the Flies.

q: Which word meaning "of Victoria's reign" comes from a british monarch?
f: Victoria came to the throne at eighteen and reigned longer than any British monarch before her. The word Victorian now suggests prudishness, though the queen herself wrote frankly in her diaries about how much she adored her husband.

q: There was a Greek town, home of Democritus. Democritus was known as the laughing philosopher for his amusement at human folly. Which word grew out of it?
f: Abdera produced Democritus, who worked out that matter is made of atoms twenty-three centuries early, and who reportedly could not stop laughing at people. The town's neighbours took the laughter personally.

q: "Acadian" is named after a place.
f: Deported Acadians who reached Louisiana were called Acadiens, then Cadiens, then Cajuns. The whole of Cajun food, music and dialect traces back to one forced expulsion from the far north.

q: There was a beautiful youth of Greek myth. Aphrodite loved him; a boar killed him, and anemones grew where his blood fell. Which word grew out of it?
f: The name is not Greek but Semitic — adon means lord, and the story came west from Phoenicia. Calling a handsome man an Adonis is therefore a compliment in a language most people using it do not know.

q: There was a Greek keeper of the winds. An aeolian harp is played by nothing but the breeze passing over its strings. Which word grew out of it?
f: An aeolian harp is left in an open window and plays itself. Romantic poets loved the idea — an instrument with no performer — and used it as an image for inspiration arriving from somewhere outside you.

q: There was a Greek fabulist. His animal fables carried their real meaning underneath the surface story. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aesop was said to be an enslaved man who won his freedom through cleverness. In Soviet Russia, Aesopian language meant writing your real point in code — because the fable was still the safest way to criticise power.

q: There was a king of the Phaeacians in the Odyssey. He gave the shipwrecked Odysseus a feast, gifts and a ship home, asking nothing first. Which word grew out of it?
f: Alcinous had a garden where fruit ripened all year round and never failed. He also had the good manners to feed his exhausted guest for two days before asking him who he was.

q: There was an English scholar at Charlemagne's court. He led the palace school and drove the revival of learning across the Frankish empire. Which word grew out of it?
f: Alcuin's scribes developed a clear rounded script called Carolingian minuscule to replace the tangle scribes had been using. Renaissance printers copied it, and the lower-case letters you are reading now descend directly from it.

q: There was a goat who nursed the infant Zeus. One of her horns broke off and filled forever with whatever its holder wished for. Which word grew out of it?
f: Amalthea's broken horn became the cornucopia — the horn of plenty still drawn overflowing with fruit at harvest festivals. Zeus later set her among the stars in gratitude for the milk.

q: "Ammonian" is named after a person.
f: Camel caravans camped at the temple of Amun, and a white salt crusted the ground where they did. Romans called it sal ammoniac, salt of Amun. Every bottle of ammonia is named after an Egyptian god by way of camel dung.

q: There was a Roman emperor. His reign was the calm centre of what Gibbon called the happiest period in human history. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Antonine Wall was built across Scotland under him, north of Hadrian's, and abandoned within about twenty years. Rome kept the older wall — the one named after the emperor who did less building.

q: There was a Roman gourmet of the first century AD. The oldest surviving cookbook in the West carries his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: The recipes attributed to Apicius include flamingo and dormice stuffed with pork. Legend says he poisoned himself on discovering he had only a modest fortune left and could no longer eat as he wished.

q: There was a French poet. He coined the word surrealism and wrote poems shaped like the objects they described. Which word grew out of it?
f: Apollinaire wrote calligrammes — poems typeset in the shape of a horse, the Eiffel Tower, falling rain. He also invented the word surrealism, three years before the movement that took it existed.

q: There was a Greek scholar and critic. As librarian at Alexandria he marked doubtful lines of Homer with a severity that became proverbial. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aristarchus went through Homer marking every line he thought was a later addition, using a small horizontal stroke in the margin. That stroke is the ancestor of the obelus, and the dagger symbol still used in footnotes.

q: There was an English poet and critic. He defined culture as the best which has been thought and said in the world. Which word grew out of it?
f: Arnold spent his working life as a school inspector, travelling England examining classrooms, and wrote criticism in the gaps. He argued that culture was the antidote to what he called anarchy, by which he mostly meant the middle classes.

q: Which word meaning "of Athens or Athena" comes from a Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare?
f: Athena and Poseidon competed for the city. He struck the rock and produced a salt spring; she planted an olive tree. The citizens chose the olive, and the city took her name.

q: "Attic" is named after a place.
f: Attic salt means dry Athenian wit. The attic in your house is the same word: architects called a small decorative upper storey in the Athenian manner an attic storey, and the name slid up into the roof space.

q: There was a prince in a tale from the Arabian Nights. He served a starving beggar a magnificent banquet of entirely empty dishes. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Barmecide describes each imaginary course in loving detail while the beggar mimes eating it. The beggar plays along, then pretends to be drunk on imaginary wine and punches him — at which the prince laughs and serves a real dinner.

q: There was a dante's idealised love. She guides him through Paradise in the Divine Comedy after Virgil can go no further. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dante met Beatrice when they were both about nine and spoke to her only a handful of times. She married someone else and died at twenty-four. He put her in charge of heaven.

q: There was an English philosopher. He proposed judging every action by how much happiness it produced overall. Which word grew out of it?
f: Bentham also designed the panopticon, a prison where one unseen guard could watch every cell. It was never built to his plan, but the idea has been borrowed by everyone writing about surveillance since.

q: There was a Roman philosopher. Awaiting execution, he wrote The Consolation of Philosophy and its image of Fortune's turning wheel. Which word grew out of it?
f: Boethius wrote his masterpiece in a cell while waiting to be executed for treason. The wheel of fortune he described — lifting people up only to drop them — became the standard medieval image for how luck works.

q: There was a Flemish painter. He filled his canvases with crowds of peasants at work, at play and at their worst. Which word grew out of it?
f: Bruegel painted a hundred children's games in a single picture and a village wedding where you can count the pies. In his Icarus, the boy falls out of the sky and every farmer in the painting keeps working.

q: There was a Scottish physician. He taught that all disease came from too much or too little excitement in the body. Which word grew out of it?
f: Brown reduced medicine to one dial: too stimulated or not stimulated enough. Treatment was opium or alcohol accordingly. It was wrong, wildly popular across Europe, and probably killed more patients than it saved.

q: "Carolingian" is named after a person.
f: Charlemagne ruled most of western Europe and worked at learning to write late in life, keeping a tablet under his pillow to practise. He never quite managed it, but he made sure his empire's scribes could.

q: There was a Trojan prophetess of Greek myth. Her prophecies were always right and never believed. Which word grew out of it?
f: Apollo gave Cassandra prophecy hoping to win her affection. When she refused him he could not take the gift back, so he added a condition: she would always be right, and nobody would ever act on it.

q: There was a Roman poet. He wrote short, direct, intensely personal poems about love and hatred. Which word grew out of it?
f: Catullus survives by luck — a single manuscript turned up in Verona around 1300 and vanished again after being copied. His most famous poem is two lines long and begins by saying he hates and loves at the same time.

q: Which word meaning "of Chaldea" comes from a region of southern Babylonia?
f: Chaldean astronomers kept night-sky records for centuries and could predict eclipses. Greeks and Romans used Chaldean to mean fortune-teller, which was rather like calling an astronomer a horoscope writer.

q: There was a Roman orator. Italian guides who talked at length about the sights were nicknamed after the most talkative Roman. Which word grew out of it?
f: Eighteenth-century travellers on the Grand Tour hired local guides and named them ciceroni — after Cicero, whose reputation for eloquence had by then drifted into a reputation for not stopping.

q: There was a Roman emperor. Dismissed as a stammering fool, he proved a capable administrator who conquered Britain. Which word grew out of it?
f: Claudius survived the purges that killed the rest of his family precisely because nobody thought him worth killing. The Praetorian Guard found him hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder and made him emperor.

q: There was an English poet. His dreamlike Kubla Khan and Ancient Mariner defined the visionary side of Romanticism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Coleridge said Kubla Khan came to him complete in a dream, and that he was writing it down when a person from Porlock knocked on the door about business. By the time he got rid of the visitor, the rest of the poem was gone.

q: "Corneillean" is named after a place.
f: Corneille's Le Cid was so popular that the French Academy was pushed to condemn it for breaking the rules of classical drama. Audiences kept going anyway, and the phrase beau comme le Cid entered the language.

q: There was an English soldier and Lord Protector. He led Parliament's army, signed a king's death warrant, and ruled without a crown. Which word grew out of it?
f: Cromwell told his portrait painter to include everything, warts and all, or he would not pay for it. Two years after his death the restored monarchy dug up his body and executed it anyway.

q: There was a small Greek island, birthplace of Apollo. It was the sacred centre of an Athenian-led alliance whose treasury was kept there. Which word grew out of it?
f: Delos was so sacred that no one was allowed to be born or to die on it. There is also the Delian problem: an oracle demanded the islanders double a cube-shaped altar, which turns out to be impossible with compass and straightedge.

q: There was a Greek god of wine and theatre. His festivals combined drinking, masks and the first performances of Greek drama. Which word grew out of it?
f: Western theatre started as a religious festival for Dionysus. The plays of Sophocles and Euripides were competition entries, performed once, in an open-air theatre, at a party for the god of wine.

q: There was an Athenian lawgiver. His code prescribed death for almost every offence, including stealing a cabbage. Which word grew out of it?
f: Asked why the penalty for minor theft was death, Draco reportedly said small crimes deserved it and he could find nothing worse for the large ones. The laws were said to be written in blood rather than ink.

q: Which word meaning "of the 1900s in Britain" comes from a british king?
f: Edward waited fifty-nine years to become king — the longest apprenticeship in British history — and reigned nine. The decade named after him is remembered as one long garden party, mainly because of what came next.

q: Which word meaning "of Elizabeth I's reign" comes from a queen of England?
f: Elizabeth reigned forty-four years and refused to marry throughout, telling Parliament she was already married to England. The theatre, the language and the navy all took their modern shape while she was on the throne.

q: "Fabianism" is named after a person.
f: The Fabian Society, founded in 1884, chose the name deliberately: change by patience, not revolution. Its members included George Bernard Shaw and H. G. Wells, and it helped found the British Labour Party.

q: There was a legendary warrior band of Irish myth led by Finn MacCool. Nineteenth-century Irish republicans took the ancient warriors' name for their movement. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Fianna were mythical hunter-warriors who roamed Ireland in the old stories. When republicans organised in 1858 they reached back two thousand years for a name, which tells you how they wanted to be seen.

q: Which word meaning "of France, especially its church" comes from a Roman name for the region that became France?
f: Gaul gave French a great deal: Gallic wit, Gallicanism, and the rooster that is still France's unofficial emblem — because gallus is Latin for both a Gaul and a cockerel, and someone enjoyed the pun enough to keep it.

q: There was a paris building where the radical revolutionary club met. The club took its nickname from the address, and the name came to mean political extremism. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Jacobins were named after a building, not a person — the Paris convent where they met. Under Robespierre the club drove the Terror, and Jacobin has meant dangerous radicalism in English ever since.

q: There was a king of England. Jacobus is Latin for James, and his reign named a style of drama, furniture and Bible. Which word grew out of it?
f: The King James Bible was produced under him by six committees of scholars, and its cadences shaped English prose for four centuries. Jacobean drama went the other way entirely — revenge, poison and skulls.

q: There was an ancient region around Jerusalem. The name of the kingdom of Judah gave us both Judaea and Jew. Which word grew out of it?
f: Judaea is named for Judah, one of the twelve tribes, whose emblem was a lion. The name travelled: from the tribe to the kingdom to the Roman province, and from there into the word Jewish.

q: Which word meaning "of Napoleon" comes from a French emperor?
f: Napoleon's civil code is still the backbone of the legal system in dozens of countries. He was of perfectly ordinary height for his time — the short-Napoleon story comes from British cartoons and a confusion between French and English inches.

q: "Pauline" is named after a place.
f: Paul began as Saul, a persecutor of Christians, and changed course after a blinding experience on the road to Damascus. A Damascene conversion — a sudden complete reversal — is named from that same journey.

q: There was a French artist and inventor. He fixed an image on a silvered copper plate, producing the first practical photograph. Which word grew out of it?
f: The French government bought Daguerre's process in 1839 and gave it to the world free — except in England, where he patented it. Each daguerreotype was unique: there was no negative, so no copies could be made.

q: There was a French architect. He popularised a roof with two slopes, the lower one steep, creating a usable extra floor. Which word grew out of it?
f: Paris property was once taxed by the number of floors below the roofline, so a mansard roof added a whole storey the tax collector did not count. Good architecture and good accounting at the same time.

q: Which word meaning "the dot-and-dash telegraph code" comes from an American painter and inventor?
f: Morse was a portrait painter first. Away from home on a commission, he received a letter saying his wife was ill; by the time he got back she was already buried. He spent the rest of his life on faster messages.

q: There was a French weaver and inventor. His loom used punched cards to control the pattern automatically. Which word grew out of it?
f: Jacquard's loom read its pattern from a chain of punched cards. Charles Babbage saw one and borrowed the idea for his calculating engine, and punched cards ran computers into the 1970s. Modern computing starts with a French silk loom.

q: Which word meaning "a large short-haired guard dog" comes from a German tax collector?
f: Dobermann collected taxes in a rough district and also ran the local dog pound, which gave him unusual access to breeding stock. He set out to build the perfect bodyguard, and the breed still carries his name.

q: Which word meaning "a hairstyle with the hair swept up from the forehead" comes from a mistress of Louis XV of France?
f: Madame de Pompadour was the most powerful woman at Versailles without being queen, and set fashion for two decades. Two centuries later Elvis Presley wore a version of her hairstyle, which she would probably have enjoyed.

q: "bechamel" is named after a person.
f: Bechameil was a wealthy court official, not a cook. Another courtier complained that the man was lucky — he himself had been serving the same sauce for years before Bechameil was born, and nobody had named it after him.

q: Which word meaning "a soft creamy cheese with a white rind" comes from a village in Normandy, France?
f: The story goes that Marie Harel sheltered a priest fleeing the French Revolution, and he taught her a cheesemaking method from Brie. The round wooden box came later, and is why Camembert could travel.

q: There was a village in southern France. The blue cheese must be aged in the natural limestone caves beneath the village. Which word grew out of it?
f: Only cheese ripened in the caves of one specific village may be called Roquefort — a protection first granted by royal charter in 1411, making it one of the oldest brand protections in the world.

q: There was a town in western France. Brandy distilled from grapes grown around the town takes its name. Which word grew out of it?
f: All cognac is brandy, but only brandy from around this one town may be called cognac. The rule is strict enough that even neighbouring Armagnac, made a hundred miles away, has to use its own name.

q: What does "champagne" mean?
c: Sparkling wine from the Champagne region
f: The region's name comes from the Latin campania, meaning open country. The bubbles were originally an accident and considered a fault — the cold Champagne winters stopped fermentation, which restarted in spring inside the sealed bottle.

q: Which word meaning "a deep purplish red" comes from a region in eastern France?
f: Burgundy is one of a small group of colours named after drinks — along with claret and port. The region itself is named for the Burgundians, a Germanic people who settled there around 1,500 years ago.

q: Which word meaning "porcelain tableware" comes from the country?
f: Europeans spent centuries trying to work out how the Chinese made porcelain so thin that light passed through it. The recipe was finally cracked in Saxony in 1708, but by then the tableware was permanently called china.

q: "damask" is named after a place.
f: Damascus gave English three words: damask for the cloth, damascene for patterned steel and inlaid metal, and damson for the plum. All three arrived along the same trade routes.

q: Which word meaning "hard-wearing cotton twill fabric" comes from a city in southern France?
f: Your jeans are named after two European cities at once. The fabric is de Nimes, from Nimes in France. The trousers are from Genoa in Italy, which the French called Genes — which English turned into jeans.

q: What does "cashmere" mean?
c: Very fine soft wool from the cashmere goat
Confused mixture of voices or languages
f: Cashmere is not the goat's outer coat but the soft underlayer it grows for winter, combed out by hand in spring. One goat yields a few ounces a year, which is why a cashmere jumper costs what it does.

q: What does "angora" mean?
c: Wool from the angora goat or rabbit
Confused mixture of voices or languages
f: Angora names three different animals — a goat, a rabbit and a cat — all long-haired, all from around Ankara. Confusingly, the goat's wool is sold as mohair, and only the rabbit's is sold as angora.

q: There was a city in northern Iraq. European traders first met the fine cotton cloth there and named it for the city. Which word grew out of it?
f: The finest muslin actually came from Bengal, where weavers produced cloth so sheer it was nicknamed woven air. Europeans met it in Mosul first, so the Iraqi city got the credit and the name.

q: There was a port city in Kerala, India, now Kozhikode. Printed cotton shipped from the port took its name across Europe. Which word grew out of it?
f: Calico was so popular in England that in 1721 Parliament banned it outright to protect the wool trade. The ban lasted thirty-three years and made smuggling printed cotton genuinely profitable.

q: There was a country in North Africa. The ribbed crepe fabric took the French name for Moroccan. Which word grew out of it?
f: Marocain is simply French for Moroccan. It is one of several fabrics that arrived in Europe with a nationality attached and kept it, alongside morocco leather from the same country.

q: "cordovan" is named after a person.
f: Cordoba's leather was so famous that the workers who made shoes from it were called cordwainers — a word still used for shoemakers in Britain, six centuries after the trade with Spain dried up.

q: Which word meaning "leather with a soft napped finish" comes from the country?
f: Suede is just the French word for Sweden. Parisians bought Swedish gloves made from the underside of the skin rather than the smooth outer face, and English took the country's name for the texture.

q: There was last king of Illyria. He was said to have discovered the medicinal value of the plant's bitter root. Which word grew out of it?
f: Gentius lost his kingdom to Rome and was paraded through the streets as a captive. His one lasting monument is a small blue alpine flower, named because he supposedly found a use for its extraordinarily bitter root.

q: There was a Flemish botanist. He was physician to James I of England, and the plant was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: De l'Obel tried to classify plants by the shape of their leaves, which was wrong but useful — it was one of the first attempts to sort plants by their structure rather than by whether they were edible.

q: There was a Greek phrase meaning 'of good name'. The shrub is poisonous to livestock, so the flattering name was a superstitious precaution. Which word grew out of it?
f: The name means good name or lucky name — given precisely because the plant is poisonous to cattle. Farmers named it something pleasant in the hope of not attracting bad luck. It is also called the spindle tree.

q: Which word meaning "a garden plant with funnel-shaped flowers" comes from a Tupi word for tobacco?
f: Petunia is not named after a person or a place but after a plant it merely resembles. Petun is the Tupi word for tobacco, and petunias and tobacco really are close relatives — both in the nightshade family.

q: Which word meaning "a knitted garment" comes from a channel Island between England and France?
f: Jersey knitting was originally what fishermen wore. The island also gave its name to a small fawn-coloured cow prized for creamy milk, and to a large American state that needed a name in 1664.

q: "holland" is named after a place.
f: Holland cloth was the standard lining and window-blind fabric for centuries. The region also gave English the Dutch oven, Dutch courage and going Dutch — mostly coined by the English during periods of naval rivalry.

q: There was a French dressmaker. The sheer crinkled silk she popularised took her first name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Georgette is one of very few fabrics named after a woman, and one of fewer still named by first name rather than surname. The crinkle comes from twisting the yarn hard in opposite directions before weaving.

q: There was a town in northern France. Its lacemakers produced a fine bobbin lace with a distinctive diamond mesh. Which word grew out of it?
f: Valenciennes lace was so slow to make that a skilled worker might produce an inch and a half in a day, and only in a cool damp cellar — dry air made the linen thread snap.

q: There was a town in northern France. It was the leading medieval centre for woven wall tapestries. Which word grew out of it?
f: An arras hung a little away from the wall, which made it useful for eavesdropping. Polonius hides behind one in Hamlet to listen in, and Hamlet stabs straight through the cloth.

q: There was a capital of Syria. Its smiths inlaid steel with gold and silver in flowing patterns; also the site of Paul's conversion. Which word grew out of it?
f: Damascene carries two unrelated senses from the same city: watered patterns in steel, and a Damascene conversion — a sudden reversal of belief, from the apostle Paul's experience on the road there.

q: Which word meaning "a small dark purple plum" comes from a capital of Syria?
f: Damson is Damascus worn down by centuries of English mouths: damascenum, damascene, damson. The Romans carried the tree west, and it grows in English hedgerows now as if it had always been there.

q: Which word meaning "a thick cold sauce of egg yolk and oil" comes from a port on the island of Menorca?
f: The usual story credits the Duke of Richelieu's cook, improvising a sauce after taking Port Mahon in 1756. Rival theories point to the town of Bayonne or to the French word for egg yolk. Nobody can settle it.

q: "bologna" is named after a person.
f: Bologna's own mortadella is studded with pistachios and cubes of fat. The American version dropped nearly all of that, kept the name, and pronounced it baloney — which then became a word for nonsense.

q: Which word meaning "a hard, sharp, aged Italian cheese" comes from a city in northern Italy?
f: Real Parmigiano-Reggiano ages at least a year, and each wheel is tested by a man who taps it with a small hammer and listens. Wheels that sound wrong inside are marked and sold under a different name.

q: Which word meaning "a firm smooth Italian cheese, often smoked" comes from a southern Italian cheese name, from a word meaning a round shape?
f: Provolone means big provola. It is a pasta filata cheese — the curd is heated and stretched like dough until it turns glossy, the same technique that makes mozzarella, then hung in ropes to age.

q: There was a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. Its fortified wine survived long sea voyages and improved in the heat. Which word grew out of it?
f: Madeira was discovered to taste better after crossing the tropics twice in a hot ship's hold. Producers began heating it deliberately. American revolutionaries toasted the Declaration of Independence with it.

q: There was a Portuguese island in the Atlantic. The plain butter sponge was named not for its ingredients but for the wine served alongside it. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: There is no Madeira in Madeira cake. Nineteenth-century English hosts served the plain sponge with a glass of Madeira wine in the middle of the morning, and the cake ended up named after the drink.

q: Which word meaning "a cigar made in Cuba" comes from a capital of Cuba?
f: Havana cigars are rolled from tobacco grown in the Vuelta Abajo valley, where the soil and humidity are considered impossible to reproduce. Rollers traditionally worked while a reader read novels aloud to the room.

q: There was a German for 'sea foam'. The soft white mineral is so light that it floats, and was imagined to be foam turned to stone. Which word grew out of it?
f: Not named for a person or a place but for what sailors thought it was: lumps of white mineral washing up light enough to float, so obviously sea foam gone solid. It carves beautifully, which is why pipes were made of it.

q: "frankfurter" is named after a place.
f: Frankfurt has been making this sausage since the 1400s. German emigrants brought it to America, where it met a bread roll — and the frankfurter became the hot dog, named by someone who thought the shape looked like a dachshund.

q: Which word meaning "a small smoked sausage" comes from a capital of Austria, Wien in German?
f: Vienna and Frankfurt both claim the sausage, and each named it after the other city: Austrians call it a Frankfurter, Germans call it a Wiener. The man who first made it had trained in Frankfurt and moved to Vienna.

q: There was a city in Bohemia, now the Czech Republic. The world's first pale golden lager was brewed there in 1842. Which word grew out of it?
f: Before 1842 nearly all beer was dark and cloudy. Plzen's brewers dumped thirty-six barrels of bad beer in the street, hired a Bavarian brewer, and produced a clear golden lager. Most beer in the world today is a copy of it.

q: There was a town in Alsace, France. Monks at the town's monastery made the strong-smelling cheese; the name comes from monasterium. Which word grew out of it?
f: Munster is a worn-down form of monasterium, the Latin for monastery — so the cheese is really called monastery cheese. Irish Munster is a different word entirely, from an old Irish tribal name.

q: There was a historic duchy now split between Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany. The cheese was first made by monks in the region. Which word grew out of it?
f: Limburger's smell comes from a bacterium that also lives on human skin. Researchers have shown that mosquitoes attracted to human feet are equally attracted to a piece of Limburger, which says something about both.

q: Which word meaning "a mild Dutch cheese in a red wax coating" comes from a town in the Netherlands?
f: Edam ages slowly and barely spoils, which made it the standard cheese for long sea voyages. Dutch ships carried it worldwide, and its red wax shell is really just very effective packaging.

q: Which word meaning "a mild yellow Dutch cheese" comes from a town in the Netherlands?
f: Gouda is named for a marketplace, not a dairy. The town held the sole right to trade cheese in the region, so every wheel that passed through took the town's name regardless of which farm made it.

q: "cheddar" is named after a person.
f: Cheddar Gorge's caves stay at a steady cool temperature all year, which is exactly what the cheese needs. Cheddar is now the most-eaten cheese in the world, and almost none of it comes from Cheddar.

q: Which word meaning "a strong English blue cheese" comes from a village in Cambridgeshire, England?
f: Stilton is named after a village where it was never produced. Coaches on the Great North Road stopped at the Bell Inn there, the landlord sold cheese from Leicestershire to passengers, and they named it after the stop.

q: There was a city in England. Two chemists in Worcester made the fermented sauce in 1837, from a recipe they found unpleasant at first. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lea and Perrill mixed the first batch, tasted it, hated it, and left the barrel in the cellar. Eighteen months later they tried it again out of curiosity. Fermentation had transformed it, and they started selling it immediately.

q: What does "tabasco" mean?
c: A very hot sauce made from tabasco peppers
f: Tabasco sauce has been made on the same Louisiana island since 1868, aged three years in oak barrels with salt from the salt dome beneath. The pepper — and therefore the name — came from Mexico.

q: There was a town in Venezuela, now Ciudad Bolivar. A German army surgeon there developed the bitters in 1824 as a stomach remedy for soldiers. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dr Siegert made his bitters as medicine for Simon Bolivar's troops. The town changed its name to Ciudad Bolivar in 1846 and the company later moved to Trinidad, so the bottle now names a place that no longer exists.

q: Which word meaning "a light scented perfume" comes from a city in Germany, Koln in German?
f: Giovanni Maria Farina created his scent in Cologne and wrote that it reminded him of an Italian spring morning after rain. His company still exists — arguably the oldest perfume house in the world.

q: There was a city in Germany. Literally 'water of Cologne', the original name of Farina's 1709 scent. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: Napoleon's soldiers took eau de Cologne home in such quantities that it became the standard word for light perfume across Europe. Napoleon himself is said to have used a bottle a day.

q: "magenta" is named after a place.
f: The dye was discovered in the same year as the Battle of Magenta and named to ride the news. It is one of the four printing inks — every colour photo ever printed uses a colour named after a battlefield.

q: There was a village in northern Italy. Another 1859 battle in the same campaign gave its name to a second new dye colour. Which word grew out of it?
f: Solferino's real legacy is not the colour. A Swiss traveller named Henry Dunant saw forty thousand casualties left untended after the battle, wrote a book about it, and founded the Red Cross.

q: Which word meaning "knee-length shorts" comes from a british island territory in the Atlantic?
f: Bermuda shorts began as British army tropical kit and became ordinary office wear on the island — worn with a jacket, tie and knee socks. It is still normal business dress in Bermuda.

q: Which word meaning "heavy cotton twill" comes from a port city in Italy, Genes in French?
f: Genoese sailors wore trousers of this hard-wearing cloth, and the French called the city Genes. English heard jean. The cloth in modern jeans is denim, from Nimes, so the garment is named after two cities at once.

q: Which word meaning "printed glazed cotton with a floral pattern" comes from a hindi word meaning variegated or speckled?
f: Chintz is a rare case of an English singular made from a foreign plural — chints was the plural of chint. It was so fashionable, then so common, that chintzy came to mean cheap and gaudy.

q: Which word meaning "a checked or striped cotton cloth" comes from a Malay word meaning striped?
f: Gingham was originally striped, not checked — the checks arrived later in Manchester mills. The name is Malay, one of a handful of everyday English words that came by ship from Southeast Asia.

q: There was a village in Suffolk, England. A coarse ribbed woollen cloth was woven there from the fourteenth century. Which word grew out of it?
f: Kersey is a village of a few hundred people that named a cloth traded across medieval Europe. Along with worsted from Norfolk, it is a reminder that English wool towns once set the standard for the continent.

q: "worsted" is named after a person.
f: Worstead is now a quiet village, but in the Middle Ages its cloth funded the enormous churches that still stand across Norfolk — buildings far too large for the parishes that own them.

q: There was an Arabic word meaning 'choice' or 'select'. The Arabic name for the fine goat-hair cloth was reshaped in English as if it contained the word hair. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mohair only looks like it contains the word hair. It is Arabic mukhayyar, meaning select cloth, which English speakers reshaped into something that sounded like it made sense. That process is called folk etymology.

q: Which word meaning "a fine goatskin leather" comes from a country in North Africa?
f: Morocco leather was the standard for fine bookbinding for centuries — soft enough to work, strong enough to last. The best grade is still called levant morocco, after another region entirely.

q: There was a town in central France. A fine silk net for veils and gowns was first made there. Which word grew out of it?
f: Tulle is the stuff of every ballet skirt and wedding veil. The town that named it is a quiet place in the Correze that most French people associate with something else entirely — it is also a former presidential hometown.

q: Which word meaning "a thin transparent fabric" comes from a city on the eastern Mediterranean?
f: The Gaza origin is the traditional explanation, though some scholars trace gauze to an Arabic word for raw silk instead. Either way it arrived in Europe along Mediterranean trade routes with its name attached.

q: There was a city in present-day Uzbekistan. The crisp sheer cotton is thought to be named for the Silk Road city that traded it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Organdy is the crispest cotton made — the stiffness comes from treating the woven cloth with acid. Its name most likely travelled the Silk Road from Urgench, a city few English speakers have ever heard of.

q: There was a city in the Netherlands. Its potters imitated Chinese porcelain in blue on white tin-glazed earthenware. Which word grew out of it?
f: Delft potters were copying Chinese porcelain they could not chemically reproduce, so they faked it: white tin glaze over ordinary clay, painted blue. The imitation became famous in its own right and outlived the thing it imitated.

q: "majolica" is named after a place.
f: Majolica is named for a stopover, not a source. The pottery was Spanish, but it reached Italian buyers through Majorca, and Italians named it after the island the ships came from.

q: There was a city in northern Italy. French buyers named the tin-glazed pottery after the Italian city that supplied it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Faience and majolica are nearly the same pottery named by two different countries after two different middlemen — the French said Faenza, the Italians said Majorca. Both were describing tin-glazed earthenware.

q: There was a london street and market carriers of the eighteenth century. The strong dark beer was popular with the men who hauled goods around the city. Which word grew out of it?
f: Porter is named after its drinkers rather than a person or place — the porters who carried loads through London markets. Extra-strong porter was called stout porter, which is where stout comes from.

q: There was a port town in western Sicily. An English merchant began fortifying the local wine in 1773 so it would survive shipping. Which word grew out of it?
f: John Woodhouse's ship sheltered at Marsala, he tasted the local wine, and he added spirit so it would survive the voyage to England. Sicily got an export industry out of one storm.

q: There was a town in Andalusia, Spain. English traders pronounced Jerez as sherris, then took it for a plural and made a singular from it. Which word grew out of it?
f: English merchants heard Jerez, said sherris, assumed the s meant plural, and invented sherry as the singular. The same mistake gave English pea from pease and cherry from cerise.

q: There was an old French word meaning 'pale' or 'clear'. Medieval Bordeaux wine was lighter in colour than modern red, so the English called it clairet. Which word grew out of it?
f: Claret describes a colour, not a place — the pale red of medieval Bordeaux, which was closer to today's rose. English drinkers kept the word even after the wine got much darker.

q: There was a region of Gascony in southwest France. Brandy distilled there predates cognac by about two centuries. Which word grew out of it?
f: Armagnac is older than cognac and distilled only once rather than twice, which leaves more flavour and less polish. It is made in far smaller quantities, largely because Armagnac has no river to the sea.

q: "panama" is named after a person.
f: Panama hats are Ecuadorian. They were shipped through Panama, and when Theodore Roosevelt was photographed wearing one at the canal works in 1906, the wrong name stuck permanently to a hat from another country.

q: Which word meaning "to heat a liquid briefly to destroy harmful microbes" comes from a French chemist and microbiologist?
f: Pasteur was asked to find out why French wine kept going sour. He found living organisms in it, and that a short spell at moderate heat killed them without ruining the taste. Milk got the same treatment, and childhood deaths dropped.

q: Which word meaning "a grain crop" comes from a Roman goddess of grain and harvest?
f: Your breakfast is named after a Roman goddess. Ceres governed grain and the harvest, and the Romans called the crops themselves cerealia — her things. Four thousand years later it is written on a cardboard box.

q: Which word meaning "quick-changing and unpredictable in mood" comes from a Roman messenger god?
f: Mercury had winged sandals and never stayed anywhere long. The only liquid metal was named after him for the same reason — it rolls away the moment you touch it. A mercurial person is just as hard to hold.

q: Which word meaning "a mountain that erupts molten rock" comes from a Roman god of fire and the forge?
f: There is a small Italian island called Vulcano, named for the god the Romans thought was hammering away beneath it. Every volcano on Earth — and on Mars — is named after one god's forge.

q: Which word meaning "fragments scattered by an exploding shell" comes from a british artillery officer?
f: Shrapnel spent his own money developing the shell and worked on it for years before the army adopted it in 1803. He got a pension and a word in every language. It is not the legacy most people would choose.

q: Which word meaning "strips of facial hair grown down the sides of the face" comes from American Civil War general?
f: They were called burnsides first, after the general who wore an enormous pair. Somewhere along the way English swapped the two halves and produced sideburns — which now sounds like it describes the sides, purely by accident.

q: "dunce" is named after a place.
f: Duns Scotus was one of the sharpest minds of the Middle Ages. When fashions in learning changed, his stubborn followers were mocked as Dunses — and one of the cleverest men of his age ended up meaning the opposite.

q: There was a French writer and aristocrat. He wrote about cruelty at length and spent much of his life imprisoned. Which word grew out of it?
f: De Sade spent roughly thirty-two years locked up, and wrote much of his work in prison — including one novel on a continuous roll of paper hidden in his cell wall. A psychiatrist coined sadism from his name in 1886.

q: There was an Austrian writer. His novel Venus in Furs described a man who found pleasure in being dominated. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sacher-Masoch was a respected historian and novelist who deeply resented having his name turned into a clinical term. The psychiatrist Krafft-Ebing coined it anyway, and paired it with sadism in the same book.

q: Which word meaning "a slip in which the first sounds of words are swapped" comes from an oxford don and clergyman?
f: Spooner is supposed to have toasted our queer old dean instead of our dear old queen. Most of the famous examples were probably invented by students, but he really did make the slips — and only ever admitted to one.

q: Which word meaning "a large dark berry crossed from several species" comes from an American horticulturist?
f: Boysen gave up and left his experimental vines to die. Walter Knott tracked down the last few survivors on the abandoned farm, nursed them back, and named the berry after the man who had quit.

q: There was a French nobleman. His cook coated almonds in caramelised sugar and named the sweet after his employer. Which word grew out of it?
f: The cook, Clement Lassagne, is said to have invented the sweet after watching a kitchen boy eat spilled caramel and almonds. He named it for his employer, opened a shop, and the shop still exists in Montargis.

q: Which word meaning "a pizza of tomato, mozzarella and basil" comes from a queen of Italy?
f: In 1889 Raffaele Esposito made three pizzas for the visiting queen. She preferred the patriotic one, and he named it after her. Whether the story is strictly true is argued over, but the pizza is definitely named for a queen.

q: "salmonella" is named after a person.
f: Theobald Smith actually identified the organism. Salmon was his supervisor, and the naming followed the rank rather than the work — an old habit in science. Salmon was the first person in America to earn a veterinary doctorate.

q: There was a british surgeon. He pioneered antiseptic surgery, and the bacterium was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: Lister worked out that infection came from invisible organisms and started spraying carbolic acid in operating theatres. Death rates collapsed. He has a bacterium named after him and, less flatteringly, a mouthwash.

q: There was a Soviet foreign minister. Finns mocked his claim that Soviet bombs were food parcels, and named their petrol bombs a drink to go with the bread. Which word grew out of it?
f: Molotov said Soviet aircraft were dropping food to starving Finns. The Finns called the cluster bombs Molotov bread baskets — and named their own petrol bombs Molotov cocktails, a drink to go with the meal.

q: Which word meaning "a unit of loudness" comes from a Scottish-American inventor?
f: The bel turned out to be too big for everyday use, so almost nobody uses it — we use tenths. Bell's mother and wife were both deaf, and his work on sound began as work on teaching deaf children to speak.

q: Which word meaning "a gas burner giving a hot clean flame" comes from a German chemist?
