f: Peter Desaga, Bunsen's instrument maker, actually built the burner to Bunsen's specification. Bunsen also lost the sight in one eye to an explosion and nearly died twice of arsenic poisoning. Chemistry was more dangerous then.

q: Which word meaning "to punish without lawful trial" comes from a virginia planter and judge?
f: Lynch's court handed out floggings, not hangings — the killing sense came later and much worse. Lynch law began as a phrase for rough frontier justice and turned into a word for one of America's darkest habits.

q: Which word meaning "the first month of the year" comes from a Roman god of doorways and beginnings?
f: Janus guarded doorways and had a face on each side, so he could see where you had been and where you were going at the same time. That is exactly what people do on the first of January.

q: "march" is named after a place.
f: March was once the first month of the Roman year — the point where winter ended and armies could move again. That is also why September, October, November and December mean seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth.

q: Which word meaning "the fifth month of the year" comes from a Roman goddess of growth and spring?
f: Maia was a goddess of growing things, and her month is when growth is at its fastest. She was also the mother of Mercury, which makes May and mercurial distant relatives.

q: Which word meaning "the sixth month of the year" comes from a Roman queen of the gods, protector of marriage?
f: Juno looked after marriage, so Romans thought June the luckiest month for a wedding. Two thousand years later June is still the most popular wedding month in much of the world, for a reason almost nobody remembers.

q: Which word meaning "the seventh day of the week" comes from a Roman god of agriculture and time?
f: Saturday is the odd one out. The Anglo-Saxons swapped most Roman gods for their own — Mars became Tiw, Jupiter became Thor — but nobody found a match for Saturn, so he kept his day.

q: Which word meaning "the fifth day of the week" comes from a Norse god of thunder?
f: The Romans called it Jupiter's day; the Anglo-Saxons had their own thunder god and swapped him in. In French it is still jeudi, from Jove — so the same day is named after two different thunder gods in two languages.

q: Which word meaning "the sixth day of the week" comes from a Norse goddess, wife of Odin?
f: Friday matches Frigg to Venus — love goddess for love goddess. French kept the Roman version as vendredi. English took the Norse one, which is why our week is a mixture of two different mythologies.

q: Which word meaning "the third day of the week" comes from a Norse and Germanic god of war, also called Tyr?
f: Tyr lost his hand feeding it to a giant wolf as a pledge, knowing the pledge was a lie — the bravest act in Norse myth. His day is the plain-sounding Tuesday, which does not hint at any of that.

q: "wednesday" is named after a person.
f: Wednesday is Woden's day, and the silent d is the fossil of the missing name. Odin gave an eye for wisdom and hung from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes — none of which survives in the spelling except that d.

q: Which word meaning "a man's formal dinner jacket" comes from a wealthy village in New York State?
f: Tuxedo Park is named from a Lenape word, probably meaning something like crooked river. So the most formal jacket in English is named after a New York country club named after a Native American place name.

q: What does "ottoman" mean?
c: A low padded seat or footstool without a back
Of Phoenicia; relating to its traders and alphabet
Boldly original and defiant of limits
f: An empire that lasted six hundred years is now best known in English homes as a padded footstool. Osman's dynasty ruled from the Balkans to Arabia, and the furniture is what English kept of the name.

q: What does "spencer" mean?
f: One story says his coat-tails caught fire at a fireplace and he simply had them cut off. Another says he lost a bet. Either way the cropped jacket became fashionable and has come back roughly once a century since.

q: There was an elizabethan executioner at Tyburn. His hoisting gallows design gave its name first to the gallows and then to any lifting crane. Which word grew out of it?
f: Derrick was a convicted criminal pardoned on condition that he become the hangman. His gallows used a pivoting beam and pulley, and oil rigs use the same shape and the same name four hundred years later.

q: Which word meaning "ostentatiously luxurious" comes from a Swiss hotelier?
f: Ritz was fired from his first restaurant job for being unsuited to the trade. He went on to run the Savoy, open the Paris Ritz, and put his name into English twice — as ritzy and in putting on the Ritz.

q: Which word meaning "a giant redwood tree of California" comes from a Cherokee scholar?
f: Sequoyah could not read any language when he began, and worked for twelve years to build a writing system from scratch. Within a few years most of the Cherokee nation was literate. The largest trees on Earth carry his name.

q: "bougainvillea" is named after a place.
f: The plant was probably first described by Jeanne Baret, the expedition's botanist's assistant, who sailed disguised as a man and became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe. The plant is named after the captain.

q: Which word meaning "a small brightly coloured freshwater fish" comes from a trinidad clergyman and naturalist?
f: The guppy had already been described and named twice before Guppy sent his specimens, so his name is not the official scientific one. It is the one everybody actually uses, which he probably would have settled for.

q: There was an American judge and amateur breeder. He crossed a blackberry with a raspberry in his garden, by accident. Which word grew out of it?
f: Logan was trying to breed better blackberries and planted his varieties too close to a raspberry. The bees did the rest. He was a judge by profession and got a fruit named after him for a gardening mistake.

q: Which word meaning "a small sweet seedless citrus fruit" comes from a French missionary in Algeria?
f: Brother Clement ran an orphanage outside Oran and noticed one tree in the garden producing unusually sweet, seedless fruit. It was a chance hybrid. Every clementine sold today descends from that single accidental tree.

q: Which word meaning "a seedless variety of mandarin orange" comes from a former province in southern Japan?
f: The wife of an American ambassador sent trees home from Satsuma province in 1878 and the name travelled with them. In Japan the same fruit is called mikan — nobody there calls it a satsuma.

q: Which word meaning "a small loose-skinned orange" comes from a port city in Morocco?
f: Tangerines are named for the port they were shipped from, not where they grew — the fruit is originally Chinese. It is the same pattern as the Panama hat: the name records the harbour, not the home.

q: Which word meaning "a sweet orange-fleshed melon" comes from a papal country estate near Rome?
f: Cantalupo means something like wolf-song. The melon came from Armenia by way of a papal garden, and the sweet orange fruit in your fruit salad is named after a place where wolves were once heard howling.

q: "sousaphone" is named after a person.
f: Sousa wanted a bass instrument that would carry sound over a marching band rather than up into the sky. He wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever too, so he is one of very few people who named both an instrument and an anthem.

q: There was a Russian inventor. He built an instrument played by moving the hands near two antennas, without touching it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Theremin invented his instrument by accident while building a proximity sensor. He later designed a Soviet listening device that hung inside the American embassy for seven years, powered by nothing but the radio beam aimed at it.

q: There was an Italian violin maker. His instruments have never been convincingly matched, and his Latinised name marks them. Which word grew out of it?
f: Stradivari made about 1,100 instruments and around 650 survive. Scientists have tested the varnish, the wood density, even the effect of a colder climate on the trees, and still cannot agree on why they sound the way they do.

q: What does "steinway" mean?
c: A piano made by Steinway and Sons
f: Steinweg built his first piano in his kitchen in Germany as a wedding gift for his wife. He emigrated in 1850, changed the name to Steinway because it sounded better in English, and the firm holds well over a hundred patents.

q: There was an American engineer. He built the first widely used voltage-controlled music synthesizer. Which word grew out of it?
f: Moog started out building theremin kits as a teenager. His synthesizer reached the public through a 1968 album of Bach played entirely on it, which went platinum and put an electronic instrument in ordinary living rooms.

q: There was a French physicist. He measured the force between electric charges and the unit of charge took his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Coulomb measured forces far too small to feel by hanging a rod from a fine thread and watching how far it twisted. The same delicate trick was later used to weigh the Earth.

q: There was a Scottish physicist. His equations unified electricity, magnetism and light; a unit of magnetic flux bears his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Maxwell's four equations showed that light is an electromagnetic wave — arguably the single greatest leap in physics between Newton and Einstein. Einstein kept a photograph of him on his study wall.

q: "gray" is named after a place.
f: Gray worked out how to measure exactly how much radiation a tissue absorbs — the difference between a useful cancer treatment and a lethal exposure. It is a rare unit that is genuinely a matter of life and death.

q: There was a Swedish physicist. He mapped the solar spectrum in units of one ten-billionth of a metre. Which word grew out of it?
f: An angstrom is about the width of a hydrogen atom, which makes it the natural ruler for anything atomic. Angstrom also found hydrogen in the Sun, using nothing but the colours in its light.

q: Which word meaning "the ratio of speed to the speed of sound" comes from an Austrian physicist and philosopher?
f: Mach photographed a bullet in flight in 1887 and captured the shock wave coming off it — the first evidence anyone had seen. Mach 1 is not a fixed speed: sound travels slower in cold air, so it changes with altitude.

q: There was an American virologist. He developed the first effective polio vaccine and refused to patent it. Which word grew out of it?
f: Asked who owned the patent, Salk said the people did — could you patent the sun? Forgoing the patent may have cost him billions. Polio cases in the United States fell from around 58,000 a year to almost none.

q: Which word meaning "a diagram of overlapping circles showing set relations" comes from an English logician?
f: Venn called them Eulerian circles and never claimed to have invented them — versions appear centuries earlier. He did build a cricket bowling machine that clean bowled a visiting Australian team, which he may have preferred to be known for.

q: The word "nobel" is named after…?
f: A French paper mistakenly printed Nobel's obituary while he was alive, under the headline The Merchant of Death Is Dead. He read his own reputation, disliked it, and rewrote his will to fund the prizes.

q: There was a Hungarian-American newspaper publisher. He endowed prizes for journalism and letters in his will. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pulitzer arrived in America as a penniless immigrant recruited into the Union army, and ended up owning New York's biggest paper. He also helped pay for the Statue of Liberty's pedestal by shaming his readers into donating.

q: "oscar" is named after a person.
f: Three people claimed to have named it, all saying the statuette reminded them of someone called Oscar. The Academy could not settle the argument, gave up, and made the nickname official.

q: There was a Belgian-American chemist. He created the first fully synthetic plastic and named it after himself. Which word grew out of it?
f: Bakelite was the first plastic made from nothing that had ever been alive — no plant, no insect, entirely synthetic. Baekeland had already made a fortune inventing photographic paper, and could afford to experiment.

q: Which word meaning "a long-distance race of about 42 kilometres" comes from a plain in Greece, site of a battle in 490 BC?
f: The modern distance was set at the 1908 London Olympics so the race could start at Windsor Castle and finish in front of the royal box — which is why every marathon since has been an oddly specific 42.195 kilometres.

q: Which word meaning "a place of learning or a society of scholars" comes from a Greek hero whose sacred grove stood outside Athens?
f: Plato's school met in an olive grove sacred to a half-forgotten hero named Akademos. It ran for nearly nine hundred years, and every academy, academic and academia traces back to that one patch of ground.

q: Which word meaning "tearfully and excessively sentimental" comes from a follower of Jesus in the Gospels?
f: Medieval English pronounced Magdalene as maudlin, which is why two Oxford and Cambridge colleges spelled Magdalen are still said that way. Centuries of paintings of her in tears did the rest.

q: There was a physician to the Greek gods. Hymns of thanksgiving sung to him became the word for any song of praise. Which word grew out of it?
f: Paean was the doctor who patched the gods up when they were wounded in battle. The hymns sung to him in gratitude gave English the word for any outburst of praise.

q: There was an American engineer. His luxurious railway sleeping cars set the standard for comfortable long-distance travel. Which word grew out of it?
f: Pullman built a whole company town for his workers, then cut wages without cutting rents. The strike that followed in 1894 shut down railways nationwide. He was buried under concrete to stop anyone digging him up.

q: "hansom" is named after a place.
f: Hansom was an architect who designed a cab as a sideline, sold the patent for £10,000 and was never paid. The cab made London's streets fast; he went back to designing churches.

q: There was a Scottish statesman. He commissioned a small enclosed carriage that could turn in a narrow street. Which word grew out of it?
f: Brougham was a lawyer, a Lord Chancellor and a campaigner against slavery, and he is remembered for a carriage. He also popularised Cannes as a resort, more or less by accident, after being stranded there.

q: There was a town in Germany. A four-wheeled carriage with a folding two-part roof was first built there. Which word grew out of it?
f: The landau's roof splits in the middle and folds both ways, so passengers could be seen in fine weather and covered in bad. British royal processions still use them for exactly that reason.

q: There was a son of the sun god in Greek myth. He begged to drive the sun chariot, lost control, and scorched the earth. Which word grew out of it?
f: Phaethon took the reins of the sun for one day and nearly destroyed the world before Zeus shot him down. Naming a fast, unstable, open carriage after him was a joke that everyone at the time understood.

q: There was a spa town in Germany. Edward VII took to wearing the local stiff felt hat and made it fashionable in Britain. Which word grew out of it?
f: The future Edward VII visited the spa, liked the hat, and brought it home. Churchill wore one, and so did nearly every diplomat photographed between the wars.

q: There was a title character of George du Maurier's 1894 novel. The hat worn in the London stage version took the character's name. Which word grew out of it?
f: The novel that gave us the word Svengali also gave us the trilby — named not for the villain but for the heroine, from the hat worn onstage in the first London production.

q: Which word meaning "a hard felt hat with a rounded crown" comes from a london hatmakers?
f: It was commissioned to stop gamekeepers being knocked off their horses by branches. The customer tested the prototype by putting it on the floor and stamping on it. It held, and he paid twelve shillings.

q: "slinky" is named after a person.
f: James was designing springs to steady instruments on rough seas when he knocked one off a shelf and watched it step end over end to the floor. His wife found the word slinky in a dictionary.

q: Which word meaning "a twisting cube puzzle" comes from a Hungarian architecture professor?
f: Rubik built it as a teaching aid and only realised he had made a puzzle when he scrambled it and could not put it back. It took him a month to solve his own invention.

q: Which word meaning "interlocking plastic building bricks" comes from a Danish phrase meaning 'play well'?
f: Lego is short for leg godt, Danish for play well. By coincidence it also means I put together in Latin, which the company only discovered later and has been enjoying ever since.

q: There was an Australian opera singer. The chef Escoffier created a peach dessert and a thin dry toast in her honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: Escoffier served peach Melba in a swan carved from ice. The toast came later, when the singer was ill and could only manage something very thin and very dry. She got a dessert and a diet food.

q: Which name or term meaning "poached eggs and ham on muffin with hollandaise" comes from a new York stockbroker?
f: Benedict wandered into the Waldorf with a hangover and asked for buttered toast, bacon, poached eggs and hollandaise. The maitre d' was impressed enough to add it to the menu, swapping in muffin and ham.

q: There was a Venetian painter. A Venice barman named his peach-and-prosecco drink after a shade of pink in one of the painter's works. Which word grew out of it?
f: Giuseppe Cipriani mixed white peach purée with prosecco at Harry's Bar and thought the colour matched a saint's toga in a Bellini painting. A fifteenth-century artist therefore named a twentieth-century drink.

q: There was an Italian aristocrat. He asked a Florence barman to strengthen his Americano by replacing the soda with gin. Which word grew out of it?
f: The count had reportedly spent time in America as a rodeo rider and came back wanting something stronger than the drink named after his adopted country. The barman swapped soda for gin, and added an orange slice to mark the difference.

q: "garibaldi" is named after a place.
f: Garibaldi unified Italy and was mobbed by crowds on a visit to England. Britain honoured the liberator of a nation by naming a flat currant biscuit after him, universally known in playgrounds as squashed-fly.

q: There was a French writer and diplomat. His chef is credited with the thick centre-cut steak served with a reduction sauce. Which word grew out of it?
f: Chateaubriand was a novelist, ambassador and foreign minister, and is now mostly a steak. His cook grilled the fillet between two lesser cuts so the outer meat burned and the middle stayed perfect, then threw the outer pieces away.

q: There was French Protestant writer. The cheese-enriched white sauce is traditionally credited to him or to his household. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mornay was a Huguenot leader nicknamed the Pope of the Protestants, who spent his life on theological argument. The attribution of the sauce is shaky, which puts it in good company among French sauces.

q: Which word meaning "a smooth sharp mustard" comes from a city in Burgundy, France?
f: Dijon mustard is a recipe, not a place of origin — the name is not protected, so most of it is made elsewhere. The seeds mostly come from Canada, which would surprise a fourteenth-century Burgundian.

q: There was a town in Switzerland. The hard alpine cheese has been made in the district since at least the twelfth century. Which word grew out of it?
f: Gruyere famously has no holes, despite being the cheese most cartoons draw with them. The holes belong to Emmental, which comes from a different Swiss valley entirely.

q: There was a valley of the river Emme in Switzerland. The cheese with large holes was made in the valley's dairies. Which word grew out of it?
f: The holes are bubbles of carbon dioxide from bacteria, and dairies can control their size by adjusting the temperature. For years the holes got smaller because the milk got cleaner — fewer hay particles for bubbles to form around.

q: Which word meaning "a soft cheese with a white rind" comes from a region east of Paris?
f: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, with Europe being carved up, the delegates held a competition to name the finest cheese. Brie won, and was dubbed the king of cheeses — the only crown that congress awarded.

q: "gorgonzola" is named after a person.
f: Legend says a distracted cheesemaker left curd overnight to chase a girl, added fresh curd in the morning to hide the lapse, and invented a blue cheese. Every blue cheese has a version of this story.

q: There was an Italian word for sheep. Any Italian cheese made from sheep's milk carries the name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Not a place or a person — pecorino just means sheepish, in the literal sense. Roman legionaries were issued a daily ration of it, which makes it one of the oldest recorded packed lunches.

q: Which word meaning "a soft fresh Italian cheese" comes from an Italian verb meaning 'to cut off'?
f: Mozzarella is named after the action that makes it: the curd is heated, stretched like dough, and pinched off in lumps. The name means the cutting-off, which is exactly what the cheesemaker's hands are doing.

q: Which word meaning "country in South America" comes from a venezuelan revolutionary leader?
f: Bolivia is one of very few countries named after a real person. Bolivar liberated six nations and died poor and disillusioned, writing that he who serves a revolution ploughs the sea.

q: Which word meaning "country in South America" comes from a Genoese navigator?
f: Columbus never set foot in Colombia. The name was chosen by a revolutionary who wanted a title for the whole of Spanish America, and it ended up attached to one country.

q: Which word meaning "country in Southeast Asia" comes from a king of Spain?
f: Named in 1543 for a Spanish prince who never visited. There have been serious proposals to change it since independence, on the grounds that the country is named after a foreign monarch who colonised it.

q: There was a Dutch navigator. He was the first European to reach the island, and it was renamed in his honour in 1856. Which word grew out of it?
f: Tasman called it Van Diemen's Land after his sponsor. The name was changed in 1856 partly to shake off its association with convict transportation — so the island is named after the navigator instead of the governor.

q: "seychelles" is named after a place.
f: A hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean are named after a French finance minister who never saw them. He was in office for two years and is remembered nowhere else.

q: The word "america" is named after…?
f: Martin Waldseemuller printed the name on a map in 1507 because Vespucci had argued it was a new continent rather than Asia. He later changed his mind and removed it — but a thousand copies were already out.

q: Which word meaning "a small yellow songbird" comes from a latin for 'islands of the dogs'?
f: The bird is named after the islands, and the islands are named after dogs — canis in Latin. So a small yellow songbird is, at two removes, named after a pack of large dogs.

q: Which word meaning "a large game bird" comes from the country?
f: The bird is American and the name is a mistake. English traders met a similar African bird sold by Turkish merchants and called it turkey; when the American bird arrived it inherited the wrong name. The Turkish for it is hindi, meaning Indian.

q: There was a Swiss mathematician. His notation and results run through almost every branch of mathematics. Which word grew out of it?
f: Euler gave us the symbols e, i, f(x) and the sigma for sums. He also wrote the equation many mathematicians call the most beautiful there is, tying together five fundamental constants in seven characters.

q: There was a Russian mathematician. He studied processes where the next step depends only on the current state, not the history. Which word grew out of it?
f: Markov developed his chains partly to win an argument, analysing the vowels and consonants in a Pushkin poem to prove a rival wrong about probability. The maths now runs speech recognition and page ranking.

q: There was a Polish-French-American mathematician. He coined the word fractal and found the set that carries his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mandelbrot asked how long the coast of Britain is, and answered: it depends on the length of your ruler. Measure in smaller steps and it gets longer without limit. That question opened up fractal geometry.

q: "hamiltonian" is named after a person.
f: Hamilton solved a problem he had wrestled with for years while walking along a Dublin canal, and carved the formula into the stone of Broom Bridge with a penknife. A plaque marks the spot; mathematicians still visit.

q: There was a Norwegian mathematician. Groups where order does not matter are named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: Abel proved that no formula can solve every fifth-degree equation, settling a question three centuries old. He died of tuberculosis at twenty-six, two days before a letter arrived offering him a professorship.

q: There was a Swedish physicist. The unit measures the biological effect of radiation, not merely the energy absorbed. Which word grew out of it?
f: A gray measures energy absorbed; a sievert measures how much harm it does, which depends on the kind of radiation. The difference matters: the same energy from alpha particles is twenty times more damaging.

q: There was a Danish physicist. He noticed a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire, linking electricity and magnetism. Which word grew out of it?
f: Orsted spotted it during a lecture, in front of students, when a compass on the bench moved as he switched on a current. He said nothing at the time and spent three months checking before publishing.

q: There was an Italian physicist. He invented the barometer and proved that air has weight. Which word grew out of it?
f: Torricelli filled a tube with mercury, upended it in a dish, and found the column always fell to about the same height — leaving a vacuum above it. Philosophers had insisted for two thousand years that a vacuum was impossible.

q: Which word meaning "a violent troublemaker" comes from a disputed — probably a rowdy London family of Irish origin in the 1890s?
f: The word appears suddenly in London newspapers in the summer of 1898, already meaning street rowdy. Whether the Houlihans were a real family, a music-hall joke, or both, nobody has ever settled.

q: There was a probably legendary English weaver. Textile workers destroying machinery in 1811 signed their threats as followers of General Ludd. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Luddites were not against machines in principle — they were skilled workers whose trade was being destroyed and who had no vote to object with. Ned Ludd, in whose name they wrote, probably never existed.

q: "munchausen" is named after a place.
f: The real baron told entertaining war stories. A writer published a wildly embroidered version without asking, making him a laughing stock across Europe — he spent his last years trying to sue, and hated the book.

q: There was a queen of England. The drink is generally held to be named for the queen whose reign saw Protestant executions. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: The naming is disputed — rival theories point to a Chicago bar and a Hollywood actress. The queen's own nickname is not disputed: roughly 280 people were burned during her five-year reign.

q: There was a village and beach in eastern Cuba. An American engineer working at the nearby iron mines mixed rum, lime and sugar and named it for the place. Which word grew out of it?
f: Jennings Cox ran out of gin while entertaining guests near the Daiquiri mines and improvised with local rum. Hemingway later drank them in Havana by the dozen, and had a variant named after him in turn.

q: Which word meaning "a cocktail of whiskey and vermouth" comes from an island borough of New York City?
f: The island's own name comes from a Lenape word usually translated as place where we get bows, after the wood that grew there. So the drink is named after an island named after a bow-making forest.

q: Which word meaning "a tequila, lime and orange-liqueur cocktail" comes from a Spanish for 'daisy' — and a common given name?
f: At least six people have claimed to have invented it for a woman named Margarita. The likelier answer is dull: daisy was already a category of cocktail, and margarita is simply the Spanish for daisy.

q: What does "tarmac" mean?
c: Of a classical golden age in literature
f: Hooley noticed a stretch of road outside an ironworks that was smooth and dustless, and learned a tar barrel had burst there and been covered with slag. He patented the accident and named it after McAdam.

q: There was a latin for 'flax oil'. Frederick Walton made the floor covering from oxidised linseed oil, and built the name from Latin. Which word grew out of it?
f: Walton got the idea from the rubbery skin that forms on a tin of old paint. He never trademarked the name, and a court ruled in 1878 that it had already become generic — the first product ever to lose a name that way.

q: "plimsoll" is named after a person.
f: Plimsoll campaigned against coffin ships — overloaded and over-insured vessels worth more sunk than afloat. The shoe is named after the line too: the rubber band round the sole looks just like a ship's load mark.

q: There was a Polish-American virologist. He developed the oral polio vaccine given on a sugar cube. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sabin's vaccine could be swallowed rather than injected, which made mass campaigns possible in places with few doctors. Like Salk, he refused to patent it. The two men disliked each other for decades.

q: There was a capital of Sweden. Hostages in a 1973 bank siege there defended their captors afterwards. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: After six days in a bank vault, the hostages refused to testify against the robbers and some raised money for their defence. The psychiatrist who coined the term was himself part of the police negotiation.

q: There was a German-American instrument dealer. His firm made the theatre organs and jukeboxes that carried the name into everyday speech. Which word grew out of it?
f: Wurlitzer organs were built to replace whole orchestras in silent-film theatres — one player, hundreds of pipes, plus drums, cymbals, birdsong and a car horn. Sound film arrived and the market vanished almost overnight.

q: There was an American luthier. He carved mandolin and guitar tops like violin tops, and the company kept his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: Gibson had no formal training and carved instrument tops from a single piece of wood, arched like a violin, when everyone else bent flat sheets. He sold the patent and the company outgrew him entirely.

q: There was an American inventor. He designed the first mass-produced solid-body electric guitar and bass. Which word grew out of it?
f: Fender never learned to play the guitar. He was a radio repairman who approached the instrument as an engineering problem — bolt the neck on so it can be replaced, and the whole thing can be built on a production line.

q: There was an American actor. He was rarely filmed without a cigarette, and the slang came from his habit of letting it hang from his lip. Which word grew out of it?
f: To bogart something is to hog it, from the way Bogart kept a cigarette clamped in his mouth without ever seeming to smoke it. The word entered wide use through a 1968 song.

q: "tradescantia" is named after a place.
f: The Tradescants kept a museum of curiosities in Lambeth called the Ark, open to anyone who paid sixpence — the first public museum in England. Its collection became the founding core of Oxford's Ashmolean.

q: There was a Swedish scientist. Linnaeus named the genus after his patron and predecessor at Uppsala. Which word grew out of it?
f: Rudbeck discovered the lymphatic system as a student, and later spent decades trying to prove that Sweden was the lost Atlantis. Linnaeus named the flower for him regardless.

q: There was an American statesman and scientist. Two botanists found the tree in Georgia and named it for their friend. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Bartrams found this tree growing in one small patch in Georgia in 1765 and collected seeds. It has not been seen in the wild since 1803. Every franklinia alive today descends from those seeds.

q: There was a German botanist. The genus was named for the head gardener of the Vienna palace gardens. Which word grew out of it?
f: Its other name is dumb cane: the sap contains needle-shaped crystals that make the mouth and throat swell, temporarily robbing anyone who chews it of speech. It remains a popular office plant.

q: There was an Austrian botanist and physician. The genus was named for the emperor's physician, who was also a botanist. Which word grew out of it?
f: Hostas are grown for foliage rather than flowers, thrive in shade, and are eaten enthusiastically by slugs. Host himself was physician to the Austrian emperor and ran the imperial botanical garden.

q: Which word meaning "a word-building board game" comes from an English word meaning to scratch or grope about?
f: Alfred Butts, an out-of-work architect, counted letter frequencies on the front page of the New York Times to set the tile values. The game failed twice under other names before Scrabble stuck.

q: Which word meaning "a tower-stacking block game" comes from a swahili verb meaning 'to build'?
f: Leslie Scott's family played it with wooden blocks from a sawmill in Ghana. She named it from the Swahili kujenga, to build — which is slightly ironic for a game everyone plays in order to watch it fall over.

q: Which word meaning "a property trading board game" comes from an economic term for exclusive control of a market?
f: Elizabeth Magie invented the original in 1904 as a protest against landlords hoarding property. Decades later a man sold a version to Parker Brothers as his own invention. She was paid five hundred dollars.

q: There was an American bandmaster. He composed the marches that defined American band music and asked for a tuba to be redesigned for marching. Which word grew out of it?
f: Sousa wrote The Stars and Stripes Forever, the official national march of the United States. He also campaigned against recorded music, warning it would stop people learning instruments — a prediction with some merit.

q: There was an Italian hatmaker. His Alessandria workshop became the most famous felt hat maker in the world. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Borsalino takes around seven weeks and dozens of separate operations to make, mostly from rabbit felt. The firm was still going after more than 160 years, which very few hat companies can say.

q: There was a british surgeon. An American doctor named his antiseptic after the pioneer of antiseptic surgery. Which word grew out of it?
f: Listerine was sold first as a surgical antiseptic, then as a floor cleaner and a cure for gonorrhoea. It only became a mouthwash when the makers popularised the word halitosis to convince people they had a problem.

q: Which word meaning "a patty of minced beef served in a bun" comes from a great German port city?
f: Sailors leaving one busy German port ate a minced beef steak served flat on a plate. They carried the habit across the Atlantic, cooks there slid the patty into a bun, and the sandwich kept the port city's name.

q: Which name or term meaning "a soft stuffed toy bear" comes from an American president and keen hunter?
f: On a hunting trip a president refused to shoot a bear that had been tied to a tree, calling it unsporting. A newspaper cartoon spread the story, a shopkeeper sewed a plush bear in tribute, and the toy carried his nickname ever after.

q: Which word meaning "a team sport played with an oval ball that players may carry" comes from an English boarding school?
f: At one English school the football rules allowed a player to pick the ball up and run with it. Old boys carried the handling version to clubs everywhere, and to tell it apart from the kicking game people simply called it by the school's name.

q: "dalmatian" is named after a place.
f: A tall spotted dog that loved to trot beside horses became fashionable as a carriage escort. Early writers linked the breed to one stretch of Adriatic coastline, and although the connection is thin, the region's name stuck to the dog for good.

q: Which word meaning "a strong, friendly retriever with a short water-shedding coat" comes from a rugged region of eastern Canada?
f: Fishermen on a cold Canadian coast kept short-haired dogs that dived into freezing water after nets and fish. English gentlemen brought the dogs home, bred them for the shooting field, and named them after the coast they came from.

q: Which word meaning "a very small dog with large upright ears" comes from the largest state in Mexico?
f: American visitors to a northern Mexican state in the 1800s bought tiny dogs from villagers near the border. Nobody recorded a breed name, so the buyers simply used the name of the state, and the smallest dog in the world has answered to it since.

q: Which word meaning "a soft round fruit with fuzzy skin and a large stone" comes from the ancient empire of modern Iran?
f: The fruit really began in China, but it reached Rome along the road from Persia. Roman growers called it the Persian apple, persicum, and centuries of shortening in French wore that long name down to a single soft syllable.

q: Which word meaning "a hot drink brewed from roasted ground beans" comes from a highland region of Ethiopia?
f: Wild bushes with red berries still grow in one Ethiopian highland. Traders carried the beans to Arabia, where the brewed drink became qahwa, and every European name for it -- cafe, kaffee and the English word -- goes back to that first green hillside.

q: Which word meaning "a very large expanse of salt water" comes from the Greek titan of the world-encircling river?
f: Greeks imagined the earth as a flat disc ringed by one endless river, and gave that river the name of a titan, the eldest son of sky and earth. When sailors learned the water went on much further than they thought, the titan's name went with it.

q: Which word meaning "a device that makes a loud wailing warning sound" comes from a sea creatures in Greek myth whose singing lured sailors onto rocks?
f: In the old story, singers on a rocky island sang so beautifully that crews steered towards them and were wrecked. Odysseus tied himself to the mast to hear them safely. Centuries later an inventor gave the name to a machine whose wail means danger.

q: "cinderella" is named after a person.
f: A girl who slept beside the fireplace and was named for the cinders in her clothes went to the ball and left one slipper behind. Now any unfancied team that reaches the final, or any ignored talent that shines, gets called by her name.

q: Which word meaning "neither too much nor too little" comes from the girl in the tale of the three bears?
f: A girl in a fairy tale tried porridge too hot, then too cold, then just right. Astronomers borrowed her fussiness: a planet in the narrow band that is neither too hot nor too cold for water now sits in the zone named for her.

q: Which name or term meaning "an adult who refuses to grow up" comes from the boy who would not grow up, created by J. M. Barrie?
f: A playwright invented a boy who flew, fought pirates, and flatly refused to get any older. Psychologists later borrowed him: someone who dodges every adult responsibility and stays a delighted child is said to have his syndrome.

q: Which name or term meaning "a person who behaves in a wildly eccentric way" comes from the tea-party host in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
f: At a tea party that never ended, a hat-maker asked a riddle he could not answer and poured tea on a dormouse. Real hat-makers of the day were poisoned by the mercury they used, which is why madness and hat-making went together in the joke.

q: Which name or term meaning "a broad fixed grin" comes from the grinning cat in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland?
f: A cat in a wonderland book sat in a tree, gave unhelpful directions, and vanished slowly from the tail forwards until nothing was left but its grin. Anyone smiling that widely for no clear reason is now said to be grinning like it.

q: Which name or term meaning "something so broken it cannot be mended" comes from the egg who sat on a wall in the nursery rhyme?
f: An egg sat on a wall, fell off, and all the king's horses and men could do nothing about it. Writers now reach for his name whenever a treaty, a company or a friendship has shattered in a way no committee is going to fix.

q: Which word meaning "a resort with mineral springs or health treatments" comes from a small town in eastern Belgium?
f: A Belgian town with bubbling iron-rich springs became the fashionable place to take the waters in the 1500s. Visitors came home saying they had been to the town by name, and soon every mineral bath in Europe was borrowing it.

q: "sardine" is named after a place.
f: Fishing boats around one large Mediterranean island hauled in silver shoals of a small oily fish by the tonne. The catch was salted, shipped and eventually tinned, and it carried the island's name to breakfast tables everywhere.

q: Which word meaning "a racket game played with a shuttlecock over a high net" comes from a stately home in Gloucestershire, England?
f: Officers home from India brought back a shuttlecock game and played it in the hall of an English duke's country house on a wet afternoon. When people asked what the game was called, they answered with the name of the house.

q: Which name or term meaning "a giant upright rotating wheel with passenger cars" comes from an American bridge engineer?
f: Chicago wanted something to outdo the Eiffel Tower. A bridge engineer proposed a wheel two hundred and fifty feet across, carrying two thousand people at once. Everyone said it would collapse; it did not, and every big wheel since has borne his name.

q: Which word meaning "a blue-green mineral" comes from the land the stone was traded through?
f: The blue-green stone was mined in Persia, but it reached Venice and Paris in the packs of Turkish merchants. French buyers called it pierre turquoise, the Turkish stone, and the shortened word now names the colour as much as the mineral.

q: Which word meaning "a Mexican spirit distilled from blue agave" comes from a town in the Mexican state of Jalisco?
f: In the red volcanic soil around one Mexican town, blue agave plants grow for years before their hearts are roasted and distilled. Mexican law now says the spirit may only carry the town's name if it comes from that region.

q: Which word meaning "a very small long-haired dog with a plumed tail" comes from a historic region on the Baltic coast?
f: Big white spitz dogs pulled sleds along a cold Baltic coast. Breeders shrank them generation by generation until Queen Victoria fell for an eleven-pound one and made the miniature fashionable, and the region's name shrank onto the little dog.

q: Which word meaning "a large powerful black-and-tan guard dog" comes from a town in south-west Germany?
f: Butchers in a German market town used heavy dogs to drive cattle to market, then tied the purse of takings round the dog's neck for the walk home. Nobody robbed them. The town's name went onto the breed and stayed.

q: "siamese" is named after a person.
f: A pair of pale blue-eyed cats with sooty faces was given to a British consul by a royal court in South East Asia in 1884. They were shown in London the next year, astonished everybody, and took the kingdom's old name as their own.

q: Which name or term meaning "a small tailless rodent kept as a pet or used in experiments" comes from a stretch of West African coast?
f: The animal is not a pig and has never been near West Africa: it comes from the Andes. But it arrived in Europe aboard ships working the Guinea trade route, sailors named it after the last coast they had seen, and the mistake stuck.

q: Which word meaning "a rich coffee" comes from a port on the Red Sea coast of Yemen?
f: For two hundred years almost every coffee bean that reached Europe left through one Yemeni harbour. The beans had a chocolatey edge, so when cooks later stirred cocoa into coffee they reached for the harbour's name to describe it.

q: Which word meaning "coffee" comes from the main island of Indonesia?
f: Dutch growers planted coffee across one Indonesian island until it supplied much of the world. American sailors and soldiers took to calling any cup of coffee by the island's name, and a programming language later borrowed it as a nod to the coders' fuel.

q: Which name or term meaning "a flat pale edible bean" comes from the capital of Peru?
f: Crates of a broad flat bean left a Peruvian port stamped with the city of origin. Buyers in North America read the stamp rather than any botanical label, and started ordering the beans by the name of the city instead.

q: Which name or term meaning "a hard, tart, bright green apple" comes from an Australian orchardist?
f: An Australian orchardist threw some French crab apple cores onto a creek bank. A seedling came up, and its fruit turned out hard, sharp and green, and kept for months. Neighbours called it by her nickname and the apple never lost it.

q: Which word meaning "a hard-shelled Australian nut with rich creamy flesh" comes from a Scottish-Australian chemist and doctor?
f: A botanist studying rainforest trees in Queensland found one with a nut so hard you needed a hammer. He named the genus after a chemist friend who, as it happens, never tasted the nut that would carry his name around the world.

q: "reuben" is named after a place.
f: A grocer playing his weekly poker game in an Omaha hotel asked the kitchen for corned beef, sauerkraut, Swiss cheese and dressing between rye bread, grilled. The hotel owner put it on the menu under the player's first name, and it never came off.

q: Which word meaning "a layered pastry of puff pastry and cream" comes from the French emperor?
f: The layered cream slice began as a Naples pastry, napolitain in French. English speakers heard the more famous name in it and rewrote the word, so the dessert now honours an emperor who had nothing whatever to do with inventing it.

q: Which word meaning "a slow-cooked Italian meat and tomato sauce" comes from a city in northern Italy famous for its cooking?
f: Cooks in one wealthy northern Italian city simmered minced meat with a little tomato, milk and wine for hours, and served it with wide flat pasta. The city's name travelled with the recipe, though what most countries make of it would horrify the locals.

q: Which word meaning "ice cream in three coloured layers" comes from a southern Italian port city?
f: Ice cream makers from a southern Italian port emigrated in the 1800s and sold moulded ice cream in coloured stripes, in imitation of their national flag. Abroad the layers became chocolate, vanilla and strawberry, and kept the city's name.

q: Which word meaning "a red wine from the region around one French port" comes from a port city in south-west France?
f: For centuries English merchants bought red wine at one French Atlantic port and shipped it home in barrels. They called it by the harbour rather than the vineyard, and even now the region's most famous wines answer to the port's name.

q: Which word meaning "a deep blue-violet dye or colour" comes from the country the dye was traded from?
f: Greek traders met a deep blue dye that came in hard cakes from the East, and called it indikon, simply the Indian thing. The name outlasted the trade: the colour between blue and violet in the rainbow still carries the country's name.

q: Which word meaning "a soft reddish metal that conducts heat and electricity well" comes from the Mediterranean island whose mines supplied Rome?
f: Rome got most of its reddish metal from mines on one Mediterranean island, and called it the Cyprus metal. Latin wore aes cyprium down to cuprum, and English wore that down again, so an island's name now sits in every electrical cable.

q: "alsatian" is named after a person.
f: During the First World War British owners could not bring themselves to call the breed a German shepherd. They renamed it after a border region that had changed hands between the two countries, and in Britain the wartime alias lasted for decades.

q: Which word meaning "a small flat-faced dog with a long flowing coat" comes from the old English name for Beijing?
f: Only the Chinese imperial family could keep the little lion dogs of the palace. When British and French troops looted the Summer Palace in 1860 five were carried off, one was given to Queen Victoria, and the capital's old name went with them.

q: Which word meaning "a horse breed with a dished face, high tail and great stamina" comes from the peninsula where the breed was developed?
f: Desert tribes bred horses that could go far on little water and live close to the family tent. The line is one of the oldest kept anywhere, and almost every modern racing breed carries some of its blood along with the peninsula's name.

q: Which word meaning "a problem that grows worse each time you attack it" comes from the many-headed water serpent of Greek myth?
f: Heracles found that every head he sliced off the marsh serpent was replaced by two more, and only fire could stop the regrowth. Ever since, a difficulty that spawns two new difficulties each time you solve it has been called by the monster's name.

q: Which word meaning "a large snake that kills by constriction" comes from the great serpent of Delphi killed by Apollo?
f: A monstrous serpent guarded the spring at Delphi until Apollo shot it, and the oracle's priestess took her title from it. When naturalists needed a name for enormous constricting snakes, they reached back into the myth for the serpent's own.

q: Which word meaning "the coloured lights that glow in polar skies" comes from the Roman goddess of the dawn?
f: Romans said a goddess rose each morning to paint the eastern sky before the sun came up. When Galileo needed a name for the green and red curtains that hang over the far north, he gave them hers, adding the northern dawn.

q: Which word meaning "a person behaving wildly or foolishly" comes from the Roman goddess and personification of the moon?
f: Doctors from Rome to the Middle Ages believed that fits of madness rose and fell with the phases of the moon, and English law once separated the permanently ill from those thought to change with it. The moon goddess's name is still inside the word.

q: "big brother" is named after a place.
f: In a novel published in 1949 every wall carried a poster of a moustached face and the line that he was watching you. Nobody in the book ever meets him. Seventy years on, his name is the fastest way to say a state is watching too closely.

q: Which word meaning "american whiskey distilled mainly from corn and aged in charred oak" comes from a county in Kentucky named for a French royal house?
f: Barrels of corn whiskey floated down the Ohio and Mississippi from one Kentucky county, whose name was stencilled on the staves. By the time they reached New Orleans the oak had mellowed the spirit, and buyers asked for it by the county on the barrel.

q: Which word meaning "a cylindrical canvas bag closed with a drawstring" comes from a town in Belgium?
f: A Belgian town wove a thick coarse wool that soldiers and sailors trusted to keep out weather. Coats and kitbags cut from it carried the town's name across every navy in Europe, and the bag kept the name long after the cloth changed.

q: Which word meaning "a machine that shaves and resurfaces ice" comes from an American ice-rink owner and inventor?
f: Resurfacing a rink took five men over an hour. A rink owner in California spent nine years bolting a shaving blade, a water tank and a squeegee onto an army surplus chassis until one driver could do it in ten minutes. His name is now on the machine everywhere.

q: Which word meaning "a German luxury car marque" comes from the daughter of an Austrian car dealer?
f: An Austrian businessman raced Daimler cars under his young daughter's name because a foreign entrant needed a pseudonym. The cars won, dealers demanded that model by that name, and the factory quietly made a ten-year-old girl's name its own.

q: Which word meaning "an American luxury car" comes from the French officer who founded Detroit in 1701?
f: A French officer built a fort on a narrow strait and called it the place of the strait, which became Detroit. Two centuries later a carmaker in that city borrowed his name and his family crest, and the word came to mean the best of anything.

q: Which word meaning "an American car marque" comes from a Swiss racing driver and engineer?
f: A Swiss racing driver went into partnership with an ousted car executive, lending his famous name to a new company. He fell out with his partner over building cheap cars, sold his shares early, and watched his surname become one of the biggest in America.

q: "bowie knife" is named after a person.
f: A frontiersman was shot and stabbed in a duel-turned-brawl on a Mississippi sandbar and still killed two men with a heavy butcher's knife. Newspapers described the blade in detail, smiths were flooded with orders, and the knife took his name.

q: Which word meaning "a blade fixed to the muzzle of a rifle" comes from a fortified city in south-west France?
f: The story goes that soldiers besieged in a French border city ran out of powder and jammed their hunting knives into their musket barrels. Whether or not that happened, the city's forges made the blades, and its name went onto them.

q: Which word meaning "a hard glossy black lacquer finish" comes from the island nation?
f: Lacquered boxes arriving from East Asia in the 1600s astonished Europe with a black finish nothing local could match. Workshops in England and France tried to copy it, sold the results as the country's own name, and turned a nation into a verb.

q: Which word meaning "a close-fitting knitted woollen jumper" comes from one of the Channel Islands?
f: Fishermen on a small Channel Island knitted jumpers so tightly that seawater ran off them. Naval crews adopted the pattern, Australian footballers borrowed the word for their shirts, and the island's dairy cattle carried the same name to farms worldwide.

q: Which word meaning "a very large draught horse with feathered legs" comes from a valley in southern Scotland?
f: Farmers in one Scottish river valley crossed local mares with imported Flemish stallions to get a horse that could haul coal and plough heavy clay. The breed grew to a tonne, kept its white feathered legs, and carried the valley's name to the world.

q: Which word meaning "a small dried grape used in baking" comes from a Greek city and port?
f: Medieval traders bought tiny seedless dried grapes at a Greek port and sold them in England as raisins of that city. The phrase wore down over centuries until only a mangled version of the city's name was left on the packet.

q: Which word meaning "a small mild onion that grows in clusters" comes from an ancient port in the Levant, now Ashkelon?
f: Returning crusaders brought back a small onion that grew in clusters and tasted milder than the ones at home. They said it came from one Levantine port, called it the onion of that place, and French cooks wore the phrase down to a single word.

q: "pheasant" is named after a place.
f: Greek sailors returning from the Black Sea brought back a spectacular long-tailed bird and said it lived along one particular river. They called it the bird of the Phasis, and every European language still carries a worn-down version of that river's name.

q: Which name or term meaning "a knobbly edible tuber from a sunflower relative" comes from the Italian word for sunflower, misheard as a city name?
f: The knobbly tuber is a North American sunflower and has never grown near the Middle East. Italians called the plant girasole, turning to the sun; English ears heard a famous city in that word, and the wrong name has stuck for four hundred years.

q: Which word meaning "a warm sauce of egg yolk, butter and lemon" comes from the Dutch region?
f: French cooks named several sauces after foreign countries to suggest a style rather than an origin. This one, whisked from yolks and warm butter until it thickens, was labelled Dutch, possibly because the Netherlands supplied the butter.

q: Which word meaning "a warm sauce of egg yolk, butter, tarragon and shallot" comes from a region in the French Pyrenees?
f: A chef outside Paris invented a herbed butter sauce at a restaurant named for Henry IV, who was born in a Pyrenean region and nicknamed for it. The sauce took the region's name, though nobody there had ever made it.

q: Which word meaning "a dry red Italian wine" comes from a hilly wine region in Tuscany?
f: A grand duke drew a boundary round some Tuscan hills in 1716 and declared that only wine from inside it could carry the region's name. It was one of the first protected wine areas anywhere, three centuries before such rules became normal.

q: Which word meaning "a light fruity red wine" comes from a wine region north of Lyon in France?
f: Growers in a French region north of Lyon make a light red from gamay grapes and release the newest vintage on the third Thursday of November. Bottles race to Paris and beyond overnight, and the region's name goes with every cork.

q: Which word meaning "a white wine grape" comes from a village in the Maconnais, Burgundy?
f: A small Burgundy village gave its name to a green-skinned grape that turned out to grow almost anywhere, from Champagne to California to Australia. It is now the most planted white wine grape on earth, still carrying one village's name.

q: "rioja" is named after a person.
f: When disease wrecked French vineyards in the 1800s, Bordeaux winemakers crossed the Pyrenees and taught growers in a northern Spanish valley to age wine in oak barrels. The region kept the technique, and its name now means oak-aged Spanish red.

q: Which word meaning "a loud musical instrument of steam whistles" comes from the Greek Muse of epic poetry?
f: An inventor in 1855 mounted a keyboard on a row of steam whistles loud enough to be heard eight miles away. He named it for the Muse of epic poetry, whose name means beautiful-voiced, which anyone who has stood near a circus one may dispute.

q: Which word meaning "a crude, loud, uncultivated person" comes from the brutish human-like creatures in Gulliver's Travels?
f: On his last voyage Gulliver meets talking horses ruling over filthy, howling creatures that look uncomfortably like humans. Swift meant it as a mirror. The creatures' name became an insult, and much later a search engine picked it up as a joke.

q: Which word meaning "a problem whose only solution is blocked by the problem itself" comes from the impossible rule in Joseph Heller's 1961 novel?
f: A bomber pilot could be grounded for insanity, but asking to be grounded proved he was sane enough to fly. Heller's invented regulation was so exact a picture of bureaucratic traps that its number entered the dictionary within a decade.

q: Which word meaning "deliberately ambiguous or misleading official language" comes from the shrinking official language in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four?
f: In Orwell's novel the state shrinks the dictionary every year, on the theory that a thought you have no word for cannot be thought at all. The invented language's name is now used for any official wording designed to blur rather than explain.

q: Which word meaning "holding two contradictory beliefs at the same time" comes from the mental habit demanded by the Party in Nineteen Eighty-Four?
f: Orwell's Party required citizens to believe two opposite things at once and to be sincere about both, forgetting the contradiction and then forgetting the forgetting. The coined word escaped the novel and is now used of real politics every week.

q: Which word meaning "a pattern of coloured diamonds" comes from the acrobatic trickster servant of Italian commedia dell'arte?
f: A masked servant character in Italian street comedy wore a patched costume that hardened over time into neat coloured diamonds. He tumbled, schemed and chased Columbine through two centuries of theatre, and left his name on the pattern itself.

q: "zany" is named after a place.
f: In Italian street comedy the servant clowns, named from a dialect form of Giovanni, copied their masters' gestures badly on purpose. English audiences took the troupe's name for the behaviour, and it now describes any cheerfully absurd person.

q: Which word meaning "the lightest inert gas, used to fill balloons" comes from the Greek sun god?
f: During an eclipse in 1868 astronomers saw a yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched no known element. They named the unknown gas after the Greek sun god. Twenty-seven years passed before anyone found any of it on earth.

q: There was an English baronet. He imported the plum from France, and the labels were lost in transit. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English baronet imported plum trees from a French monastery, and the labels were lost on the way. His gardener, needing something to call the green ones, combined the colour with his employer's surname, and the plum has answered to it since.

q: There was a Massachusetts merchant. He distributed the English Williams pear in America under his own name. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An English variety called the Williams pear was already growing on a Massachusetts farm when a merchant bought the land. Not knowing the name, he propagated and sold it under his own. The same fruit still has two names on two sides of the Atlantic.

q: There was a Soviet tank sergeant turned weapons designer. He designed the rifle while recovering from wounds in 1942. Which word grew out of it?
f: A wounded Soviet tank sergeant lay in hospital listening to comrades complain that German troops had better automatic weapons. He sketched a design built to work when filled with mud or sand. Over a hundred million have been made, all carrying his name.

q: There was a German firearms designer. His bolt-action rifle became the pattern copied by most armies. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German designer perfected a bolt action so reliable that armies from Spain to Japan bought or copied it, and hunting rifles still use his locking system a century later. His surname is stamped on more military rifles than almost any other.

q: There was a German physicist. He found that energy comes in fixed packets set by one small number. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A German physicist trying to explain the colour of hot glowing objects found the maths only worked if energy came in indivisible packets. He called the idea a desperate act. It founded quantum theory, and the tiny number in it carries his name.

q: "bohr model" is named after a person.
f: A Danish physicist proposed that electrons could only sit in certain orbits and jumped between them by swallowing or spitting out exact packets of light. It explained hydrogen's spectrum precisely, was wrong in detail, and is still the first atom every student draws.

q: There was a French physicist. He hung a heavy pendulum in the Pantheon to show the earth turning beneath it. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: In 1851 a French physicist hung a sixty-seven-metre wire from the dome of the Pantheon with a heavy iron ball on the end. As it swung, its path slowly rotated. Paris could watch the planet turning for the first time, in a public hall.

q: There was an Italian physicist and priest. He showed that fluid speeds up and its pressure drops in a narrowing pipe. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An Italian priest and physicist showed that squeezing a pipe makes the fluid inside run faster and press outwards less. Carburettors, atomisers, aircraft instruments and hospital suction all use the trick, and all carry his name for it.

q: There was an Irish-born engineer. He found a single number that predicts whether flow will be smooth or turbulent. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An engineer injected a thread of dye into water flowing down a glass pipe. Below a certain speed the thread stayed straight; above it, the dye burst into swirls. He reduced the whole question to one dimensionless ratio that now bears his name.

q: There was a Japanese-American meteorologist. He rated tornado strength by the damage left behind. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A meteorologist who had surveyed the blast damage at Nagasaki applied the same eye to tornado wreckage, working backwards from broken buildings to wind speed. His damage-based scale, from a snapped branch to a house swept clean off its slab, still rates every twister.

q: There was an English mathematician. He showed how to rebuild a function from its derivatives at a single point. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An English mathematician showed that if you know a curve's height, slope, curvature and every higher rate of change at just one point, you can rebuild the entire curve as an endless sum. Almost all of numerical computing rests on that trick.

q: There was a German mathematician. He generalised ordinary geometry to spaces with infinitely many dimensions. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A German mathematician extended ordinary distance and angle into spaces with endlessly many directions. It sounded like pure abstraction until quantum mechanics arrived and turned out to need exactly that geometry to describe the state of a particle.

q: "jacobian" is named after a place.
f: A German mathematician studied the grid of partial derivatives that says how much a change of coordinates stretches or twists each direction. Its determinant is the factor by which volume changes, which is why it appears in every multiple integral.

q: There was a German mathematician. He studied the square array of second derivatives that describes curvature. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A German mathematician assembled all the second derivatives of a function into one square array. Its signs tell you whether a flat point is a peak, a valley or a saddle, which is why every optimisation algorithm reaches for it.

q: There was a plateau town in the Veneto, northern Italy. The cow's-milk cheese has been made on that plateau for centuries. Which word grew out of it?
f: Shepherds on a high plateau in northern Italy once made this cheese from sheep's milk. When cattle replaced the flocks the recipe changed but the name did not, and European law now protects it for that plateau alone.

q: There was a small town in Wisconsin. A cheesemaker's son invented the washed-curd cheese there in 1885. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Wisconsin cheesemaker's teenage son washed the curds in cold water instead of letting them cook dry, and got a softer, milder, moister cheese than cheddar. It was the first cheese invented in America, and it took the little town's name.

q: There was an experimental farm outside Copenhagen. A Danish cheesemaker developed the cheese at that farm in the 1800s. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Danish woman toured European dairies, came home to an experimental farm outside Copenhagen, and worked out a semi-soft cheese full of tiny irregular holes. The farm's name went onto it, and Denmark's best-known cheese was born on a research plot.

q: There was the northern Italian city. The city's cooks breadcrumb and fry veal, and saffron their risotto. Which word grew out of it?
f: A northern Italian city gave its name to two very different dishes: a veal cutlet beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried in butter, and a risotto turned gold with saffron. Vienna's schnitzel is very probably the same cutlet under another flag.

q: There was a French city famous for its cooking. Dishes finished with sliced onions are named for the city's style. Which word grew out of it?
f: One French city is so serious about food that its small restaurants have their own name, bouchons. Any dish labelled with the city's adjective on a French menu comes with sliced onions browned in butter, whatever else is on the plate.

q: "provencal" is named after a person.
f: The name of a southern French region on a menu promises the same three things every time: tomato, garlic and olive oil, usually with herbs from the dry hills. The region's Roman name simply meant the province, the first one Rome held outside Italy.

q: There was the miserly old Venetian merchant of commedia dell'arte. His tight leg-covering costume gave its name to trousers. Which word grew out of it?
f: A stock character in Italian street comedy played a mean old Venetian merchant in tight full-length hose, unusual when other men wore breeches. Audiences named the garment after him, French shortened it, and the word ended up as plain pants.

q: There was the boastful cowardly soldier of commedia dell'arte. His swagger and swift retreat made his name a word for a boastful rogue. Which word grew out of it?
f: A stock character in Italian comedy strutted in black with a sword, boasted of battles he had not fought, and ran at the first real threat. His name, from a word meaning skirmish, became the English word for exactly that sort of man.

q: There was the hypocritical architect in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit. He preached morality endlessly while behaving badly, so his name means smug hypocrisy. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dickens created an architect who never designed a building, lived off his pupils' work, and lectured everyone he met about virtue while cheating them. His name became the exact English word for moralising that the moraliser has no intention of following.

q: There was an Austrian physicist. He wrote the wave equation that governs how a quantum state evolves. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An Austrian physicist on a winter holiday in the Alps wrote down a wave equation that predicted the hydrogen spectrum exactly. He later invented a thought experiment about a cat to show how absurd he found the standard reading of his own equation.

q: There was a German physicist. He showed that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A young German physicist working alone on Helgoland realised that the sharper you pin down where a particle is, the vaguer its momentum must become, and not because your instruments are poor. The limit is built into nature, and it carries his name.

q: There was an Austrian physicist. He showed that no two electrons can share the same quantum state. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An Austrian physicist, famous for a scathing tongue and for equipment that broke when he entered the room, showed that two electrons can never sit in exactly the same state. That single refusal is why atoms have shells and why matter takes up space.

q: "rydberg constant" is named after a place.
f: A Swedish physicist hunting for pattern in the coloured lines of glowing gases found one formula that fitted them all, with a single number in it. He had no idea why it worked; Bohr's atom explained it thirty years later.

q: There was an Austrian physicist. He linked the temperature of matter to the statistics of its moving particles. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An Austrian physicist argued that heat is just particles jostling and that entropy counts the ways they can be arranged. Colleagues mocked the idea for decades. His formula is carved on his gravestone, and the constant in it carries his name.

q: There was a German mathematician. He built a set by repeatedly deleting middle thirds, and founded set theory. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A German mathematician took a line, cut out the middle third, cut the middle third from each remaining piece, and kept going forever. What is left has no length at all yet contains uncountably many points, which is the sort of thing that made his colleagues furious.

q: There was a French mathematician killed in a duel at twenty. He linked the solvability of equations to the symmetry group of their roots. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A French student twice failed his entrance exams, was expelled for politics, and spent the night before a duel writing out his mathematics with a note in the margin saying he had no time. He died at twenty. The theory reshaped algebra.

q: There was a French lawyer and mathematician. He claimed a proof in a book margin and never wrote it down. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A French lawyer scribbled in the margin of a book that he had a proof but the margin was too small to hold it. Three and a half centuries and thousands of failed attempts later, Andrew Wiles finally proved it, using mathematics that did not exist in the margin-writer's lifetime.

q: There was a Scottish mathematician. He invented both logarithms and a set of numbered rods for multiplying. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: A Scottish laird who also invented logarithms cut multiplication tables onto strips of ivory. Line the rods up beside a number and the products can simply be read off and added. It was the pocket calculator of the seventeenth century.

q: There was an American pathologist. He identified the tick-borne bacteria and died of the fever he was studying. Which word grew out of it?
f: An American pathologist traced spotted fever to ticks, then went to Mexico to study typhus. He caught it from the lice he was working with and died at thirty-nine. The genus was named for him a few years later.

q: "shigella" is named after a person.
f: During a dysentery epidemic that killed a fifth of those infected, a young Japanese bacteriologist isolated the organism from patients' stools and proved it was the cause. He was twenty-six. Both the genus and the toxin it makes carry his name.

q: There was a German-Swiss microbiologist. The genus of pneumonia-causing bacteria was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German microbiologist who also spotted the diphtheria organism under his microscope gave his name to a genus of rod-shaped bacteria wrapped in a thick slimy capsule. That capsule is exactly what makes them so hard for the immune system to grip.

q: There was a Swiss-French bacteriologist. He identified the plague bacterium in Hong Kong in 1894. Which word grew out of it?
f: Two researchers found the plague organism in Hong Kong within days of each other in 1894, and for decades the credit was muddled. The genus now carries the name of the one whose samples were clean, who also worked out that rats and their fleas carried it.

q: There was a German-Austrian paediatrician. He first described the gut bacterium in infants in 1885. Which word grew out of it?
f: A paediatrician studying infant digestion described a rod-shaped bacterium living harmlessly in the gut. It was renamed in his honour after his death, and the species is now the most studied organism on earth after ourselves.

q: There was a Scottish microbiologist and army surgeon. He identified the organism behind Malta fever in 1887. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Scottish army surgeon posted to Malta traced the fever wrecking the garrison to an organism in goats' milk. Stopping the milk ration ended the epidemic almost overnight, and the genus was named after him.

q: There was a spa town in central France. A chef named the chilled leek and potato soup after the region of his childhood. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chef working at a New York hotel served the leek and potato soup of his childhood cold instead of hot, on a hot summer day. He named it after the spa town near his home, and a Manhattan invention now sounds thoroughly French.

q: There was a Greek colony in Cilicia whose settlers spoke poor Attic Greek. Athenians mocked the colonists' broken grammar and named the fault after their town. Which word grew out of it?
f: Athenian visitors to a distant Greek colony were appalled by the dialect the settlers had drifted into, and turned the town's name into an insult for any mangled sentence. The word later widened to cover social blunders as well as grammatical ones.

q: "meander" is named after a place.
f: One river in Asia Minor looped so extravagantly across its flat valley that Greek writers used its name as a byword for anything that would not go straight. Geographers still use it as the technical term for a river bend.

q: There was the king of Macedon and father of Alexander. Demosthenes delivered a famous series of attacking speeches against him. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Athenian orator spent years warning his city about the ambitions of a northern king, in speeches so fierce that the king's name became the word for any blistering public attack. Cicero later borrowed the form to go after Mark Antony.

q: There was the Hebrew prophet of the Book of Lamentations. His long laments over Jerusalem's fall gave the name for any prolonged complaint. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Hebrew prophet warned his city for forty years that disaster was coming, was thrown into a cistern for saying so, and then watched it happen. The book of laments that followed gave English a word for any lengthy, gloomy tirade.

q: There was a sorcerer in the Acts of the Apostles. He offered money for the power to give the Holy Spirit. Which word grew out of it?
f: A sorcerer watched the apostles lay hands on people and offered them cash for the same power. Peter's refusal was blistering. His name became the church's legal term for buying office, and a serious offence for the next eighteen centuries.

q: There was the river of the Greek underworld. Its dark waters gave the word for gloom that is total. Which word grew out of it?
f: Souls were ferried across one black river to reach the land of the dead, and the gods swore their most binding oaths on its water. Anything gloomy enough to suggest that crossing is described with the river's name.

q: There was the Roman queen of the gods. Her stately imposing figure became the compliment for a tall commanding woman. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Roman queen of the gods was pictured as tall, broad-browed and unmistakably in charge, never girlish. Painters and novelists borrowed her name as a compliment for a woman built on the same commanding scale.

q: There was the Athenian grove sacred to Apollo Lykeios where Aristotle taught. Aristotle's school met in that grove, so its name came to mean a place of learning. Which word grew out of it?
f: Aristotle taught in a grove outside Athens sacred to Apollo under one of his titles, walking as he lectured. The grove's name became the word for a lecture hall, and in France it still names the secondary school itself.

q: "gradgrind" is named after a person.
f: Dickens opened a novel with a schoolmaster demanding facts, nothing but facts, and a girl punished for defining a horse poetically instead of anatomically. His name is now the English word for anyone who measures everything and understands nothing.
