q: There was the cheerfully insolvent optimist in Dickens's David Copperfield. He waited endlessly for something to turn up, so his name means hopeful improvidence. Which word grew out of it?
f: Dickens created a man permanently one letter away from ruin who assured everyone that something would turn up. Economists borrowed his budgeting advice, and his name became the word for waiting for rescue instead of arranging one.

q: There was an American-British inventor. He built the first fully automatic machine gun, recoil-operated. Which name or term grew out of it?
f: An American inventor in London decided that the surest way to make money in Europe was to help Europeans kill each other more efficiently. He used the recoil of each shot to load the next, and one man could suddenly do the work of a hundred riflemen.

q: There was an American firearms designer. He designed the pistols and machine guns that armies bought for a century. Which word grew out of it?
f: A gunsmith's son in Utah filed his first patent at twenty-four and ended with a hundred and twenty-eight. He designed the pistol the US Army carried for seventy-four years, and died at his workbench in Belgium with a design half finished.

q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the tube linking the middle ear to the throat. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist working before the printing of good anatomical plates described the narrow tube that lets the middle ear equalise pressure. It is why your ears pop in a lift, and it has carried his name for four centuries.

q: There was an Italian anatomist and surgeon. He described the tubes running from ovary to womb. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist who died at thirty-nine described the delicate tubes running from ovary to womb, comparing their flared ends to trumpets. He got the function wrong but the anatomy right, and the tubes still bear his name.

q: There was an English physician. He described the microscopic canals running through compact bone. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English physician put thin slices of bone under an early microscope and found it was not solid at all but drilled through with a network of tiny tunnels carrying blood vessels. Bone turned out to be plumbing, and the canals took his name.

q: "pacinian" is named after a place.
f: An Italian anatomist found onion-layered capsules buried deep in the skin and joints that fire when pressed or vibrated. He also saw the cholera bacterium thirty years before Koch, and got credit for neither in his lifetime.

q: There was a Dutch physician and anatomist. He described the fluid-filled follicle that releases an egg. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Dutch physician described the fluid-filled blisters on the ovary and argued they held the egg. He was nearly right: they hold the follicle that releases it. He died at thirty-two, embittered by a priority quarrel with a colleague.

q: There was an Italian physician and microscopist. He gave his name to structures in the kidney, spleen and insect gut. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian microscopist was the first to see capillaries, red blood cells and the filtering knots of the kidney. So much of the invisible body was his discovery that his name now attaches to structures in three separate organ systems.

q: There was a German physician. He described the oil glands along the rim of the eyelid. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German physician described rows of tiny oil glands along the eyelid margin. Their oil stops tears evaporating too fast; when they clog, eyes feel gritty and dry. Modern eye clinics still name the condition after him.

q: There was a Danish physician and antiquary. He described the small extra bones found in skull sutures. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Danish physician described the small irregular islands of bone that sometimes form inside the wavy joints of the skull. They are harmless in most people but crowd in on certain bone diseases, which is why radiologists still count them.

q: There was a Dutch physician and anatomist. He described the deep cleft dividing the temporal lobe from the rest of the brain. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Dutch physician traced the deep cleft that separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. It is the most obvious landmark on the side of the human brain, and the artery running along it carries his name too.

q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the central furrow dividing motor from sensory cortex. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist mapped the deep furrow running down the top of the brain. In front of it lies the strip that commands movement; behind it, the strip that receives touch. A whole class of childhood epilepsy is named from that furrow.

q: "purkinje" is named after a person.
f: A Czech physiologist who founded the world's first independent physiology department described both the fibres that carry the heart's electrical signal and the huge fan-shaped neurons of the cerebellum. Two entirely different cells carry the same name.

q: There was a German physiologist. He described the cells that wrap nerve fibres in insulating sheaths. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German physiologist proposed that all animal tissue is built from cells, then found the ones that spiral around nerve fibres like insulation on wire. Without them a nerve signal would crawl instead of race.

q: There was an Italian physician and Nobel laureate. His silver staining method revealed a stack of membranes inside the cell. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian physician invented a silver stain that made single nerve cells stand out black against pale tissue. It won him a Nobel Prize shared with a rival he publicly disagreed with, and it revealed the cell's packaging depot, now named for him.

q: There was a Baltic German anatomist. He described the scavenging cells lining the liver's blood channels. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Baltic German anatomist described star-shaped cells stationed in the liver's blood channels. They swallow bacteria and worn-out red cells as blood filters past, making the liver a checkpoint as well as a chemical works.

q: There was an Italian physiologist. He described the nurse cells that support developing sperm. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian physiologist, still a student when he made the discovery, described tall cells in the testis that cradle developing sperm and feed them through their whole maturation. They are among the few true nurse cells in the body.

q: There was a German zoologist and anatomist. He described the testosterone-producing cells of the testis. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German zoologist described clusters of cells sitting between the sperm-making tubes rather than inside them. Their job turned out to be chemical, not reproductive: they make the hormone that drives male development.

q: There was a German anatomist. He described the touch receptor cells at the base of the epidermis. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German anatomist described cells sitting at the base of the outer skin layer that report steady pressure and fine texture. They are why you can feel the difference between paper and silk with a fingertip.

q: "meissner" is named after a place.
f: A German anatomist described egg-shaped bundles of nerve endings packed just under hairless skin. They fire on the lightest brush and go quiet if the touch holds still, which is why you stop noticing your own clothes.

q: There was an Italian anatomist and embryologist. He described the stretch-sensing endings in skin and joint capsules. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist described spindle-shaped nerve endings that report sustained stretch rather than momentary touch. They tell your brain where your fingers are without your having to look, which is how you can type in the dark.

q: There was an English surgeon and histologist. He described the capsule that collects filtrate in the kidney. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English surgeon showed that the kidney works by filtering blood through a knot of capillaries into a cup, rather than by secreting urine directly. The cup is named after him and the filtering knot after Malpighi.

q: There was a German physician and anatomist. He described the hairpin loop in the kidney tubule that concentrates urine. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German anatomist traced a hairpin bend in the kidney's tubules that dips down into the organ and back. The bend lets the kidney pull water back out of urine, which is why land animals can survive on so little of it.

q: There was a Swiss anatomist. He described the patches of lymph tissue in the wall of the small intestine. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swiss anatomist described oval patches of immune tissue studding the lining of the small intestine. They sample everything passing through, which makes them the gut's border control and the first place typhoid attacks.

q: There was a Swiss anatomist. He described the alkaline-secreting glands of the duodenum. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swiss anatomist described glands in the first stretch of intestine that pump out alkaline mucus. Their job is defensive: they neutralise the flood of stomach acid before it can burn the gut wall downstream.

q: There was a German anatomist and neuropathologist. He described the nerve network in the gut wall that drives its muscle waves. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German neuropathologist found a full nerve network woven between the muscle layers of the gut. It runs the waves that push food along without asking the brain, which is why the gut is sometimes called a second nervous system.

q: "wernicke" is named after a person.
f: A German neurologist found patients who spoke fluently in complete nonsense and could not understand a word said to them. The damage sat behind the ear, in a region that turns sound into meaning, and it carries his name.

q: There was a French physician and anthropologist. He located the brain region whose damage destroys fluent speech. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French physician examined a patient who understood everything but could say only one syllable. The autopsy showed a lesion in the left frontal lobe. It was the first hard evidence that a single mental function lives in one patch of brain.

q: There was an Italian anatomist. He described the sensory organ of the inner ear that converts sound to nerve signals. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist dissected the spiral of the inner ear and found a ribbon of hair cells sitting on a membrane. Each responds to a different pitch, so the ear separates a chord into notes before the brain hears anything.

q: There was a Danish surgeon and anatomist. He described the accessory smell organ in the nasal cavity. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Danish surgeon described a second smell organ tucked into the nasal cavity. In snakes and cats it reads chemical signals from other animals, which is why a snake flicks its tongue into the roof of its mouth.

q: There was a Danish anatomist. He described the pair of lubricating glands at the vaginal opening. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Danish anatomist from a family of three generations of anatomists described a pair of pea-sized lubricating glands. His father named the lymphatic system's thoracic duct; the family put its surname on a remarkable amount of the body.

q: There was an English surgeon and anatomist. He described the pair of glands that secrete pre-ejaculatory fluid. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English surgeon described a pair of pea-sized glands below the prostate. He also republished another anatomist's plates under his own name, causing one of the ugliest plagiarism rows in the history of anatomy.

q: There was an English physician and anatomist. He named the submandibular salivary duct and the jelly inside the umbilical cord. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English physician who stayed in London through the plague of 1665 while most doctors fled described the duct draining the salivary gland under the jaw. The jelly that cushions the vessels inside an umbilical cord also carries his name.

q: "stensen" is named after a place.
f: A Danish anatomist found the duct draining the big salivary gland in front of the ear when he was twenty-two. He then left medicine, worked out how fossils form and how rock layers stack, and ended his life as a bishop.

q: There was a German pathologist. He described the hormone-producing islands scattered through the pancreas. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German medical student described strange islands of cells scattered through the pancreas and admitted he had no idea what they did. Forty years later they turned out to make insulin. He died of tuberculosis at forty-one.

q: There was an English physician and pioneer of neurology. He described the ring of arteries supplying the base of the brain. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English physician traced a ring of arteries at the base of the brain that lets blood reach it from more than one direction. If one vessel blocks, the ring can reroute around it, which is why some strokes cause far less damage than expected.

q: There was an Italian anatomist and surgeon. He described the deep membranous layer of the abdominal wall. Which word grew out of it?
f: An Italian anatomist described the deep membranous sheet in the abdominal wall that limits how far leaked fluid can spread. He was so disliked that after his death a colleague kept his severed head on display in the university museum.

q: There was a French surgeon and naturalist. He described the thickened band of tissue running to the groin. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French surgeon described the thickened cord of tissue running from the hip bone to the pubic bone. Every hernia repair works around it, and the two kinds of groin hernia are distinguished by which side of it they emerge.

q: There was a German anatomist. He described the ring of lymphoid tissue guarding the throat. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German anatomist described the ring of tonsils and lymph tissue circling the entrance to the throat, catching whatever is breathed or swallowed. He also coined the words neuron and chromosome, which outlasted the ring in fame.

q: There was a Baltic German anatomist. He described the thin membrane dividing chambers of the inner ear. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Baltic German anatomist described a membrane just two cells thick separating two fluid chambers of the cochlear spiral. The fluids on either side carry different salts, and that difference is what powers hearing.

q: "bruch" is named after a person.
f: A German anatomist described the thin layered membrane between the retina and its blood supply. It thickens with age and cracks, and those cracks are where the blood vessels of macular degeneration break through.

q: There was an English physician and microscopist. He described the whorled bodies found in the thymus. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English microscopist described onion-like whorls of flattened cells buried in the thymus. He also used his microscope on London's drinking water, and his drawings of what lived in it helped force the city to build proper sewers.

q: There was a German neuropathologist. His stain revealed granular bodies in the nerve cell body. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German neuropathologist invented a dye that turned the protein factories inside nerve cell bodies deep blue. When a nerve is injured the granules scatter and fade, so the stain became a way of reading damage directly.

q: There was a Ukrainian anatomist. He described the giant motor neurons of the cerebral cortex. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Ukrainian anatomist described the largest cells in the human cortex, giant neurons whose fibres run all the way down the spinal cord. Each one commands muscle directly, and a single cell can be a metre long.

q: There was a French pathologist and histologist. He described the gaps in a nerve's insulating sheath where the signal jumps. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French histologist noticed that the insulation around a nerve fibre is not continuous but broken by regular tiny gaps. The signal leaps from gap to gap instead of crawling along, which makes a nerve impulse fifty times faster.

q: There was a Romanian surgeon and anatomist. He described the fibrous envelope around the kidney. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Romanian surgeon described the fibrous envelope wrapping each kidney in its bed of fat. Surgeons still name the plane by him, because a tumour contained inside that envelope is a far better prospect than one that has broken out.

q: There was a French surgeon and anatomist. He described the fascial layer between rectum and prostate. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French surgeon described a thin sheet of fascia separating the rectum from the prostate. Two centuries later it decides the outcome of prostate surgery: staying on the right side of that sheet is what spares the nerves.

q: "banksia" is named after a place.
f: A wealthy young botanist paid his own way onto Cook's Endeavour and came home with fourteen hundred plants nobody in Europe had seen. He later ran Kew Gardens for four decades, and the bottlebrush-flowered shrub carries his name.

q: There was an English botanist and rector. A botanist named the butterfly bush in his memory. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English country rector spent his spare hours cataloguing mosses and grasses so carefully that Linnaeus later used his work. He never saw the shrub named for him: it came from China decades after his death, and now colonises railway sidings everywhere.

q: There was a Spanish vicereine of Peru said to have been cured by the bark. The malaria-treating bark took her title, though the story may be legend. Which word grew out of it?
f: The bark of a Peruvian tree was the only cure for malaria for three centuries. Linnaeus named the genus after a vicereine said to have been saved by it, then misspelled her title. The story is probably invented; the spelling error certainly was not.

q: Which word meaning "a scented South African flower grown from a corm" comes from a German physician?
f: A German botanist collecting in South Africa found a small scented flower on a one-sided spike and named it after a doctor friend back home. It became one of the most popular cut flowers in the world on the strength of its smell alone.

q: Which word meaning "a large brightly coloured daisy from South Africa" comes from a German naturalist and physician?
f: A German doctor ran a botanical garden in Moscow and explored the Volga collecting plants before dying at thirty-three. A colleague named a South African daisy after him, and it is now the fifth most sold cut flower on earth.

q: There was a German botanist and physician. The bell-flowered houseplant was named for him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German botanist writing in the 1780s had a genus of velvet-flowered tropical plants named after him. Confusingly, the plant sold in shops under his name today belongs to a different genus entirely, which botanists have given up trying to correct.

q: There was a British collector and founder of the Royal Horticultural Society. A botanist named the Australian genus after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A British collector who helped found the Royal Horticultural Society had a large Australian genus named after him. There are over three hundred and fifty species, from ground creepers to trees, and almost all of them are pollinated by birds rather than insects.

q: "rafflesia" is named after a person.
f: The plant has no leaves, no stem and no roots. It lives inside a vine and erupts as a metre-wide reddish flower that smells of rotting meat to draw flies. It was named for the colonial official who founded Singapore.

q: There was a Russian grand duchess who became Queen of the Netherlands. A Dutch-funded expedition named the tree after their queen. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German botanist working for the Dutch named a Japanese tree after the Russian grand duchess who had become Queen of the Netherlands. It grows faster than almost any hardwood, up to five metres in a single season.

q: There was the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition. A botanist named the alpine flower from specimens he collected. Which word grew out of it?
f: An American explorer crossing the Rockies collected a low plant with fleshy leaves whose root the local tribes ate. It survived being pressed, dried and carried across a continent, and then sprouted in a Philadelphia garden.

q: There was the American explorer of the Lewis and Clark expedition. The wildflower was named for the second leader of the expedition. Which word grew out of it?
f: The other leader of the great American overland expedition got his name on a genus of showy pink wildflowers found along the route. His companion got a different plant, so the two men who crossed the continent together are commemorated in separate genera.

q: There was the Swedish botanist who invented modern biological naming. He chose a small modest twinflower to carry his own name. Which word grew out of it?
f: The man who named tens of thousands of species reserved one for himself, and pointedly chose a tiny creeping woodland plant with two nodding pink bells. A colleague wrote that it was lowly, insignificant and flowered only briefly, like its namesake.

q: There was a German chemist and botanist. The flowering shrub was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German chemistry professor who also taught botany had an East Asian flowering shrub named after him. Robert Fortune brought it out of China in the 1840s on the same journeys that smuggled tea plants to India.

q: There was an English horticulturist and orchid collector. He coaxed a discarded orchid into flower and it was named for him. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English collector was sent a crate of Brazilian mosses packed in what looked like dead stems. He planted the packing material anyway. It flowered into an orchid nobody had seen, and the genus took his name.

q: "kalmia" is named after a place.
f: Linnaeus sent a student to North America to find plants that might survive Swedish winters. He came back with an evergreen shrub whose stamens are spring-loaded and fling pollen at visiting bees. Linnaeus named it after him.

q: There was a Scottish physician and patron of Linnaeus. Linnaeus named the henna plant after the man who funded his great work. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Scottish army physician paid the printing costs of the book in which Linnaeus first laid out his system of classification. In return Linnaeus named the henna shrub after him, so the dye on a thousand years of hands carries a Scot's surname.

q: There was a French-Canadian surgeon and naturalist. The pitcher plant genus was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French surgeon in Quebec sent European botanists a plant whose leaves form tall tubes half full of liquid. Insects walk in on downward-pointing hairs and cannot climb out. The genus was named after him.

q: There was a French royal gardener. The false acacia was named after the gardener who first grew it in Europe. Which word grew out of it?
f: A gardener to three French kings planted a North American tree in Paris around 1601. One of the specimens he or his son planted is still alive, propped on crutches, making it the oldest tree in the city.

q: There was a Finnish physician and botanist. Linnaeus named the air plants after him as a joke about water. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Finnish botanist was so violently seasick on one voyage that he walked home round the Gulf of Bothnia instead. Linnaeus, who found this funny, gave his name to a genus of plants that seem to repel water and live on air.

q: There was a Baltic German naturalist and ship's surgeon. A shipmate named the California poppy after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Baltic German ship's surgeon sailed round the world twice on Russian expeditions. His friend and shipmate named the golden poppy of the Californian hills after him, saddling the state flower with one of the hardest genus names in botany.

q: There was a French botanical illustrator. The trailing rock plant was named after the artist. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French botanical artist who drew plants on expeditions to the Levant had a low cushion-forming rock plant named after him. It is the sheet of purple that spills over garden walls in April.

q: "gunnera" is named after a person.
f: A Norwegian bishop who catalogued his country's flora between sermons had a genus named after him whose largest species carries leaves three metres across, big enough to shelter under. Nothing in Norway grows remotely like it.

q: There was a German physician and botanist. The red hot poker plant was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German physician published books illustrated by pressing inked plants straight onto the page. A South African plant whose flower spike burns from red at the top to yellow at the bottom was later named after him.

q: There was a Spanish physician and botanist. Linnaeus named the aromatic herb after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Spanish physician in Seville wrote the first European account of the plants coming back from the Americas, including tobacco and sunflowers, without ever crossing the Atlantic himself. Linnaeus named a fragrant mint-family herb after him.

q: There was a German colonial administrator. He sent the African violet's seed to his botanist father. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German administrator in East Africa found a small purple flower growing in the shade of a rock and posted seed home to his father. It became one of the most popular houseplants in the world, and the genus took the family name.

q: There was a British sealing captain and navigator. He sailed further south than anyone had and both a sea and a seal took his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: A British sealing captain pushed his ship further south than anyone before him through an unusually ice-free summer. The sea he found and the seal that lives in it both took his name; the seal can hold its breath for eighty minutes.

q: There was a Russian explorer of Central Asia. He described the last truly wild horse. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Russian explorer brought back a skull and hide from the Mongolian steppe that proved a genuinely wild horse still existed, never domesticated. It went extinct in the wild in the 1960s and was brought back from twelve captive animals.

q: There was a German naturalist on the Russian Bering expedition. He described a sea cow, a jay, a sea eagle and a sea lion in a few weeks. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German naturalist got ten hours ashore in Alaska and used them so well that six species now carry his name. He described a nine-metre sea cow that was hunted to extinction within twenty-seven years of his sighting it.

q: "adelie" is named after a place.
f: A French explorer charting the Antarctic coast named the land he found after his wife, waiting at home in France. The small penguins nesting on it took the same name, so the commonest penguin in Antarctica is called after a Frenchwoman who never went there.

q: There was a German city and grand duchy. The grand duke's court bred the grey hunting dog. Which word grew out of it?
f: The court of a German grand duchy bred a grey gundog for hunting big game, then kept the bloodline closed to outsiders for a century. When Americans finally got some in the 1920s, the breed carried the duchy's name.

q: Which word meaning "a very large gentle dog bred for water rescue" comes from a large island off eastern Canada?
f: Fishermen on a cold Canadian island bred an enormous dog with webbed feet and a waterproof coat to haul nets and pull drowning men out of the surf. One is recorded as having saved twenty people from a single wreck.

q: There was an ancient city in southern Arabia. The desert hunting hound is thought to take its name from the town. Which word grew out of it?
f: A slender hound bred to run down gazelle across open desert appears in Egyptian tomb paintings four thousand years old. Bedouin tribes let them sleep in the tent, an honour no other dog received, and their name traces to an Arabian town.

q: There was a valley in Yorkshire, England. Mill workers in the valley bred the large terrier. Which word grew out of it?
f: Mill workers in a Yorkshire river valley crossed terriers with otterhounds to get a dog that could hunt on land and in water. It grew into the largest terrier of all, and served as a messenger dog in the trenches of the First World War.

q: Which word meaning "a short-haired cat with a distinctive ticked coat" comes from the historic name of Ethiopia?
f: A cat shown in London in 1871 was billed as having been brought back from an Ethiopian campaign. The claim is doubtful and the breed's real origins are probably Indian Ocean coastal, but the country's old name stuck to it.

q: There was the French chemist and microbiologist. The genus of animal-borne bacteria was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: The Frenchman who proved germs cause disease had a whole genus named after him: rod-shaped bacteria that live harmlessly in cats' and dogs' mouths and cause fast, angry infections in bitten humans.

q: "bordetella" is named after a person.
f: A Belgian immunologist grew the whooping cough organism from his own infant son's cough in 1906. He won a Nobel Prize for separate work on how blood destroys bacteria, and the genus carries his name.

q: There was a German physician and bacteriologist. He identified the bacterium causing gonorrhoea. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German bacteriologist aged twenty-four identified the coffee-bean-shaped paired bacteria behind one venereal disease, staining them from patients own samples. The same genus includes the organism that causes the most feared and fastest-moving form of bacterial meningitis.

q: There was a French bacteriologist. The corkscrew-shaped bacteria were named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French bacteriologist gave his name to a genus of loosely coiled corkscrew bacteria. One species, carried by ticks that feed on deer and mice, causes Lyme disease and can hide in the body for years.

q: There was a United States veterans' organisation. An outbreak at their 1976 convention revealed the organism. Which word grew out of it?
f: In 1976 a hundred and eighty delegates at a veterans' convention in Philadelphia fell ill and thirty-four died. It took six months to trace it to bacteria breeding in the hotel's cooling tower, and the organism took the delegates' name.

q: There was a French zoologist. The intestinal parasite was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French zoologist had a pear-shaped single-celled parasite named after him. It clamps onto the lining of the small intestine with a sucking disc, and hikers who drink from clear mountain streams have been discovering it ever since.

q: There was a Scottish pathologist and army officer. He identified the parasite behind a fatal tropical fever. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Scottish army pathologist found tiny bodies in the spleen of a soldier dead of a wasting Indian fever. The parasite is spread by sandflies, and in its worst form it destroys the liver and spleen and kills within two years.

q: There was an American pathologist. The insect-infecting bacteria were named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: An American pathologist gave his name to bacteria living inside the cells of most insect species on earth. They manipulate their hosts' reproduction so thoroughly that scientists now use them deliberately to stop mosquitoes carrying dengue.

q: "serratia" is named after a place.
f: An Italian pharmacist investigating why polenta turned blood-red overnight found a bacterium making a scarlet pigment, and named it after a countryman he thought had been cheated of credit for the steamboat. It is now a serious hospital infection.

q: There was a German physician and Nobel laureate. The tick-borne bacteria were named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: The German who invented chemotherapy and the first cure for syphilis had a genus of tick-borne bacteria named after him. They hide inside the very white blood cells sent to destroy them, which is why the infection is so hard to spot.

q: There was a French veterinarian and microbiologist. He isolated the branching bacteria from cattle disease. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French veterinarian isolated a branching, thread-like bacterium from cattle on Guadeloupe. It lives in soil and dust and mostly troubles people whose immune systems are already failing, which is why it became far better known after 1980.

q: There was a Romanian bacteriologist. He identified the blood parasite in cattle. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Romanian bacteriologist found parasites inside the red blood cells of cattle with a wasting fever. It was the first proof that a tick could carry disease, and the discovery reshaped how doctors thought about insects entirely.

q: There was a Swiss-South African veterinary scientist. The cattle blood parasite was named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swiss veterinarian who lost an arm in an accident became the founding figure of South African veterinary science. The tick-borne parasite named after him kills cattle across east and southern Africa, and shaped the whole continent's livestock trade.

q: There was a Brazilian-German physician. He found the worm larvae behind elephantiasis. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German physician working in Brazil found thread-like worm larvae in the urine of patients with grotesquely swollen limbs. The adult worms clog the lymph vessels, and the disease they cause still affects tens of millions of people.

q: There was the husband-and-wife pioneers of radioactivity. The element was named for the couple who founded the study of radioactivity. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element ninety-six was made by bombarding plutonium with helium nuclei in 1944 and kept secret until the war ended. It was named for the husband-and-wife team who discovered radium, the only element honouring two people at once.

q: "einsteinium" is named after a person.
f: Element ninety-nine was first found in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test in 1952. Its discovery stayed classified for three years, and it was named after the physicist whose equation had made such bombs conceivable.

q: There was an Italian-American physicist. The element was named after the builder of the first nuclear reactor. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred appeared in the same hydrogen bomb debris as its neighbour. It was named after the physicist who built the first nuclear reactor under a Chicago squash court, and who had died the year before the name was announced.

q: There was the Russian chemist who devised the periodic table. The element honours the man whose table predicted where elements would fall. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and one was made one atom at a time, seventeen atoms in the first experiment. Naming it after the Russian who invented the periodic table was a deliberate Cold War gesture from an American team.

q: There was a New Zealand-born physicist. The element honours the man who split the atom and found the nucleus. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and four was claimed by both Soviet and American labs, and the two names fought it out for nearly thirty years. The winner honours the New Zealander who discovered that atoms have a dense nucleus at all.

q: There was an American nuclear chemist. The element was named for him while he was still alive, which broke precedent. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and six was named after a living chemist, which caused a formal objection: no element had ever honoured someone still breathing. He had co-discovered ten elements himself, so the rule bent rather than held.

q: There was an Austrian-Swedish physicist. The element honours the physicist who explained nuclear fission. Which word grew out of it?
f: She worked out the theory of nuclear fission in exile after fleeing Nazi Germany, and her collaborator took the Nobel Prize alone. Element one hundred and nine was named for her decades later, an apology written into the periodic table.

q: There was the Polish astronomer who put the sun at the centre. The element honours the man who displaced the earth from the centre of the cosmos. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and twelve was announced on the five hundred and thirty-seventh anniversary of the astronomer's birth. The team chose him to honour a scientist whose ideas took a century to be accepted and then changed everything.

q: "gadolinium" is named after a place.
f: A Finnish chemist analysed a black stone from a Swedish quarry and found an entirely new kind of earth in it. That single quarry eventually yielded eight elements, and both a mineral and this metal carry his name.

q: There was a Russian mining official. The mineral named after him yielded the element. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Russian mining official who supplied specimens to chemists had a mineral named after him, and the element later teased out of that mineral inherited the name. He is the first person ever to have a chemical element named after him.

q: There was the Swedish inventor of dynamite and founder of the prizes. The element honours the man whose fortune funds the science prizes. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and two was claimed first by a Stockholm team whose result nobody could reproduce. The name they had chosen, honouring the founder of the prizes, survived even though their discovery did not.

q: There was an American physicist and inventor of the cyclotron. The element honours the inventor of the particle accelerator that made such elements possible. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and three was named for the physicist who invented the cyclotron, the machine that hurls particles fast enough to build new elements at all. Nearly every element past uranium exists because of his machine.

q: There was the Danish physicist who modelled the atom. The element honours the architect of the quantum atom. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element one hundred and seven honours the Dane who worked out that electrons sit in fixed shells. The team originally proposed a form of the name that would have been confused with boron, and had to be talked out of it.

q: There was the continent, itself named after a navigator. The element was named for the Americas, by analogy with europium. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element ninety-five was named after a continent to mirror the element named for Europe directly above it in the table. It is the only synthetic element sitting in ordinary homes: a speck of it makes smoke detectors work.

q: There was the American state and its university. The element was named for the state and university where it was made. Which word grew out of it?
f: Element ninety-eight was named for the state and the university where it was created. The team joked that they had skipped the tradition of honouring a person because getting to California had been hard enough for the pioneers.

q: "berkelium" is named after a person.
f: Element ninety-seven was named for the university town where it was made, following the pattern of the element above it in the table, which had been named for a Swedish village. Both sit in the same column by design.

q: There was the continent. The rare earth element was named after the continent. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chemist separated a new rare earth in 1901 and named it after his continent. It glows a distinctive red under ultraviolet light, which is why euro banknotes carry a trace of it as an anti-forgery mark.

q: There was the country. Its German discoverer named it after his homeland. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German chemist found a new element in a silver ore in 1886 and named it for his country. It filled a gap Mendeleev had predicted almost exactly, and its properties matched the prediction so closely that the periodic table was suddenly beyond argument.

q: There was a marie Curie's homeland. She named her first new element after the country of her birth. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Polish-born chemist working in Paris isolated a new element and named it after her homeland, which at the time did not exist as an independent state. It was a deliberate political act disguised as a chemical one.

q: There was the country. Its French discoverer named it after her homeland. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chemist found the last naturally occurring element to be discovered in 1939 and named it after her country. There is thought to be less than thirty grams of it in the entire earth's crust at any moment.

q: There was the northern European region. Its Swedish discoverer named it after the region. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swedish chemist separated a new element from a Scandinavian mineral in 1879 and named it for the region. It turned out to be one of the elements Mendeleev had predicted and left a blank space for a decade earlier.

q: There was a village and quarry near Stockholm. The quarry's black mineral yielded four elements named after the village. Which word grew out of it?
f: One small quarry on a Swedish island produced a black mineral that turned out to contain eight new elements. Four of them were named after the village itself, which makes it the most honoured place name in the periodic table.

q: "strontium" is named after a place.
f: A mineral dug from lead mines in a Highland village turned out to contain a new element that burns crimson. It is the only chemical element named after a place in Scotland, and it is why fireworks can be red.

q: There was a French geologist and mineralogist. He described the rock, and both it and a mountain range took his name. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French geologist noticed that some Alpine limestone did not fizz in acid the way limestone should. It proved to be a different mineral entirely. Both the rock and the spectacular Italian mountain range made of it now carry his name.

q: There was the German poet, playwright and naturalist. A mineralogist named the iron oxide after the poet, who collected minerals. Which word grew out of it?
f: Germany's greatest poet was also a serious mineral collector with eighteen thousand specimens. A mineralogist named the commonest iron oxide after him, so the substance that rust is mostly made of is named for the author of Faust.

q: There was an English chemist and mineralogist. He distinguished the zinc carbonate mineral, and his fortune founded the Smithsonian. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English chemist showed that two minerals long lumped together were chemically different. He never visited America, but left his entire fortune to found an institution there, and both the mineral and that institution carry his name.

q: There was a Swedish-German pharmacist and chemist. He identified the acid in the tungsten ore now named after him. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swedish apothecary discovered oxygen, chlorine and several other elements, then largely lost the credit for each by publishing late. He had a habit of tasting his compounds, which probably killed him at forty-three.

q: There was an English chemist and physicist. The calcium silicate mineral was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: An English chemist discovered palladium and rhodium, and made a fortune quietly selling purified platinum. A needle-crystalled calcium silicate was named after him, and the dark lines he first noticed in sunlight became the science of spectroscopy.

q: There was a Russian mineralogist and statesman. The mineral was named after him, and now names a whole class of crystal structures. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Russian mineralogist had one obscure titanium mineral named after him. Its crystal arrangement turned out to be shared by hundreds of compounds, and materials built on that pattern are now the great hope of cheap solar power.

q: "alexandrite" is named after a person.
f: A green gem found in the Urals was presented on the day the future tsar came of age. Under candlelight it turned raspberry red. Since those were the Russian imperial military colours, the stone became instantly fashionable.

q: There was the American banker and gem collector. A gemmologist named the pink beryl after his greatest patron. Which word grew out of it?
f: A New York gemmologist persuaded a banker to fund the assembly of two of the finest gem collections in the world, both later given to museums. He named a newly recognised pink beryl after his patron.

q: There was an American mineralogist and gem expert. The pink spodumene was named after its describer. Which word grew out of it?
f: A self-taught mineralogist joined Tiffany at twenty-three and became the most influential gem buyer alive. He described a pale lilac stone from California that fades in sunlight, and colleagues named it after him.

q: There was a French chemist and Nobel laureate. He found the silicon carbide crystals in a meteorite crater. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chemist picking through fragments from a meteorite crater found crystals he first took for diamond. They were silicon carbide, almost unknown in nature. Grown in laboratories, they now outsparkle diamond and cost a tenth as much.

q: There was an American chemist and founder of a leading science journal. The aluminium silicate mineral was named in his honour. Which word grew out of it?
f: An American chemist founded the journal that became the backbone of nineteenth-century American science and analysed the first meteorite fall studied in the United States. A high-temperature aluminium silicate was named after him.

q: There was a diamond-mining city in South Africa. The diamond-bearing volcanic rock was first identified there. Which word grew out of it?
f: Diggers at a South African hill found diamonds in a strange bluish rock filling an ancient volcanic pipe. The rock had come up from a hundred and fifty kilometres down, fast enough that the carbon stayed diamond, and it took the town's name.

q: There was the South American mountain range. The volcanic rock is characteristic of the range's volcanoes. Which word grew out of it?
f: The volcanoes running down the spine of South America erupt a rock midway between basalt and granite in composition. It was named for the range, and the boundary where that rock type appears around the Pacific carries the same name.

q: "bauxite" is named after a place.
f: A French geologist described a reddish rock near a Provencal village in 1821. It turned out to be the world's only economic source of aluminium, so every drinks can and aeroplane wing traces back to a name from southern France.

q: Which word meaning "magnesium sulphate, used dissolved in baths" comes from a town in Surrey, England?
f: A farmer noticed his cattle would not drink from one spring on a Surrey common. The water was bitter with magnesium sulphate. Boiled down it became a famous purgative, and the town grew into a spa on the strength of it.

q: Which word meaning "of the random jittering motion of tiny particles suspended in a fluid" comes from a Scottish botanist?
f: A Scottish botanist watching pollen grains in water saw them jitter endlessly and could not explain it. Eighty years later Einstein showed the jittering was invisible water molecules knocking them about, which finally proved atoms are real.

q: There was a Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate. He explained the blue glow given off by particles moving faster than light in water. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Soviet physicist explained the eerie blue glow around nuclear reactor cores. Light slows down in water, so a particle can outrun it there, and the glow is the optical equivalent of a sonic boom.

q: There was a Welsh physicist and Nobel laureate. He predicted current tunnelling between superconductors separated by a barrier. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Cambridge graduate student predicted that a supercurrent would tunnel straight through an insulating gap between two superconductors. Senior physicists doubted it. He was twenty-two, was proved right, and the effect now defines the standard volt.

q: There was a Baltic German physicist. He found that a temperature difference across joined metals produces a voltage. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Baltic German physicist joined two different metals, heated one junction, and found a compass needle nearby swung. He had made electricity out of a temperature difference. Every thermocouple in every industrial furnace uses the effect.

q: There was a French watchmaker turned physicist. He found that passing current across joined metals moves heat. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French watchmaker who retired at thirty to do physics found the reverse of the thermoelectric effect: run a current through joined metals and one junction gets cold. Camping fridges and chip coolers run on it.

q: "lenz" is named after a person.
f: A Baltic German physicist established that nature pushes back: a current induced by a changing magnetic field always flows so as to oppose that change. Drop a magnet down a copper pipe and it floats down slowly because of it.

q: There was a German physicist. He formulated the rules for current and voltage in electrical circuits. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German physicist stated his two circuit rules while still a student: charge in equals charge out at any junction, and voltages round any loop sum to zero. He also co-founded spectroscopy and named the black body.

q: There was a German chemist and Nobel laureate. His equation links a cell's voltage to the concentrations inside it. Which word grew out of it?
f: A German chemist derived the equation linking an electrochemical cell's voltage to what is dissolved in it, then went on to state the third law of thermodynamics. Every nerve impulse in your body obeys his equation.

q: There was a Swedish chemist and Nobel laureate. His equation describes how reaction rate rises with temperature. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swedish chemist nearly failed his doctorate for proposing that salts split into charged particles in water. He later won a Nobel Prize for it, and was the first person to calculate how carbon dioxide warms the planet.

q: There was a French chemist. His law relates a solution's vapour pressure to its composition. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chemist found that dissolving something in a liquid lowers how readily that liquid evaporates, in exact proportion to how much is dissolved. It is why the sea freezes later than a pond and why antifreeze works.

q: There was a French chemist. His principle predicts how a system at equilibrium answers a disturbance. Which word grew out of it?
f: A French chemist stated that a chemical system at balance always shifts to undo whatever you do to it: squeeze it and it shrinks its own pressure, heat it and it absorbs heat. Industrial chemistry is largely the art of exploiting this.

q: There was a Swiss mathematics teacher. He found the formula fitting hydrogen's visible spectral lines. Which word grew out of it?
f: A Swiss schoolteacher with a taste for numerical puzzles found, at fifty-nine, a simple formula that fitted the four visible lines of glowing hydrogen exactly. He had no physical explanation. Bohr supplied one thirty years later.

q: "waals" is named after a place.
f: A Dutch schoolteacher who taught himself physics at night wrote an equation for real gases that accounted for molecules taking up space and pulling faintly on each other. Those faint pulls are why geckos can walk up glass.
